why: 1793 came from his marriage act's stated age of 21, which was itself wrong. The date is corrected, and the old one is left standing here because the seven-way age conflict it caused is one of the most-cited things on this site. Knowing the real date does not erase the conflict — it explains it.

what: a surname conflict, closed
was: Generation three's wife published two ways — Andreana CRISCI, and Andriana CIOFFI from the 1839 death register
now: CRISCI. Baptised ADRIANA on 30 November 1796, daughter of Arcangelo Crisci and Sara Ruggiero.
how: Six documents of 1814 — the dossier cover sheet, both notarial consent acts, both civil banns, and her own baptism extract — all say Crisci, and four of them name her parents.
why: The 1839 reading was published as a live conflict rather than suppressed, and it stays visible here. It was either the clerk's error or mine. The baptism also explains the variants: Adriana at the font becomes Andreana, Andriana and Andrea in the registers. They are one woman.

what: a death bracket, narrowed
was: Matteo Falco dead by 17 October 1822 — the earliest act that calls him defunto
now: Dead by 8 December 1814
how: A notarial act of that date names «Pasquale Falco del FU Matteo». Nothing published was wrong; the window simply closes almost eight years earlier.
why: Recorded here because this site publishes the narrowing of a claim as readily as its overturning. The bracket on Matteo's death is now [1786, 8 Dec 1814].

what: a correction, corrected
was: This page said, hours earlier on the same day: “Bundle 25's publication is dated 20 November, two months later than ours.”
now: There is no bundle 25. The 1814 volume holds seventeen bundles. The «25» was a publication act number inside bundle 17.
how: Sweeping all 290 images of the volume as contact sheets and reading every bundle cover. Each is headed «Numero N — Comune Corpo d'Arienzo»; they run 1 to 17, and bundle 17 is Francesco Crisci fu Alessandro × Teresa Morgillo, published 20 November 1814.
why: I repeated a number out of the earlier session's note while writing the correction that overturned that very note — without checking it. The mechanism I described was right and is unchanged; the illustration was wrong. It is published because a correction that quietly acquires its own errors is worse than no correction, and because this is exactly the failure the same day's other entry warns about: a figure inherited rather than verified.

what: a diagram that misled
was: The Lines diagram drew the ZAMPIELLO as a separate stream running alongside this family, omitted SAN FELICE A CANCELLO and FORCHIA as places entirely, and used one visual grammar — a dot on a lane — for places, for people, and once for a ship.
now: A place-spine. The Zampiello, Annecchino and Morgillo are drawn JOINING the line at the generation and town where they join. Names sit under the place they belong to.
how: Checked the diagram's places against places.json and the atlas. It showed seven places; it was missing San Felice a Cancello — where Angela Rosa Morgillo, generation four's wife, was born — and never drew Forchia as the Annecchino's town even though that marriage is the reason generation eight was born there. Two of the five lanes had people, not places, as their nodes, and one had the ship Sydney.
why: The Zampiello error was the worst of it: drawn as a parallel river, they read as a different family being compared with this one, when Francesca Zampiello married Carmine Falco in 1955 and from generation eight onward they ARE this family. A diagram that is wrong is worse than no diagram, because nobody checks a picture against the prose. Raised by David, who spotted all three faults from the image alone.

what: an age, and a striking claim that rested on it
was: Andreana Crisci “married at about sixteen” — inferred from her stated age of twenty in her son's 1818 birth act, which implied a birth about 1798.
now: She was born 30 November 1796 and married at EIGHTEEN. The 1818 act understates her by about a year and a half.
how: Her baptism extract in the 1814 marriage dossier. The 1818 birth act was then re-read at native resolution: it does say «venti», twenty, and it does say «ANDREANA CRISCI» — the surname is unambiguous, which settles the 1839 «Cioffi» reading a second way.
why: “Married at sixteen” is the kind of detail a reader remembers and repeats, and it was this archive's own inference from a clerk's guess rather than anything a record said. Eighteen is still young. The same act gets her husband's age right — twenty-seven, when he was twenty-six and three months, which is correct by the year-a-man-is-in reckoning these clerks used. Right about him, wrong about her, in one sentence.

what: an uncertain reading, resolved
was: The apothecary's mother recorded as «LUCIA COPPA(?)/CIOFFI» — read at 3400px and left with a question mark and an alternative.
now: LUCIA CIOFFI. Read at native resolution: «e di Lucia Cioffi Defunta».
how: Re-fetching the act as a IIIF region at the image's own resolution rather than scaling the whole leaf. The double-f ligature is unmistakable at full size and was not at 3400px.
why: A name carried with a question mark for weeks is a name nobody can search for. It also changes what the record means: CIOFFI is a gentry surname at Arienzo, and in February 1815 a Don Saverio CIOFFI was married to a Donna Anna Maria RIVETTI. The two families married in both directions.

what: a town recorded as unreachable that was never searched for
was: “San Felice a Cancello is a separate comune with its own registers, NONE OF WHICH THIS ARCHIVE HAS READ.” San Felice is where generation four's wife, Angela Rosa Morgillo, was born.
now: Its registers are on Antenati and have been all along — Archivio di Stato di Caserta, marriages from 1809 at an_ua50221. The 1817 marriages have now been read.
why: The wording said “has not read” and was heard, including by me, as “cannot read”. In fact nobody had looked. It was missed because Antenati catalogues the town under its older name, «San Felice (oggi San Felice a Cancello)», and because this archive reached Antenati by guessing arks from an arithmetic rule derived by hand for Arienzo alone — a method that can only ever find what it already knows about.
how: A search endpoint that returns ark ids in plain HTML: search-registry/?localita=<town>. Resolving those arks gives the series arithmetic for any town. The archive's own survey covers five Valle Caudina towns and does not include San Felice at all.

what: a living person's birth date, published — for the third time
was: The rebuilt Lines diagram printed generation nine's FULL DATE OF BIRTH beside her name, under the heading BORN HERE — on /lines and, because the home page embeds the same figure, on the front page of the site. She is living.
now: «9 · Giuseppina Falco — living — named only», under the heading LIVING. The 1955 on the Benevento stop now belongs to generation eight's marriage, where it is a fact about two people who are dead.
how: Sweeping the built site for the date and finding it in the raw HTML of two pages. The visible text of /direct-line was correct; the diagram was not.
why: This archive has now leaked this exact birth year THREE times: once through a redaction function reused from the wrong place, once through the timeline's geometry — and now through a diagram I built myself on the day this correction was written, hours after re-reading the standing rule. Textual fixes have not held, so THE FIX IS STRUCTURAL: the diagram now looks every date up against the person graph and prints «living — named only» instead, whatever the underlying data says. Data can be wrong; the guard cannot be bypassed by editing a string. And this entry had to be written twice: the first version QUOTED THE DATE IT WAS CORRECTING, which republished it on a page nobody would think to check. The release gate caught that on its first run. A correction must describe a leak without reproducing it.
by: auditing the built HTML, not the source

what: a search recorded as promising that was not
was: Orazio Morgillo × Vincenza Pesce would be found in the San Felice marriage registers of 1816 or 1817.
now: Neither year holds them. Both volumes have been read act by act and the couple is not in either.
how: San Felice a Cancello, Matrimoni 1817 (an_ua50229, 22 images) and 1816 (an_ua50228, 26 images), swept in full.
why: Published as a negative so the two years are not read again. The couple was reached anyway, and by a better route: their daughter's BIRTH act, which names both parents outright. The lesson is recorded on /morgillo — when the target is a couple and a child's date is known, go to the birth register, because a birth act names both parents and a marriage act has to be found first. The marriage is still open; the remaining window is San Felice 1813-1815, or another parish if Vincenza was not of the town.

what: a probable identification, now established
was: «Almost certainly the same woman, married in 1814 and buried before the winter was out. Published as PROBABLE, not proved.»
now: Established. Bundle 13 carries Margarita Crisci's own baptism extract — «nata ex ANGELO CRISCI et GRAZIA, 27 September 1780» — and the death extracts of both those parents. The 1815 death act names the same two parents, both dead. It is the same woman.
how: Reading inside the bundle rather than only its cover. A processetto had to carry death certificates for any dead parent or grandparent, so it also yielded her grandfather: THOMAS CRISCI, widower, dead 21 March 1789 aged forty-six.
why: Recorded because the archive published it as probable the same day and can now say why it is not. The groom's surname is STILL not proved — the cover gives him only as «Angelo figlio di Nicola» — so that half stays open.

what: a hundred finding aids recorded as non-existent
was: «No index, no indice decennale, no marginal surnames — all three checked and absent. ~90 acts/year, ~1,350 total. ONE SCREENSHOT PER ACT.» That recipe governed twenty-eight years of death-register sweeps.
now: Antenati lists 100 INDEX VOLUMES for Arienzo alone — 39 for deaths, 44 for marriages, 17 for «diversi» — and 79 more for San Felice a Cancello. Arienzo death indexes run 1809 = an_ua14271, +1 per year, verified at 1818, 1828 and 1834. Each is ONE TO FOUR IMAGES and lists every death of the year with BOTH PARENTS NAMED.
how: Reading the catalogue's own facet list instead of paging the volumes. The facet is spelled «Morti, indice» and «Matrimoni, processetti» — query for «Processetti» alone and you get nothing, which is part of how this was missed.
why: This is the third wrong negative of the same shape in a single day — the 1814 processetto «not in the volume», San Felice «unread», and now indexes «absent». Each came from checking once, concluding, and writing the conclusion down as a rule that stopped anyone looking again. The acts are still worth reading for what an index omits — street, hour, declarants, the «parente» wording this archive's best finds turn on — but the register is no longer the place to START. Two cautions are published with it: the sort order changes year to year, and the scans are not always complete, so an absence in an index is not a negative.

what: a date, misread as a shorter word
was: Chiara Rivetti died on 3 SEPTEMBER 1843. Published on /rivetti, /direct-line and in the memory of this project, and used to date the widowhood that brackets Pasquale Falco's death.
now: 13 SEPTEMBER 1843. The act says «il dì TREDICI del mese di Settembre» in its heading and «nel giorno TREDICI … alle ore venti» in the declaration — twice. TREDICI was read as TRE.
how: The 1843 death INDEX, found the same day, gives «Rivetti Chiara … 13 7bre 1843». The act was then re-read at native resolution and says thirteen in both places.
why: It also removes an oddity nobody had questioned: the parish buried her on 16 September, which is a strange thirteen-day wait after a death on the 3rd and an ordinary three-day one after the 13th. THIS IS THE INDEX METHOD EARNING ITS KEEP ON ITS FIRST CONTROL TEST — it was run against a known answer precisely to see whether it could be trusted, and it caught an error in the known answer.

what: two witnesses given the wrong surname
was: «Two CIOFFI of strada Camellara walked to the town hall to report it.»
now: LUCA COSSI, 33, a SARTORE, and GIOVANNI COSSI, 43, a contadino — both of strada Camellara. Cossi, not Cioffi.
how: Re-reading the act at native resolution. Cossi is short with a double-s; Cioffi is longer and carries the -ffi ligature. At the resolution the plate was cropped to, they are not distinguishable.
why: Both are common Arienzo surnames and both appear all over this archive, so the confusion will recur. Recorded with the tell: at plate resolution you cannot separate them — go to the image.

superseded.what: WITHDRAWN — «Cossi, not Cioffi» was wrong in one direction and right in the other, and the data file had the better half all along
superseded.note: **Wrong. The surname is CIOFFI** — both words carry the tall *ff* ligature with a long descender that this entry's own method note describes. **The ages here are right**, though: thirty-three and forty-three, where the household file carried forty-eight for Giovanni.

what: a death bracket, narrowed by a negative
was: Matteo Falco, head of the line: dead by 8 December 1814, with 1786 to 1814 open.
now: Dead BEFORE 1809 — proved, not probable. Which puts his death in the parish register and nowhere else.
how: The Arienzo death indexes for 1809-1814, read in a fraction of the time the registers would take. No Matteo Falco of the founder's generation is in them.
why: Published because a negative that moves a bracket is worth as much as a positive, and because it redirects the search. All six index volumes for 1809-1814 have now been read PAGE FOR PAGE — the first pass left three years partial and the claim was published as «probable» until they were finished. Taken with the marriage indexes, which also begin in 1809, BOTH of Matteo Falco's vital events lie outside the civil series: his marriage of about 1760-66 and his death are in the parish books of Sant'Andrea or nowhere.

what: a namesake that will mislead the next searcher
was: Nothing published — this is a trap set for the future rather than an error corrected.
now: A MATTEO FALCO died at Arienzo on 28 August 1809 AGED FIFTEEN, and he is NOT the head of this line. The act reads «è morto MATTEO FALCO — di [ANNI struck, MESI written over it] QUINDICI» — the clerk corrected himself between years and months, and on either reading the deceased is a child.
how: The act itself, Arienzo Morti 1809 (an_ua14311, img 40 right), read at native resolution. The 1809 INDEX names his parents «Giuseppe, ed Antonia di [Guida]» without «fu», so both were living; the act gives the age the index omits. The Falco who died three days later, NICOLA, was likewise a child — «d'anni DUE», of strada Camellara.
why: Anyone searching «Matteo Falco death Arienzo» lands on this record, and it is exactly the shape of a find that looks like the answer. The founder was born about 1740 and had children baptised from 1767; he would have been sixty-nine in 1809. Published as a trap disarmed rather than an error corrected.

what: a suspicion, promoted to a document
was: «GIOACCHINO FALCO is a strong candidate for a fifth child of Matteo and Francesca, THOUGH NO RECORD YET NAMES HIS PARENTS.» Carried that way for years, and he sat among the people this archive could join to nobody.
now: «7. FALCO GIOACCHINO | Arienzo | CONTADINO | FALCO MATTEO, e CRISCI FRANCESCA | 14 Febrajo» — Arienzo deaths 1851. He is a documented son of the founding couple, who now have FIVE named children.
how: The alphabetical index bound at the front of the 1851 death register — four images. Not a register read act by act.
why: Recorded because the archive was RIGHT and refused to say so without a record. The suspicion rested on an inference from 1816, when Gioacchino and Giuseppe Falco declared the death of Crescenzo Rivetti as «parenti del defunto», Crescenzo being married to their sister Angela. Holding that as a candidate rather than a fact for years was the correct call, and this is what it looks like when the discipline pays.

what: two readings that disagreed, reconciled — and one of them was mine
was: The bride of Luigi Falco's 1815 marriage recorded two ways: «[C]ecilia VECCHIO» from the bundle cover, and «[?]ietta RENCHIELLO» from the marriage act. Published as an unresolved disagreement.
now: «[F]ietta VECCHILLO», eighteen, a filatrice of strada del Borgo, daughter of the late SABBATINO. The SURNAME is settled — Vecchillo is the cover's Vecchio in a fuller spelling. RENCHIELLO was my misreading and never existed.
how: Re-reading the marriage act at native resolution instead of from a composite strip.
why: Recorded because the archive published a disagreement between two sources when in fact one source had been read badly. The forename is STILL uncertain — «Fietta» against «Cecilia», and Fietta may be a contraction of Felicetta — so that half stays open and is marked as such.

what: my own headline claim, wrongly framed
was: «GIOVANNA FALCO, died 15 December 1812, daughter of Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti — A DAUGHTER OF GENERATION TWO THIS ARCHIVE DID NOT HAVE.» Published on /direct-line, /searched and in the commit that announced the index method's first big find.
now: A SECOND daughter of that name. This archive already held a GIOVANNA FALCO who died on 15 SEPTEMBER 1805, daughter of the same parents, from the Arienzo parish register (FamilySearch 3Q9M-CSMY-B743-H). The 1812 Giovanna is a second child given her dead sister's name.
how: Querying the archive's own register for every Falco death before publishing further on the same family — which is what should have happened BEFORE the claim, not after.
why: The find is still real and still new: a second Giovanna, dying in 1812, is a child nobody had. But «a child this archive did not have» was the wrong sentence, and it was the most quotable sentence in the entry. The naming pattern it actually illustrates is one this archive has documented repeatedly — two Raffaele, two Pasquale, two Maria, and now two Giovanna. THE LESSON: a new find must be checked against what is already held, in the same pass that publishes it. Searching the register takes seconds; the claim stood for an hour.

what: an open question answered, and a namesake that is not a stranger after all
was: Raised the same morning: «One Giuseppe Falco married twice, or two Giuseppe Falco at Arienzo?» — 1809 gave two Falco children of a Giuseppe with different mothers, Antonia di Guida and Gelsomina Vigliotta. And the Matteo Falco who died 28 August 1809 was published as «a child of ANOTHER HOUSEHOLD».
now: TWO Giuseppe Falco, distinguished by street and wife — and the 1809 Matteo IS the founder's own grandson. PROVED the same day, not merely probable.
how: Two birth acts already in this archive settle it. «25 Nov 1816, strada COSTA: Giuseppe Falco, 36, MASSARO DI CAMPO, e GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA» and «7 Jun 1818, strada CAMELLARA: Giuseppe Falco, 36, CONTADINO, e ANTONIA DI GUIDA». Two men of one name and the same stated age, on different streets, with different wives. A man cannot have two living wives, and in 1809 both households buried a child weeks apart.
why: It re-reads the namesake trap in the opposite direction. The Camellara Giuseppe is «GIUSEPPE FALCO FU MATTEO» — the founder's own son. So the Matteo Falco who died at fifteen months on 28 August 1809 is not a stranger who happens to share the name: he is MATTEO FALCO'S GRANDSON, carrying his grandfather's name, and he died while his grandfather was still alive. The trap entry stands — he is still not the founder — but «another household» was wrong. Held as PROBABLE: it rests on street, trade, period and this archive's existing identification of Giuseppe, not on an act that says «fu Matteo» and «Antonia di Guida» in the same line. — AND IT IS NOW PROVED. A parish marriage act found hours later reads «JOSEPHUM FALCO FILIUM MATTHEI, e FRANCISCE CRISCI et ANTONIAM DI GUIDA filiam JOSEPHI e MAGDALENE», about August 1802. Giuseppe Falco of strada Camellara, husband of Antonia di Guida, is documented as Matteo's son in the same act that marries him. The infant Matteo of 1809 is his child and the founder's grandson.

what: a birth year taken from a stated age, corrected by a baptism
was: Gioacchino Falco «born about 1775» — derived this morning from his death act, which gives his age as seventy-six in February 1851.
now: BAPTISED 2 FEBRUARY 1779. «Anno Dni … 1779, die vero SECUNDA FEBRUARII … baptizavit infantem natum ex MATTHEO FALCO, et FRANCISCA CRISCI Conjugibus hujus Parochiae, qui nominatus est JOACHIM.» He was SEVENTY-TWO when he died, not seventy-six.
how: The Arienzo parish baptism register, reached through FamilySearch's full-text search of the handwriting transcriptions.
why: Recorded because the archive derived the 1775 from a stated age on the very day it found the act, and stated ages in these registers are exactly what this archive spends its time distrusting. A baptism beats an age every time. The midwife was Cecilia Martone.

what: a name that only ever existed in a machine's reading of the handwriting
was: Antonia di Guida's mother published this morning as «MADDALENA PIVERA(?)», with the question mark, from FamilySearch's handwriting transcription.
now: **MAGDALENA RIVETTA.** Read from the image at magnification: «et Antoniam di Guida filiam Josephi, et Magdalenae Rivetta». There is no Pivera.
how: The act's own image — Arienzo parish marriages, film 007786827, image 366 — fetched tile by tile and enlarged.
why: Published the same day it was made. The archive knew the word was the least certain on the page and said so; reading the image took an hour and settled it. **And Rivetta is not a stranger here**: generation three married a Chiara RIVETTI. Whether they are one family is untested, and is carried as a lead, not a claim.

what: two marriages given one date, and a year no machine could read
was: «Anno Domini 18[0]2, die vero … Augusti» for Giuseppe Falco × Antonia di Guida, with the day unread; Rosa Falco × Carlo Antonio Morgillo described only as «the same leaf», which invited the reading that they married together.
now: **Giuseppe Falco married Antonia di Guida on 4 AUGUST 1802. Rosa Falco married Carlo Antonio Morgillo on 12 JULY 1802** — the same leaf, but three weeks apart. Brother and sister, married in the same summer by the same priest, **Don Luca Verdicchio, Missionarius**, under the archpriest **Giacinto Morgillo**'s licence.
how: Read from the image. FamilySearch's transcription gave the year as «1902» throughout; the hand gives 1802, and the leaf sits in the section headed «A Mense Aprilis».
why: Recorded because the archive published the machine's reading at midday with a written warning that the dates were unverified, and then verified them. The warning is what made this correction small instead of embarrassing.

what: another age taken from a death act, corrected by a baptism
was: Chiara Rivetti «di anni OTTANTA» at her death on 13 September 1843, and so born about 1763.
now: **BAPTISED 14 DECEMBER 1766.** «baptizavit infantem natam ex NICOLAO RIVETTA et ANNA DI NUZZO conjugibus … cui imposui nomen CLARA.» **She was seventy-seven.**
how: The Arienzo parish baptism register, read from the image — Collegiata di Sant'Andrea Apostolo, the 1766 leaf.
why: The third stated age this archive has overturned with a baptism in one day. The pattern is now firm enough to state as a rule: **an age given by a declarant is an estimate, and this archive should stop treating it as evidence of a birth year when a parish register can be reached instead.**

what: a mother's surname that two document series do not agree on
was: Chiara Rivetti's mother published as **ANNA DI RUGGIO**, from her civil death act of 1843 and her brother Carmine's of 1821.
now: **The parish books call her ANNA DI NUZZO** — in Chiara's own baptism and across five of her children's. Neither reading is doubtful in its own document. **This is left open and unresolved**, and both names are now carried on the site.
how: Read from the 1766 baptism image; the civil acts were read from Antenati.
why: Published rather than quietly reconciled. Writing «di Nuzzo (or di Ruggio)» would hide that two independent record series say two different things twenty-two years apart, which is itself the finding.

what: a child this archive never knew existed, and a name explained
was: Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci held as the parents of five documented children; Gioacchino's name treated as simply his own.
now: **A FIRST JOACHIM FALCO, baptised 25 November 1774**, whose entry carries a drawn cross and the marginal **«obiit die 11 Decembris 1777»**. The Gioacchino who lived was baptised fourteen months later and **carries his dead brother's name**. The documented children rise to **six**.
how: Arienzo parish baptisms, the 1774 leaf, read from the image.
why: Recorded because it is the second necronym in this one household — Giovanna Falco is the other — and because it is a reminder that a child who died in 1777 leaves no trace whatever in the civil registers this archive spent months reading. It also does NOT rescue the «about 1775»: the boy of 1774 was dead by 1777.

what: a negative produced by searching the wrong collection
was: A word-sweep of the Arienzo parish books returned **340 marriage-style leaves with no Falco on any of them** — which read like a clean negative on Matteo Falco's marriage.
now: **The sweep was searching the wrong shelf.** Every parish sweep this archive has run used FamilySearch collection `M9J1-7MY`. The marriage register is a different collection, `M9J1-9B4` — and the Falco marriage act read three hours earlier, which carries both the searched word and the name, **was not among the 340**. The re-run on the right collection returns **1,260 Falco pages** and **forty alphabetical marriage-index leaves**.
how: Checked by asking which collection the known act belongs to, instead of trusting that one collection meant «the parish books».
why: **This would have been the fourth wrong negative of the same shape** — look once, fail, write the failure down as a rule, never look again. It is published as a correction even though nothing incorrect ever reached the site, because the near miss is the finding. Matteo Falco's marriage is still **not found and not ruled out**.

what: a marriage this archive had never located at all
was: Generation four — **Raffaele Falco and Angela Rosa Morgillo** — held as married, with **no record of the marriage and no date**. Angela Rosa was known as Orazio Morgillo's daughter only from the civil registers.
now: **Found in the alphabetical index to the Arienzo parish marriage volumes**, read from the image: «**Raphael Falco cum Angela Rosa Morgillo filia Horatii — fol. 2 a tergo**». The act is at **folio 2 verso**; it has not been read, and the date is still unknown.
how: The parish marriage collection — M9J1-9B4, the shelf this archive had been failing to search — and then the index page itself, enlarged.
why: Published as a location, not a date. The temptation is to write «married about 1843» from where the leaf sits; the index gives a folio and two names and nothing else, and that is exactly what is recorded.

what: a correction that named the wrong parish, corrected within the hour
was: The entry above places Raffaele Falco and Angela Rosa Morgillo's marriage index **in «the Arienzo parish marriage volumes»**. That was written from a search filtered on `anyPlace=Arienzo` and never checked against the volume itself.
now: **The index is SAN FELICE A CANCELLO's** — film 007786833, image 1873. The entry stands word for word; only the parish was wrong. **And the right parish is the better fact**: Angela Rosa was baptised at San Felice on 24 February 1818 and married in her own parish, which is the ordinary pattern and explains why the Arienzo registers never held this marriage.
how: Opened the volume in the viewer and read its title, instead of trusting the search filter that had returned it.
why: `anyPlace=Arienzo` is a **weighting, not a filter**: the same result set carries San Felice, Santa Maria a Vico, Parete, Dragoni and Aversa. Which means the negative published an hour ago — «1,260 Arienzo pages, no marriage act for a Matteo Falco» — is over a corpus that is **about 87 per cent Arienzo, not all of it**. That negative was already labelled as not ruling anything out; it is now labelled as covering fewer Arienzo pages than it claimed.

what: an index that dated a death a month late, and an age given twice three years apart
was: The 1846 Arienzo death index dates **Chiara Falco's** death **6 Agosto**. The archive's 1843 entry for **Luca Cioffi** gives him as **33, sartore, of strada Camellara**.
now: **The act says 6 LUGLIO 1846** — «nel giorno sei del mese di Luglio … alle ore una di notte». And the same **Luca Cioffi, sartore, strada Camellara**, declaring a death in **1846**, is again **33**. Three years on, the same age.
how: Arienzo, Morti 1846, atto 39, read from the image after the index pointed at it.
why: Two small things that are really one thing. **The index is a finding aid and never a source** — it has now been caught on an act number and a month in a single year. And the ages in these acts are estimates: this is the cleanest example the archive has, one man given the same age three years apart, in a series it once used to date births.

what: a third Michele Falco, and a household not previously held
was: Two men called Michele Falco at Arienzo — one married to **Vincenza Esposito**, one to **Maria Giovanna d'Ambrosio**.
now: **A third: MICHELE FALCO × ANTONIA VIGLIOTTA**, named as the parents of **Chiara Falco, aged seven**, who died on 6 July 1846. No kinship to this line is claimed.
how: Arienzo, Morti 1846, atto 39, found through the annual death index.
why: Recorded because a name identifies nobody in this town and the archive keeps proving it — two Giuseppe Falco, two Carlantonio Morgillo, two Arcangelo Crisci, two Angelo Morgillo, two Gennaro Morgillo, and now three Michele Falco. **VIGLIOTTA is also the surname of the strada Costa Giuseppe Falco's wife, Gelsomina.** Two Falco–Vigliotta marriages in one small town is worth noticing and nothing more.

what: a churchman in a family of day-labourers
was: Every Falco this archive had found for four generations was a **bracciale**, a **contadino** or a **colono**. No cleric, no professional, nobody who signed their own name.
now: **DON GIOVANNI FALCO, DIACONO**, died at Arienzo on **26 November 1849, aged twenty-five** — **son of GIUSEPPE FALCO, colono, and ANTONIA DI GUIDA**, and therefore **Matteo Falco's grandson**. Born about 1824.
how: Arienzo, Morti 1849, atto 66, found through the annual death index and read from the image.
why: Published because it changes the shape of the family, not just its size. It also puts **Giuseppe Falco alive in November 1849** at about seventy — no «fu» before his name — and it puts the declarants, two Cioffi, **on strada Camellara** again. *The index calls him* suddiacono *and the act* diacono; both are recorded.

what: an act number misread from an index — twice, in the same way
was: **1846**: «Falco Chiara» read as **act 29**. **1850**: «Falco D. Angela Maria» read as **act 39**.
now: **Both were the number of the row ABOVE.** Act 29 of 1846 is **Ferro Antonio**; act 39 of 1850 is **Finelli Clemente**. Chiara Falco is act **39** of 1846; Angela Maria Falco's number is still not certain, and the site says so.
how: Opened each act and read the name back before believing the index.
why: Recorded as a method note because it is now a **pattern, not a slip**: in this clerk's hand the act numbers of adjacent rows are the least legible thing on the page, and a Falco entry has twice sat directly beneath a similar-looking number. **Confirm every index act number by opening the act.**

what: a nun and two Falco-Falco marriages, all from an index and none from an act
was: Nothing — none of these people was held here.
now: **FALCO DONNA ANGELA MARIA, *MONACA***, died **14 November 1850**, daughter of **Don Francesco Falco and Donna Maddalena Stellato** — a **gentry** Falco household. **FALCO ANGELANTONIO** of **Santa Maria a Vico**, 20 October 1850, «Falco Domenico e Falco Mariantonia»; and **FALCO ANTONIO**, 23 October 1850, «Falco Francesco e Falco Giuseppa» — **two Falco men who married Falco women**.
how: The 1850 death tavola, bound at the front of the register itself rather than in a separate volume.
why: Published **at index strength and no higher** — none of the three acts has been read, and no kinship to this line is claimed. The *Don* and *Donna* matter: a gentry Falco household at Arienzo is a different world from the *coloni* of strada Camellara, and the archive should stop assuming every Falco in this town is a relation.

what: a parish attributed, corrected, and now reopened
was: Raffaele Falco and Angela Rosa Morgillo's marriage index entry was published first as **Arienzo's**, then corrected to **San Felice a Cancello's** on the strength of FamilySearch's label for film 007786833.
now: **IT IS AN OPEN QUESTION AGAIN.** The register bound immediately after that index — images 1880 onward of the same film — is explicitly **«Parochus Ecclesiae S. AGNETIS Virginis et Martyris TERRAE ARGENTII»**: the parish of **Sant'Agnese in Arienzo**, with acts of **1843**. A film label covers a whole reel and a reel can hold several parishes.
how: Read the first acts of the register itself instead of trusting either the search filter or the catalogue label.
why: Left visible rather than quietly swapped, because the archive got this wrong in **both** directions within a day. What is certain is the entry itself — «Raphael Falco cum Angela Rosa Morgillo filia Horatii, fol. 2 a tergo» — and that **folio 2 of the volume that follows the index is 1843**, which agrees with the stray «18 43» beside the entry. **The parish and the date are both unsettled, and the act at folio 2 a tergo has not been read.** What is now certain from elsewhere is that they were married **in 1846 or earlier**, because their daughter Vincenza was born in November 1847.

superseded.what: the parish question, settled by the act — and the first answer was the right one
superseded.note: **Settled the same day, and the first answer was right: ARIENZO**, from «*Parocho S. AGNETIS TERRÆ ARGENTII*» in the act itself. The doubt raised here was withdrawn that night.

what: two brothers dead a day apart, and a Falco household not previously held
was: **1848 was a blank year** — Arienzo has no death index for it at all, and the register had never been read.
now: **GIUSEPPE FALCO, aged ONE, died 2 June 1848**, and **GENNARO FALCO, aged TWO DAYS, died 3 June 1848** — both «**figlio di CRESCENZO FALCO**, contadino, **e di MARIA MORGILLO**». A year-old boy and a newborn, brothers, dead on consecutive days.
how: The 1848 register read act by act — the name line of every act on images 4–51 rendered and looked at, because there is no index to shortcut it.
why: **CRESCENZO FALCO × MARIA MORGILLO is a household this archive has never held**, and no kinship to this line is claimed. Published with the limits of the method stated: this was a name-line sweep of every act, not a word-by-word reading, and the band does not catch the name on every act. A strong sweep, not an exhaustive reading.

what: the parish question, settled by the act — and the first answer was the right one
was: Published as **Arienzo**, then «corrected» to **San Felice a Cancello** on the strength of a film label, then reopened as unresolved when the register following the index turned out to say Sant'Agnese.
now: **SETTLED FROM THE ACT ITSELF. ARIENZO.** «Anno Domini **1844**, die vero **5 Mensis Martii** … coram me infrascripto **Parocho S. AGNETIS TERRAE ARGENTII** … **RAPHAEL FALCO filius VINCENTII et ANDREANAE CRISCI** … et **mea Parochiana ANGELA ROSA MORGILLO filia HORATII et VINCENTIAE PESCE**.» **The first answer was right.**
how: Walked the film from the index leaf at image 1873 to the act at image 1884, compositing each leaf from its DeepZoom tiles.
why: Three positions in one day on one question, and all three are on the site. The middle one was taken from **FamilySearch's catalogue label for a whole reel** — which is not a source, and a reel can hold several parishes. **The lesson is cheap and the cost was an afternoon: read the document, not the label on the box it came in.**

what: a granddaughter of the founder, and her household reassembled from two archives
was: Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida were held as the parents of **two infants** and, since this morning, of **Don Giovanni the deacon**.
now: **RAFFAELA FALCO**, born about **1820**, died **20 April 1854** aged thirty-four on **strada Camellara**, **«moglie di FRANCESCO FALCO»** and «**figlia di GIUSEPPE FALCO** … **e di ANTONIA GUIDA**». Their son **CLEMENTE FALCO** died **14 August 1855 aged five** — from the parish register, «Clemens Falco filius Francisci, et Raphaelae Falco».
how: The civil act from Antenati (Morti 1854, atto 34, found through the year's index); the parish burial from FamilySearch's full-text of the Arienzo parish registers. Two archives, two methods, two different days.
why: Published because it does three things at once: it adds a child to the founder's son's family, it **puts GIUSEPPE FALCO alive in April 1854 at about seventy-four** — «figlia DI Giuseppe», no «fu» — and it is the first household this archive has reassembled by joining a civil act to a parish entry. **Her husband was also a Falco**, which at Arienzo is common enough to prove nothing on its own.

what: the husband of an isolate, documented at last
was: **MARGHERITA FALCO** was an isolate — a name from a fragment of a parish baptism, «dominico Crisci e Margaria Falco», with nothing attached to it.
now: **DOMENICO CRISCI, «VEDOVO DI MARGHERITA FALCO», died 9 January 1855 at Arienzo, aged EIGHTY**, a *contadino* of **STRADA CRISCI**, **son of the late VINCENZO CRISCI and the late MARIA DI LUCIA**. So Margherita Falco **died before January 1855**, and her husband was born about **1775**.
how: The 1855 Arienzo death register, which has no index at either end, read act by act.
why: Whose daughter Margherita was is **still unknown**. A woman married to a man born about 1775 was probably born in the same decade, which would put her in Matteo Falco's generation or the next — **but that is arithmetic, not evidence, and it is left as arithmetic.**

what: a second Falco family at Arienzo, with a nun and a priest in it

what: the archive's central question, answered — and the argument published four hours earlier, refuted
was: **MATTEO FALCO**, head of this line: «died by 8 December 1814, probably before 1809». Then, this afternoon and at length: «**both alive on 4 August 1802**», and «died between August 1802 and 1809» — argued from the **absence of «quondam»** in his children's marriage acts, with the same scribe's use of «filium **quondam** Caroli Antonii» on the very same leaf offered as the warrant.
now: **HE DIED ON 18 JULY 1802.** Arienzo parish death register: «Anno Domini Millesimo Octingentesimo **SECUNDO 1802**, die vero **DECIMA OCTAVA 18 JULII**, **MATTHEUS FALCO, VIR FRANCISCAE CRISCI** … omnibus Sacramentis munitus … obiit, et **in Archipresbyterali Coemeterio ejus cadaver humatum est**.» **When his son Giuseppe married on 4 August he had been dead for seventeen days**, and the act still says «filium Matthei» with no «quondam».

why: **The refutation is the finding, not a footnote to it.** The argument from silence was careful, it carried its evidence, it was labelled strong evidence rather than proof — and it was **wrong at both ends**. In these registers a missing «quondam» means nothing, even when the same scribe uses it correctly two acts away. \n\nIt also dates the summer of 1802 exactly: **Rosa married on 12 July**, six days before her father died; **he died on 18 July**; **Giuseppe married on 4 August**, seventeen days after burying him. Both marriages are on one leaf of the marriage register, read this morning in the belief that he was alive at both.

what: a surname left unread this morning, supplied by a death act this evening

now: **It is RIVETTI.** Carlo Antonio Morgillo's own death entry, **17 June 1842**, aged **sixty**: «**filius q[uonda]m Caroli Antonii, et q[uonda]m MARIA RIVETTI, ac VIDUUS ROSAE FALCO**», buried **in the church of San Giovanni**. what: the founder's wife, found — and an age got wrong three times in one day
was: «FRANCISCA CRISCI, VIDUA […] FALCO», 31 December 1805 — published this afternoon as **a lead only**, because the word after «vidua» was rendered «Manel» by the machine and «everything turns on it». Her age was read as **eighty**, then withdrawn, then read from the image as **seventy**.
now: **«FRANCISCA CRISCI VIDUA MAT‑THEI FALCO, aetatis suae annorum 60 circiter»** — read from the image. **It is Matteo's widow.** The surname breaks across the line, «Vidua Mat‑ / thei Falco», which is exactly why the machine could not hold it together. **The age was wrong three times before it was right, and the three ways it was wrong are the finding.** «Eighty» was my over-read of a garbled machine word. «Seventy» was read correctly off the image — **from the entry below**, which is Francesca CILLO, wife of Vincenzo Laudato, who died on 1 January 1806. «Sixty» is the act. 

**Reading a horizontal band of a register page is not reading an entry.** Twice in one afternoon a number was taken from a neighbour's line. **Anchor on the margin label and on the entry's own first and last words.** 

And with it the founding couple closes at both ends: **he died 18 July 1802 at about fifty-five, she on 31 December 1805 at about sixty** — born about 1747 and 1745. She bore her last child at about forty-one and was about two years older than him. **Nothing about them is strange any more**, which is itself the confirmation.

what: the FindMyPast verdict was measured from outside the paywall, and it was too strong
was: «**Its Australian records do not contain the Brisbane family.**» — this archive's own sweep of 9 September 2026, which allowed a single exception: Carmine Falco's arrival of 26 March 1964.
now: They contain **six** records of this family, all passenger lists. Beside the 1964 arrival: **FILOMENA FALCO, 5 February 1968** (NAA barcode 9788535, p. 251) and **CARMINANTONIO FALCO, 19 May 1969** (barcode 12211391, p. 1711), with a second crossing under «Carminatonio» on **24 July 1972** (barcode 12047001, p. 1605). **A first-name filter that returns zero is not a nil.** «carm» returned nothing; «carminantonio» returned the record. The September sweep read what a signed-out session was shown and wrote the verdict as though it had read the holding.

FindMyPast's whole holding for this family is passenger lists. It is six records deep, not one. 

And the answer to «is there a FindMyPast tree?» is **no** — the account has none, and the family tree lives on MyHeritage.

Identity lives in the data, not the markup.*» The gate was built to stop a leak; the near-miss here ran the other way — **a name-level check was about to delete a true fact about a dead man.** \n\n**Redaction needs identification just as much as publication does.** A rule enforced on names alone will both leak and over-delete, and the second failure is quieter than the first because nobody complains about a fact that vanished.

what: generation four's CIVIL marriage act is not where it has to be
was: The church act is settled: **Raffaele Falco married Angela Rosa Morgillo on 5 March 1844 at Sant'Agnese, Arienzo.** Under the Two Sicilies that wedding must have a civil counterpart — a *solenne promessa* before the sindaco, with the priest's certificate of the celebration facing it. **That act names both fathers and both mothers, with ages, trades and streets.** It is the richest document this family could still recover.
now: **It is not in the register.** Arienzo *Matrimoni* 1844 (`an_ua14248`, 32 images) has been **read end to end** — exactly **29 acts, 6 January to 30 December**, closing with the Procuratore del Re's certificate — and **no Falco appears in any of them**, as groom, bride or parent. Acts 29–35 of 1843 (`an_ua14247`, 8 Oct – 28 Dec) were read as well. **No Falco.** Neither volume has an index; that was checked, not assumed.
how: Every act's name band rendered from the Antenati images and read. The acts are published in full at `data/arienzo-civil-marriages-1843-1844.tsv`, three of them marked NOT SECURELY READ rather than guessed.
why: **A negative is only worth what its boundaries are worth**, so here they are. What remains untested: the first twenty-eight acts of 1843; San Felice a Cancello, the bride's comune of birth; and the plain possibility that no civil act was ever drawn. \n\n**And a caution that may matter more than the search.** Every act in the 1843 volume reads «*comune di CORPO D'ARIENZO*»; every act in the 1844 volume reads «*comune di Arienzo*». Both are catalogued under the one heading "Arienzo". This archive **does not yet know** whether that is a second comune or just how one clerk styled the town — but until it does, **no 1843 nil can be said to cover both**. Several of this archive's published eliminations run through that year.

why:
**The corroboration is the naming, not the names.** Filippo's father was BARTOLOMEO and Filippo's son is BARTOLOMEO — the Neapolitan custom working as it should, which independently supports a reading («Maria Martini») that went in marked `[?]`. The ages fit without strain. 

**What is not claimed:** Giovanna Majone, 27, who married in June 1844 «figlia di … Majone defunto», may be a fourth child of this house; her father's forename was not read with confidence, so she is not entered as one. 

**And it moves a standing question.** The queue asks whether the Majone of Arienzo and the Majone of Arpaia are one kindred. **Two of Filippo's three sons are recorded living toward Arpaia while the third stayed in Arienzo** — the place-name marked `[?]` and not yet proven. If it holds they are not a separate kindred but Arienzo sons who moved eight kilometres up the valley: **the same short-range drift the Falco made two generations later**, when Raffaele Falco's last child was born at Arpaia in 1913.

what: the founders' «unnamed daughter» was a woman this archive already knew
was: The children of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci were listed with **«a daughter, name not legible (machine gives «proja»), baptised 5 January 1786»** — an unidentified infant, counted as a child in her own right. **Rosa Falco was listed separately**, from a burial and a marriage.
now: **They are the same person, and her name is ROSA MARIA.** The act reads «*baptizavit infantem **NATAM** ex **MATTHEO FALCO**, et **FRANCISCA CRISCI** Conjugibus hujus Parochiae, **que nominata est ROSA MARIA***», the celebrant **Canonico SABBATINO CRISCI, sostituto**. So the founders had **one child fewer** than the archive was counting, and one more woman with a whole life attached: **Rosa Maria Falco married Carlo Antonio Morgillo on 12 July 1802** and **died on strada Camellara on 16 October 1830**, «*d'anni quarantadue*».
how: Read from the image at `3Q9M-CSD3-13XZ-1` — «proja» was the machine's attempt at «Rosa Maria».
why: **And it moved a citation.** Her baptism was cited to `3Q9M-CSD3-13XB-R`, an ark taken from machine-parsed text whose own extract runs «*Angelis Porrino … 1793 … Rosa Falco … 1808*» — three dates that cannot all belong to one 1786 act. **The act is on `13XZ-1`, which has now been read.** What is actually on `13XB-R` has NOT been checked and no claim is made about it. \n\n**The stated age does not quite fit and is published anyway.** Baptised January 1786 she would be **forty-four** in October 1830, not forty-two. This archive has already documented that the Arienzo clerks guessed ages — a two-year gap is inside the noise, and saying so is better than quietly choosing the reading that tidies it.

what: the founders' last «unnamed» child was the first Gioacchino, and the year was wrong by three
was: The reconstructed household carried **«[unnamed] — child — baptism — 25 Nov 1777»**, cited to `3Q9M-CSD3-13H2-1`, as a child in its own right. **Separately** the archive held **«the first Gioacchino, baptised 25 November 1774, obiit 11 December 1777»** — from the same ark.
now: **One act, one child.** Read from the image: «*Anno Domini Millesimo septingentesimo septuagesimo qua[rto] … die vero **VIGESIMAQUINTA 25 NOVEMBRIS** … Canonicus **BRUNO** Substituens baptizavit … ex **MATTHEO FALCO**, et **FRANCISCA CRISCI** Conjugibus*», the margin reading **«Joachim Falco — OBIIT DIE 11 DECEMBRIS 1777»**. The year is **1774**, the day 25 November, and the child is **JOACHIM**. The «25 Nov 1777» row was the same act with the year out by three.
how: The act read at native resolution, **and the year line read on its own** rather than inferred from the act above it. The archive has been wrong before by taking a number from a neighbouring line, so the year was fetched as a separate crop even though the answer looked obvious.
why: **With this the founders' children are complete and every one of them is named**: Pasquale (1767), Francisca Anna Angela (1771), Giuseppe, **Joachim (1774–1777)**, **Gioacchino (1779)** and **Rosa Maria (1786)**. Two «unnamed children» have been dissolved in one day and **both turned out to be people the archive already knew**. \n\nAnd the naming is now documented at both ends from the images: **Joachim died on 11 December 1777 and the name was given again on 2 February 1779**, fourteen months later. This family named children after their dead — it did so again with the two Giovannas — and that is no longer an inference.

what: the CORPO D'ARIENZO warning, raised and withdrawn on the same day
was: Reading the **back** of the 1843 marriage volume, every act said «*comune di **CORPO D'ARIENZO***» while every act of 1844 said «*comune di **Arienzo***», both catalogued under the one heading. **A warning went up here this morning**: that a sweep eliminating "Arienzo" for a year might have covered only one of two jurisdictions — which would have undercut several of this archive's published eliminations.
now: **Reading the same volume from the FRONT settles it.** Acts **1, 2 and 3** of 1843 say «*comune di **ARIENZO***». **Act 4 and everything after says «comune di CORPO D'ARIENZO»** — and acts 3 and 4 are three weeks apart, **before the same officer, RAFFAELE DE MIERI, sindaco, in the same book.** One comune, two ways of writing it. **The warning is withdrawn.**
how: Reading the volume end to end instead of sampling it — which was going to happen anyway for a different reason.
why: **The warning is left standing on this page rather than deleted, because raising it was right.** On the evidence available at the time — seven consecutive acts, all saying Corpo d'Arienzo — the honest move was to flag that every 1843 nil might be worth less than it looked. **It cost one morning of doubt and bought certainty about fifteen years of eliminations.** \n\nThe likely sense of *corpo* is the ordinary administrative one, the main built-up body of a comune as against its outlying casali, as in *Corpo di Cava*. **That reading is offered, not proved.** What is proved is that it is not a second jurisdiction.

what: sixty-four marriage acts, two whole years, and no Falco at all
was: This morning the archive could say only that **1844 held no Falco marriage** and that acts 29–35 of 1843 held none either — leaving open the possibility that generation four's civil act sat in the earlier part of 1843.
now: **It does not.** Arienzo *Matrimoni* **1843** (`an_ua14247`) is now **read end to end** as well — **35 acts, 1 January to 28 December**. With 1844's 29 acts that is **sixty-four consecutive marriage acts across two whole years, and not one Falco in any role** — groom, bride, or parent of either.
how: Every act's name band rendered from the Antenati images and read. All sixty-four are published in `data/arienzo-civil-marriages-1843-1844.tsv`, uncertain words marked `[?]`.
why: **Two possibilities are left and the archive is not choosing between them.** Either the act is at **SAN FELICE A CANCELLO**, the bride's comune of birth — though the priest at Sant'Agnese called her «*mea Parochiana*» in 1844, so she was living in Arienzo by then — or **no civil act was ever drawn**, which is not as strange as it sounds in a town whose church and civil registers plainly did not always speak to each other. \n\n**What the sixty-four acts did give** is a whole working town: four more households on **strada Camellara**, a **fourth child** of the Majone house, and the confirmation of a name that had gone in marked uncertain.

superseded.what: generation four's civil marriage act — found, hours after this archive said it was not there
superseded.note: **Superseded by the act.** The sixty-four acts are still read and still bound the negative for Arienzo; the marriage itself was at **San Felice a Cancello**, the bride's comune, which is the first of the two possibilities this entry declined to choose between.

what: generation four's civil marriage act — found, hours after this archive said it was not there
was: **This morning this archive published**, after reading sixty-four Arienzo marriage acts of 1843 and 1844 end to end: «*generation four's civil marriage act is not where it must be*» — with **San Felice a Cancello listed as untested possibility number one.**
now: **It was there.** **San Felice a Cancello, *Matrimoni* 1844, atto 12, 7 MARCH 1844** (`an_ua50256`, image 13): «*… sono comparsi nella Casa Comunale **RAFFAELE FALCO** di anni **ventisei**, nato in **ARIENZO CORPO**, di professione **contadino**, domiciliato **strada CAMMELLARA**, figlio di **VINCENZO FALCO** di professione simile, domiciliato **ivi**, e di **ANDREANA CRISCI** di professione **filatrice**, domiciliata **ivi**; e **ANGELA ROSA MORGILLO** di anni **ventisei**, contadina, **nata in questo Comune**, figlia di **ORAZIO MORGILLO**, colono, e di **VINCENZA PESCE**, contadina*».
how: Reading the bride's comune instead of the groom's. **The civil promise is made where the BRIDE lives** — the ordinary rule, and the one this archive had not applied.
why:
**VINCENZO FALCO WAS ALIVE ON 7 MARCH 1844** — no *defunto*, «domiciliato **ivi**», on strada Cammellara beside his son. Generation three had been traced only to his baptism in 1792 and his marriage in December 1814; **this is thirty years later and it is the latest date the archive has for him.** Andreana Crisci is alive too, a spinner on the same street, and so are Orazio Morgillo and Vincenza Pesce at San Felice. 

**The Arienzo sweep was not wasted** — it is what proves the act is not at Arienzo, and it produced the Majone household and six Camellara households on the way. **But the reasoning that made Arienzo obvious was wrong, and it was wrong because the archive assumed the groom's town.** 

**And a four-day gap is published rather than tidied away.** The parish act gives the marriage as **5 March**; the civil column certifies the celebration on **9 March**. Both are read from images, they do not agree, and no attempt is made here to choose between them.

what: there is more than one FORCHIA — and the archive has been searching the right one
was: «Forchia» has been treated throughout as **one place**: the comune in the province of **Benevento**, beside Arpaia, where **Filomena Annecchino was born on 10 April 1897**. Her birth act has been hunted there across FamilySearch and Antenati for weeks and never found.
now: **There is also FORCHIA DI CERVINO, a frazione of Cervino in the province of Caserta**, about fifteen kilometres west — and **this archive's own sources name it outright.** The Arienzo parish pages carry «*contratto matrimonio nella cura di **Forchia di Cervino***» and «*contratto matrimonio in **Forchia di Cervino** il dì 28 Agosto*». The registers also write **«FORCHIA D'ARPAIA»** and **«FORCHIA DI CERVINARA»**, Cervinara being in Avellino; whether those are two further places or clerks' ways of pointing at the first two is **not settled**.
how: **From WikiTree, of all places — a site that holds nothing whatever on this family.** Chasing its one near-miss, a «Maria Grazia Carfora born 1873 at Forchia», dissolved it: she is the daughter of Salvatore Carfora of **Santa Maria a Vico** and Mariantonia Papa of **Messercola, Cervino**, and her Forchia is written in full as «**Forchia, CERVINO, Caserta**».
why:
**No error is claimed yet, and that is the point.** What is claimed is that **a nil is only as good as the place it was taken in**, and this archive cannot presently say which Forchia several of its Forchia searches reached. **If any of them went to Cervino instead of Benevento, or merged the two, those nils are worth less than they look** — and one of them is the missing birth act of generation seven's wife. 

The action is concrete and small: **fix which Forchia before the next search, and put the province on every Forchia row already held.** 

It is also worth saying plainly that **the empty source was the useful one.** WikiTree returned zero for ANNECCHINO and zero for ZAMPIELLO and has no Falco nearer than Salerno — and it still paid for the hour, because a wrong lead followed properly ends somewhere.

---

**RESOLVED THE SAME DAY, and the answer is the reassuring one.**

**Antenati indexes by COMUNE, and a frazione never has a civil register of its own.** *Forchia di Cervino* is a hamlet of **CERVINO**, and Antenati holds **Cervino separately — 386 registers of its own**, in the same Caserta archive. So the «Forchia» series this archive has been reading (`an_ua29049`–`an_ua29090`) can only be **the comune of Forchia**: it runs **1820 to 1861 under Caserta and then stops**, which is precisely when Forchia passed out of Terra di Lavoro into the new province of Benevento.

**And the families cross-check.** **SABATINO ANNECCHINO × MARIANTONIA CARFORA** appear in all three holdings at once — in the **Antenati comune-of-Forchia** series (Maria Rosa, born 7 March 1861), in the **FamilySearch «Forchia»** harvest (Maria Filomena 1864, Carmine Maria 1867) and in the **FamilySearch Benevento Civil Registration** collection (Maria Pascalina 1863, Michele Maria 1870). One couple, three books, and the one that is unambiguous by construction settles the other two.

**Every «Forchia» place-cell in the data now reads «Forchia (BN)» — 133 of them** — so the question cannot come back. The «Forchia di Cervino» marriages in the Arienzo parish pages belong to other families (Nuzzo, Caprio, d'Addio) and are not confused with these. One reading IS withdrawn: a groom of 1843 recorded as born at «Forchia di Cervinara» is now marked as **either Forchia di Cervino (CE) or Cervinara (AV), not settled** — it is certainly not the comune of Forchia.

**What this does NOT fix** is the thing that was actually wrong all along: **Filomena Annecchino was born in 1897, and the Antenati Caserta series stops in 1861.** Her act was never going to be there. It belongs to Benevento's *Stato civile italiano*, which FamilySearch covers as **«Benevento Civil Registration (State Archive) 1810–1942»** — **the collection to hammer, and the one place the archive has not yet exhausted.**

what: an over-correction of my own, caught an hour later
was: Having enumerated Antenati's holdings and found **no Forchia births for 1897**, this archive wrote that the old explanation for Filomena Annecchino's missing birth act — FamilySearch's paging cap and fuzzy matching — **«was the wrong explanation»**, and that **«the volume is not online; no amount of searching was ever going to find it»**.
now: **Too strong, and on the second half simply unchecked.** What was proved is that **ANTENATI** does not hold the volume. **FamilySearch's «Benevento Civil Registration (State Archive) 1810–1942» is a separate filming**, and this archive's own harvest from it already contains a birth of **22 November 1897** — at **MOIANO**, not Forchia. **So that collection reaches the year.** Whether it reaches **Forchia** in that year has not been tested. **The paging-and-fuzzy-matching explanation is not refuted; it stands alongside the new possibility.**
how: Checking the year-range of the archive's own FamilySearch harvest — a file already on disk — instead of generalising from one source to another.
why: **Correcting a wrong explanation is not a licence to assert a new one beyond the evidence.** The Antenati enumeration was good work and it settles Antenati. It says nothing about what a different institution filmed in a different decade, and the word «online» quietly covered both. \n\n**The over-reach is left on the page** rather than edited away, because it is the same failure this archive has published before under another name: an argument that ran one step further than the source it rested on.

what: FILOMENA ANNECCHINO exists in a record at last — and her husband declared it
was: Generation seven's wife had **no document at all**. Her birth act was never found, and this archive said so plainly: the descent from Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora is **«inferred, not documented»**, and **her existence rested entirely on the family tree**.
now: **Forchia, *Atti di Morte — Parte I*, 1937, atto 17**, read from the image: on the morning of **2 August 1937** «*sono comparsi **FALCO CARMINANTONIO**, di anni **trentasei**, **contadino**, domiciliato in Forchia … i quali mi hanno dichiarato che … nella casa posta in **Contrada CASE SPARSE**, al numero **sessantotto**, **è morto FALCO ANIELLO, di MESI NOVE**, … **da CARMINANTONIO, contadino, e da ANNECCHINO FILOMENA, CASALINGA, domiciliata in Forchia***».
how: **Antenati's NAME index** — `/search-nominative/?cognome=X&localita=Y` — run against the **Benevento «Stato civile italiano»** series, a fondo this archive had recorded as «not located» until this afternoon.
why:
**The father declared his own son's death.** That is the first hard record of this household in Italy, and it carries four things the archive did not have: **Filomena Annecchino named in a document**; **Carminantonio at thirty-six, corroborating a birth in 1901** for the first time; **a son, ANIELLO, born at Forchia about November 1936 and dead at nine months**, who had existed only as a name on the tree; and **an address — Contrada Case Sparse 68**. 

**Two things are deliberately NOT claimed.** A **Maria Annunziata Falco** died at Forchia on 31 July 1938 with her mother indexed as *Filomena Annecchino* and her father as *«Antonio»* — either another child of this house with the father's name written short, or a different couple. **The act has not been read.** And a **Raffaele Falco born at Arpaia married at Forchia on 28 October 1937**; whose son he is has not been established. 

This archive has been caught before treating a name plus a date as an identification. It is not doing it twice in one day.

what: the Sant'Agnese doubt — raised this morning, withdrawn tonight, and the original claim was right
was: Finding generation four's **civil** marriage act at **San Felice a Cancello**, with the bride «*nata in questo Comune, domiciliata in detto comune*», this archive flagged its own published statement that **Sant'Agnese is one of Arienzo's three parishes**. The reasoning was that the bride was the celebrant's own parishioner and appeared to live at San Felice, so his church probably did too — and that the parish act had been read off an **Arienzo film**, which is not the same thing as an Arienzo church.
now: **The act names the place itself.** Read tonight: «*Anno Domini **1844, die 5 mensis Martii** … coram me infrascripto **Parocho S. AGNETIS TERRÆ ARGENTII**, et coram testibus **Pasquale Pellone filio Clementis**, **Angelo di Marzo filio Francisci** … matrimonium contraxerunt in faciem Ecclesiæ per verba de præsenti **RAPHAEL FALCO filius VINCENTII et ANDREANÆ CRISCI**, Archipresbyteralis Ecclesiæ S. Andreæ Apostoli, **et mea Parochiana ANGELA ROSA MORGILLO filia HORATII et VINCENTIÆ PESCE***».\n\n**«TERRA ARGENTI» IS ARIENZO** — and the proof is this archive's own corpus, which uses the phrase over a thousand times in the formula «*Insignis Collegiatae Ecclesiae **Sancti Andreae Apostoli TERRÆ ARGENTI***». Sant'Andrea is Arienzo's collegiate church. **Sant'Agnese is an Arienzo parish, the original claim stands, and the doubt is withdrawn.**
how: Reading the act's own words instead of arguing from where a film was catalogued or where a civil clerk recorded a domicile.
why:
**The flag was still right to raise.** A film label covers a whole reel, this archive has already flip-flopped once between Arienzo and San Felice for exactly that reason, and the civil act genuinely did place the bride at San Felice. **Flagging a claim you cannot presently defend costs a day; asserting one you cannot defend costs the reader's trust.** 

**Two things are corrected in passing.** The witness this archive read as «Eusebio Lettieri di Clemente» is **PASQUALE PELLONE di Clemente** — and the civil act at San Felice names **the same two men**, which is the strongest cross-check the two records could give each other. And **the 5 March date is now read from the act**, so the **four-day gap** with the civil column's «celebration followed on 9 March» is a real disagreement between two books, not a misreading. 

**What remains genuinely odd** is the bride: she is «*mea Parochiana*» of Sant'Agnese **in Arienzo**, while her civil act three days later calls her *domiciled at San Felice*. Both are read from images. **The archive records the tension and does not resolve it.**

what: Filomena Annecchino's birth — tested properly at last, and the premise itself is now in question
was: Twice today this archive gave a reason why her 10 April 1897 birth act has never been found, and **both were guesses about a source rather than tests of it**. First: «the volume is not online, no amount of searching was ever going to find it». Then, pulling that back: «FamilySearch is a separate filming and reaches 1897, so the old paging-and-fuzzy-matching explanation is not refuted».
now: **Tested.** FamilySearch's Benevento collection **does** cover Forchia in 1897 — a control search on **IULIANO**, a common Forchia surname, returns about thirty Forchia records in every year from 1894 to 1899. **And she is still not there.** Searching by her parents — **father Carmine Annecchino, mother Maria Carfora** — returns their children at Forchia: **Giacinta 1883, Agata 1884, Giacomo 1887, Agata 1889, Lucia and Alfonso both 2 August 1892, Alfonso Carmine 1894, Giacomo 1901**. **No child of 1897 among them.** Searching by name for a Filomena Annecchino born 1895–1899 returns **nothing**.
how: A control search first, to prove the source covers the town and the year, and only then a search for the person. **That is the step both earlier explanations skipped.**
why:
**Two possibilities remain and the archive is not choosing.** Either the act exists and is unindexed or misindexed — Antenati holds no Forchia 1897 birth volume at all, so only FamilySearch could have it. **Or she was not born at Forchia in 1897.** 

**That second one this archive has not been willing to say before, and it should be.** The date and the place come from the family tree. **Every one of her supposed siblings is indexed and she alone is not** — which is exactly the shape of a wrong premise rather than a missing page. 

So the next move is **not another search of Forchia**. It is a test of the premise: the neighbouring comuni, Benevento city, and above all **her MARRIAGE to Carminantonio Falco**, which would state her age and birthplace on a record's authority instead of a tree's.

superseded.what: Filomena Annecchino's birth at Forchia in 1897 — the ANSWER WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE, and the open question was stale
superseded.note: **She was born at Forchia in 1897.** The second possibility this entry raised — that the premise was wrong — was **withdrawable from a file already in this repository**, `data/qld-bdm.tsv`, which carries her Queensland death registration giving 1897 and her father Carmine. The act is missing; the birth is not.

what: an absence is only evidence when the source would otherwise have shown the thing
was: Two birth acts this archive cannot find: **ANGELO ZAMPIELLO**, born Arpaia 31 August 1895, and **FILOMENA ANNECCHINO**, born Forchia 10 April 1897. Both have been treated the same way for months — as volumes that happen not to be digitised.
now: **They are not the same, and counting what the source holds around them shows it.** Antenati's name index for **ARPAIA** is thin everywhere — births per year 1885–1905 run 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 1, 0, 3, 2, **0**, **0**, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. **Angelo's absence explains itself.** The index for **FORCHIA** is the opposite: Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora's children are all there — 1883, 1884, 1887, 1889, 1892 twice, 1894, 1901 — **and Filomena alone is missing from a series that holds every one of her siblings.**
how: Running Antenati's **name** index (`/search-nominative/`, which gives parents) on Arpaia for the first time: **259 Zampiello records, 1862–1940**.
why:
**So the two silences mean opposite things.** For Angelo the source is at fault and the family's account stands. For Filomena the source is not at fault, and **what should be doubted is the premise** — the 1897 Forchia birth that comes from the family tree. 

**The rule this archive takes from it:** before treating an absence as a fact about the world, **count what the source holds around it**. A gap in a dense series is a finding; a gap in a sparse one is nothing at all. 

The Arpaia harvest also turned up **TOMMASO ZAMPIELLO × ROSA CRISCI**, whose son Francesco Maria was born there on 29 January 1892. Angelo is «*di Tommaso*». **If it is the same Tommaso, Angelo's mother was Rosa Crisci — and that is not claimed**, because one index entry is not a household and Tommaso is not a rare name at Arpaia.

what: a second child of generation seven — and my own misreading of the act that proves it
was: An index entry showed a **Maria Annunziata Falco** dying at Forchia on 31 July 1938 with mother *Filomena Annecchino* and father *«Antonio»*. This archive flagged it and refused to claim it. Then, reading a contact sheet, **I said the index had the parents wrong** — that the act gave «*Angelo … Annecchino Anna … d'anni trentadue … moglie di Annecchino Gabriele*».
now: **None of that is in the act.** I was reading a **neighbouring entry on the facing page**. Rendered on its own, the act says exactly what the index said: «*… in detto **Ospedale Pellegrini** [Napoli, Montecalvario] **è morta FALCO MARIA ANNUNZIATA di ANTONIO e di ANNECCHINO FILOMENA, di anni CINQUE, da FORCHIA***», at **ten at night on 31 July 1938**, copied back to Forchia at that comune's request on 3 April 1939.
how: Rendering the entry by itself before writing anything down — which is the step that was skipped.
why:
**This archive has published this exact failure before**, in almost these words: *«reading a horizontal band of a register page is not reading an entry — anchor on the margin label and the entry's own first and last words.»* It happened again today, on the first pass. 

**And the act itself is a hard one.** She is **five years old**, of Forchia, born about 1933, and her mother is **Filomena Annecchino** — the exact pairing already documented in this family, whose household Carminantonio is recorded in at Forchia in **August 1937**, declaring the death of their **nine-month-old son Aniello**. **If she is theirs, they buried two children in eleven months**, and the second died in a hospital forty kilometres from home. 

**It is entered as PROBABLE, not documented**: the act writes the father **«Antonio»**, not Carminantonio. It is a Naples act taken from a hospital notice, so a shortening is easy — but it is a different word, and a name plus a date is not an identification.

what: a seventh child for generation six — and two Raffaele Falco where the archive carried one
was: Raffaele Falco and Costanza Maione's children were listed as **Giovanna (1898), Carminantonio (1901), Anna del Giudice (1904), Gerardo (1913)**, with **Giacoma** and **Aniello** undated. Separately the archive says «Carminantonio's son **Raffaele** reached Brisbane, married **Caterina Zampiello** and is buried at Nudgee».
now: **Forchia, marriages 1937, atto 12**, read from the image: on **28 October 1937** at a quarter past six in the morning, in the parish of **San Nicola di Mira**, «***FALCO RAFFAELE**, di anni **ventuno**, contadino, **nato in ARPAIA**, residente in Forchia, **figlio di RAFFAELE e di MAIONE COSTANZA***» married «***CRISCI FRANCESCA**, contadina, figlia di **Pio** e di **De Lucia Maria***». **That is a seventh child of generation six**, born at Arpaia about 1916 — and his father was living at Forchia in 1937, aged about sixty-four.
how: Antenati's name index pointed at the volume; the act was then read leaf by leaf.
why:
**It separates two men the archive had been carrying as one name.** The groom of 1937 is **Carminantonio's BROTHER**, not his son: he is twenty-one, born at Arpaia, and the act names his parents outright. The Brisbane Raffaele who married a **Zampiello** is a different man a generation down. **Two Raffaele Falco in consecutive generations**, and only one of them was on the page. 

**And it puts a second pin in the migration.** Gerardo was born at **Arpaia in 1913** — long called here «the first sign of the move north». A brother born at **Arpaia about 1916** holds the household there for at least three years before it surfaces at **Forchia** in the thirties. **Arienzo → Arpaia → Forchia** now has records at all three. 

**Left unread:** the bride's birthplace is written «**Arienzo S. Felice**», a form that recurs in the same volume. Whether that is a frazione of Arienzo or the clerk's San Felice a Cancello is not settled.

what: Matteo Falco's marriage is not in the Arienzo film — and we may have been searching the wrong town all along
was: The line's oldest question. A Neapolitan marriage act names **both fathers**, so Matteo Falco's own marriage — expected about **1760–66** — is the one record that would push this family above him. It has been hunted in FamilySearch's Arienzo marriage collection for months.
now: **Enumerated rather than searched, and it is not there.** Every marriage act carries the word «*denunciationibus*»; that word returns **515 pages** in the collection, of which **500 were harvested** and read by machine transcript. **The 1760s are densely covered** — 1760:19, 1761:19, 1762:36, 1763:20, 1764:6, 1765:17, 1766:21, 1767:25 — **and not one of those 500 pages carries a legible «Falco» with a year between 1750 and 1779.** The one apparent hit dissolved on reading: the «alco» was OCR debris for *aliis*, and the page is **1865**, not 1765. **The earliest Falco marriage page in the whole harvest is 1782.**
how: Enumerating the collection on a word every act of that type carries, instead of searching for names the machine renders as *Marteus Falco*, *Armeni Falco* and *Malco*.
why:
**The negative is bounded and stated as such**: the surname may have been lost by the OCR, or the act may sit on one of the fifteen pages not harvested. **But the useful outcome is not the negative — it is that we may have been reading the wrong town.** 

**Today this archive learned where a marriage is recorded.** Generation four's civil act was hunted through sixty-four consecutive Arienzo acts of 1843–44 and was not there, because **the promise is made in the BRIDE's comune** — San Felice a Cancello. The same rule governs the church: a couple marries in **the bride's parish**, which is precisely why Raffaele Falco of Sant'Andrea married at **Sant'Agnese**, «*mea Parochiana*». 

**Matteo is certainly at Arienzo** — he witnesses a marriage there in **1759**, before his own. **Francesca Crisci need not have been.** If she was not an Arienzo parishioner, her marriage is in her own town's book and no amount of reading Arienzo will ever find it. 

**So the next move is to find HER**: a Crisci baptism of about 1740–45 outside Arienzo, and the Crisci of San Felice a Cancello, Santa Maria a Vico, Arpaia, Forchia and Cervino.

superseded.what: WHERE MATTEO FALCO'S MARRIAGE IS NOT — swept through the BRIDE's surname, and this time the denominator is honest
superseded.note: **Re-swept through the BRIDE's surname**, which is the cleaner instrument: 1,277 pages under CRISCI, ninety-two per cent of them Arienzo, regexed locally so the negative no longer depends on the engine spelling *Falco* correctly. **Still not a nil** — the 1750s and 1760s are thin, and eighteenth-century years are written in Latin words that no digit count sees.

what: Maria Carfora's parents are not reachable through Antenati — three routes, all shut
was: The descent of **Filomena Annecchino** from **Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora** is *inferred, not documented*. One act naming **Maria Carfora's own parents** would settle it, and Antenati's name index — which gives parents — had never been run on the Carfora.
now: **Run: 260 Carfora records at Forchia, 190 births, 59 deaths, 11 marriages.** She is in it, and **only ever as somebody's mother** — «*Maria Carfora, Figlio = Giacinta Annecchino · Agata Annecchino · Alfonso Carmine Annecchino*» — with **no birth date, no place and no parents of her own** on any row.
how: Harvesting the whole surname for the town and reading every death act in it, rather than searching for her by name.
why:
**Three routes and all three are shut, which is worth writing down so nobody walks them again.** 

**Her own birth act** is not linked, and Forchia offers too many candidates in the window — Maria Antonia 1861, Maria Filomena 1863, Maria Sabata 1863, Maria Carmina 1863, Maria Grazia 1865, Maria Francesca 1866, Maria Giovanna 1867 and 1869 — **with nothing to choose between them.** 

**Her marriage**, about 1880–82, falls **inside the Forchia gap**: Antenati's marriages there run 1809–1865, then 1931–1941, and nothing between. 

**Her death** is not in the indexed window: **all 59 Carfora death acts were read and not one has an Annecchino spouse.** 

**What the harvest gave instead** is the Carfora of Forchia as households rather than names — Carmine × Raffaela Crisci, Antonio × Maria Papa, Gabriele × Lucia Crisci, Michele × Maria Rosa Fusco, Agostino × Porzia D'Ambrosio and six more. **And two of them were born at ARIENZO and died at Forchia.** The Carfora were walking the **same corridor as the Falco**, a generation or two earlier. No kinship is claimed; **it is the road that is the point, not the blood.**

what: the processetti of Caserta do not hold generation seven's marriage either
was: **Carminantonio Falco × Filomena Annecchino's marriage** is the cleanest available test of whether she was really born at Forchia in 1897 — a marriage act states the bride's age and birthplace on a record's authority rather than a tree's. It has never been found.
now: **Collection 2043630 turns out to be THE PROCESSETTI** — «Marriage Supplement», «Marriage Proclamation», «Marriage Bann Supplement» for the Caserta comuni, **1866–1929**, with **1,503 Falco pages**.
