what: THE 1823 BIRTH REGISTER READ END TO END — one Pasqua in the year, and she is not joined to the line
was: Every search route to **Pasqua Falco**, Giovanna Arricale's mother, was closed: the index blind to her, the 1823 and 1822 *tavole* both physically obstructed, no death act in this archive's sweeps of 1816–1858. What remained was reading.
now: **Read.** Arienzo *Nati 1823*, `an_ua14420` — **110 image openings, about 107 acts, every one of them looked at**, by sweeping a narrow band across the «*il nome di …*» line of each act. **The year contains exactly one Pasqua**, at image 41: «*…nata da **GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA** sua moglie legittima, di anni **trentotto** … nel giorno **trenta** del mese di **Marzo** … alle ore dieci … il nome di **PASQUA***». Her father is **GIUSEPPE FALCO of strada Costa** — **the other Giuseppe Falco**, the household this archive spent months separating from its own. Her mother's age corroborates: thirty-two in 1816, thirty-eight in 1823. **And the margin records her marriage:** «*A 30 Dic. 1880 l'uff. dello stato civile d'Arienzo … Pasqua Falco con **Pasquale Carfora***», certified at Caserta 27 August 1881.
how: A band sweep rather than 110 separate page reads — the same trick as reading a margin column, applied to a whole volume: crop the one line that carries the child's name and grid thirty acts at a time.
why: **She is NOT joined to the line, and the temptation to join her is exactly why the rule exists.** Her birth falls inside the window Giovanna's act implies — «twenty-five» in December 1848 means born between December 1822 and December 1823, and this is 30 March 1823. She is the **only** Pasqua born at Arienzo that year. **But Arienzo holds at least three Pasqua Falco in these decades**: the wife of **Francesco Arricale** (Giovanna's mother), the wife of **Angelo Maione** (mother of a Francesco Maione b. 1857 and a Pasquale Majone b. 1864), and this one, who married **Pasquale Carfora** in 1880 with no widowhood indexed. They may be one woman marrying three times or three women; **nothing in any document joins them.** **And the stakes of guessing are high.** If this Pasqua were Giovanna's mother, then generation five's marriage of 1872 would have joined the Camellara Falco to the **strada Costa Falco** — the very household this archive built the «*which Falco?*» page to keep apart. **That is a claim worth making only on a document, and there isn't one.** **What the read did settle** is a new documented daughter for that other household, and that the 1823 register holds no other candidate. **The next year to read is 1822** — 132 acts, whose tavola is torn.

what: 1822 READ END TO END TOO — the whole age window holds exactly ONE Pasqua, and she belongs to the other Falco house
was: Reading 1823 had found a single Pasqua — **Pasqua Falco, born 30 March 1823 to Giuseppe Falco and Gelsomina Vigliotta of strada Costa** — and left the obvious question open: was there another in 1822, whose tavola is torn?
now: **There is not.** Arienzo *Nati 1822*, `an_ua14419` — **136 image openings, 132 acts, every one looked at** by the same band sweep. The volume restarts with a fresh «REGISTRO» title page at image 102, and the acts run on to 139. **Not one child in the year was named Pasqua.** **So the whole window closes on one person.** «Twenty-five» in December 1848 means born between December 1822 and December 1823. **Across both volumes — 239 acts — there is exactly one Pasqua**, and she is the daughter of the *other* Giuseppe Falco.
how: Five band sweeps per volume, about 250 leaf fetches in all, reading only the «*il nome di …*» line of each act.
why: **This narrows the question to two possibilities and resolves neither, and the archive's own evidence is what stops it resolving.** **Either** Giovanna Arricale's mother *is* that Pasqua Falco — in which case generation five's marriage of 1872 joined the **Camellara** Falco to the **strada Costa** Falco, the two houses the «which Falco?» page exists to keep apart, and the Pasqua who married Pasquale Carfora in 1880 was a widow remarrying at fifty-seven. **Or** the clerk who wrote «venticinque» in December 1848 was wrong, and she was born in some other year. **This archive has documented that these clerks guessed badly and often**: Giuseppe Falco is 32, 37, 36, 43, 42, 42 and 40 across nine years of acts; Carminantonio is forty-six in 1897 and fifty-five in 1902, nine years of ageing in five. **An age from these registers is worth about five years either way**, which puts the real window somewhere near 1818–1828 — ten volumes, not two. **Nothing is joined.** What the two reads bought is a hard fact — the window as stated contains one candidate and no other — and the honest knowledge that the window as stated is not to be trusted.

what: A NEW CHILD FOR GENERATION THREE — Angelandrea Falco, 12 September 1826, strada Camellara
was: Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci were known to have had Raffaele (1818), Luigi (1819), Pasquale (1830), Antonio (1843), and an Andrea, an Angelo, a Nunziata and a daughter known **only from their marriage acts** — no birth date among them. And no act had ever placed the couple themselves on strada Camellara with an age or a trade.
now: **Act 69 of 1826**, found through the register's own *tavola* and then read from the image: «*…è nato da **ANDREANA CRISCI**, di anni **ventotto**, domiciliata ivi **strada Camellara**, e da **VINCENZO FALCO marito della stessa**, di anni **trentadue**, di professione **contadino**, domiciliato con detta sua moglie, nel giorno **dodici** del mese di **Settembre** … alle ore ventidue, nella casa d'abitazione di detti conjugi … il nome di **ANGELANDREA***». **He is NOT joined** to the Angelo who married Maria Cimmino in 1847 or the Andrea who married Maria Carmela — this household already contains both, each known only from a marriage act, and «Angelandrea» may be either or neither.
how: The tavola trick, generalised: **the F page of a year's alphabetical index lists every Falco born that year, with both parents and the date, for the cost of one image.**
why: **The act does something the marriage acts could not: it ages the parents.** Vincenzo is **thirty-two** in September 1826, giving a birth about 1794 — his baptism is **1 February 1792**. Andreana is **twenty-eight**, giving about 1798 — her baptism is **30 November 1796**. **Both are two years out, in the same direction, in the same sentence, written by a clerk with both of them standing in front of him.** That is the tightest measurement this archive has of how these registers handle age, and it is the reason Pasqua Falco's «twenty-five» cannot be trusted to a year. **And the obstruction is mapped.** Of the nine birth volumes checked either side of 1823, the tavole for **1821, 1822, 1823 and 1824 are physically covered** by conservation sheets laid over the index during filming, while **1826, 1827 and 1828 are clear**. The blockage is a run of consecutive volumes, not the whole series — so the method holds, and the years it fails on are now named.

what: A SECOND MADDALENA — the name given again twenty-three months after the first one died
was: **Maddalena Falco**, daughter of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, was born on **7 June 1818** and died on **31 May 1825**, aged seven, a week short of her birthday — her baptism was read from the image earlier today and her death act has been held here for months. The household was thought to have seven children, ending with Giovanni in 1825.
now: **There was a second Maddalena.** The 1827 tavola records «*52. **Falco Maddalena** | Falco **Giuseppe**, e Guida d'**Antonia** | A dì **4 Maggio 1827***» — born **twenty-three months** after the first Maddalena was buried, and given her name. An **eighth child** for the household.
how: The F page of the 1827 alphabetical tavola, page VIII, reached by stepping back from the volume's closing certificate. **From the tavola, not the act** — `atto 52` itself has not been read, and the entry is marked so.
why: **This archive has now seen the practice five times in one family**: two Gioacchino (1774, 1779), two Giovanna, three Margherita and two Agostino among the di Guida, two Agata and two Alfonso and two Giacomo among the Annecchino, and now two Maddalena. **It is the single most reliable signal that a child has died** — and it works in reverse, which is the useful direction: a repeated forename in a sibling list is a reason to go looking for the first child's burial. **And it is exactly the trap the archive fell into once already**: a «new» Giovanna Falco that turned out to be a second daughter given a dead sister's name. **Here both are documented and both are kept**, which is the difference between a duplicate and a family.

what: SARA FALCO — a ninth child for generation three, born four days before Christmas 1828
was: Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci of strada Camellara were held as the parents of eleven children gathered from baptisms, marriages and burials, with **Angelandrea (12 September 1826)** the latest birth read from an act and **Pasquale (1830)** the next.
now: **SARA FALCO, born 19 December 1828 at twenty-one hours, in her parents' own house on STRADA CAMELLARA.** «*…è nata da **ANDREANA CRISPI**, di anni **ventisette** … e da **VINCENZO FALCO** marito della stessa, di anni **trentasei**, di professione **contadino** … il nome di **SARA***». Act **118**, folio **325**. **Declared the next day by the midwife** — «*GELSOMINA RUGGIERO, di anni sessanta, di professione **levatrice**, domiciliata … strada Porta di Sopra*» — with two illiterate witnesses, Pasquale Sansone (38) and Carlo Manna (57).
how: The **1828 alphabetical tavola**. The F group runs by act number — 43 Ferro, 82 Ferriello — and **ended the page**. Rendering the next leaf to confirm the letter was finished put **«118. Falco Sara | Falco Vincenzo, e Crispi Andreana»** on the first line. Then the act itself, found by sweeping the left margins of images 116–123 for the mother's name and reading atto 118 whole.
why:
**A false negative was four minutes from being published.** The working note already read «1828 holds no Falco birth» on the strength of a complete-looking F group; the group simply continued overleaf. **An alphabetical group in these tavole is not finished until the next page says so** — that is now a standing rule here. 

The child herself is recorded at **full strength, read from the image**. Two cautions travel with her. The **midwife who declared her** shares a name with the Gelsomina Ruggiero who stood *matrina* at this couple's son Raffaele's baptism in 1818, and Andreana's own mother was a Ruggiero — **no kinship is claimed**; the name is common at Arienzo and a midwife declaring a birth is the ordinary case. And the **mother's surname is written with a ligature this reader cannot separate from «Crispi»**: five other acts in this household give **Crisci**, and the household is fixed by the husband, the street and the trade, not by the spelling.

what: Giuseppe Falco aged forty on 2 April 1825 and forty-five on 6 April 1825
was: This archive has said for a week that **a stated age in these registers is an estimate**, and argued it each time by setting a death act or a declaration against a baptism — always across years, and always across two different records of two different kinds.
now: **Four days.** On **2 April 1825** Giuseppe Falco declared a neighbour's death as «*GIUSEPPE FALCO, di anni **QUARANTA**, di professione **MASSARO***». On **6 April 1825** he declared his own son's birth as «*GIUSEPPE FALCO, di anni **QUARANTACINQUE**, di professione **CONTADINO***». Same man, same street, same comune, same week — **five years apart, and a different trade**.
how: Both read from the image: Morti 1825 `an_ua14327` img 10r, and Nati 1825 `an_ua14422` atto 42, img 44r.
why: Published because it needs **no inference at all**. Every previous demonstration here depended on trusting a baptism to contradict an age; **this one is internal to four days of one year** and cannot be explained by a misread register, a namesake or a lost decade. It is the cleanest evidence the archive has that **these numbers were guessed at the desk**, and it is the reason no birth year in this archive is derived from a stated age alone.

what: Don Giovanni Falco's civil birth act — the hour, the house, and a check that stopped a false discovery
was: The deacon's baptism was read from the parish image on 14 September: **6 April 1825**, «*baptizavit infantem natum ex JOSEPHO FALCO et ANTONIA DI GUIDA*». **A baptism date, and no birth date** — the archive had never held one for him.
now: **Born 6 April 1825 at seventeen hours, in his parents' own house on STRADA CAMELLARA**, and declared by his father the same evening at twenty-one hours. Act **42**, folio **301**. The father is «*di anni **quarantacinque**, di professione **contadino***», the mother «*ANTONIA DI GUIDA sua moglie legitima, di anni **quaranta***». Witnesses **Arcangelo Giglio**, 22, *falegname* of strada Sant'Andrea, and **Domenico Papa**, 50, *contadino* of strada Camellara. **Baptised the same day he was born.**
how: Reading the **1825 birth register end to end** — the year's tavola is unusable (see the searched page) — and finding «*è comparso Giuseppe Falco*» at image 44.
why:
**This was written up as a new eighth child before it was checked, and the check is why it is not published as one.** The house rule here is that a find is tested against what the archive already holds **in the same pass that publishes it**; the pass found the deacon's baptism sitting on the same day, and the «discovery» became a confirmation. 

What it genuinely adds is the **hour and the house** — this family's births are almost never dated to an hour — and a father's **age and trade on a fixed day**, which is what made the *forty-in-four-days* contradiction visible at all. It also **closes the gap between birth and baptism to nothing**: he was carried to Sant'Andrea Apostolo the day he was born, and the parish returned the *notamento* that same 6 April.

what: A FOURTH Maria Falco — and the first Falco woman found married to a Diglio
was: Three women called Maria Falco were on the books at Arienzo and kept deliberately apart: one buried **24 July 1817**, daughter of Giuseppe Falco and Rosa Sossi and widow of Francesco Quotolo; one already dead by **February 1818**, wife of Nicola Majone; and one **living in June 1823 and April 1825**, wife of **Francesco Cossi**, who buried three children in three years with Giuseppe Falco standing for the house each time.
now: **A fourth.** On **30 May 1825**, **ALFONSO DIGLIO**, 32, *contadino* of **strada Camellara**, declared a daughter born «*da **MARIA FALCO** sua moglie legitima, di anni **trentatré***» — the child named **CLEMENTINA**, act **72**, folio **321**. Thirty-three in May 1825 gives **b. c.1792**.
how: Read from the image while sweeping the whole 1825 birth register for the surname. The reading was checked against the **«Foglio»** trap — a real Arienzo surname that this hand renders almost identically, and which has generated false Falco hits here before — by magnifying the word itself rather than trusting the sweep.
why:
**She cannot be the wife of Francesco Cossi**, who was alive that same month; a woman does not have two living husbands. So the register holds **two Maria Falco alive at Arienzo in 1825**, both attached to strada Camellara, and neither of them yet attached to a household. 

**Which Falco house she comes from is open.** Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti baptised a Maria on **30 October 1790**, which would make her thirty-four here rather than thirty-three — inside this register's proven margin, and **not enough**. What is new and solid is the **tie to the Diglio**, who until now appeared only as the Falco's neighbours and co-declarants on Camellara: Aniello Diglio stood beside Giuseppe Falco on 2 April 1825, and **Cesare Diglio witnessed this very act**. They were marrying each other, not just living alongside.

She is the daughter of **Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti**, died 25 April 1826, identified through her husband Alfonso Diglio's second wedding.

what: The deacon was Matteo Falco's GRANDSON, not his great-grandson — this archive contradicting itself in its own corrections
was: The entry of **14 September** that published Don Giovanni Falco's baptism day calls him «**the founder's great-grandson**» — and then, in the same sentence, lays out the descent that disproves it: «*Matteo Falco → Giuseppe Falco × Antonia di Guida → Giovanni*». **Three names is a grandson.** The earlier entry of 13 September had it right: «Matteo Falco's grandson».
now: **Grandson.** Matteo Falco → **Giuseppe Falco** × Antonia di Guida → **Don Giovanni Falco**, *diacono*, born 6 April 1825, died 26 November 1849.
how: Found while checking today's civil birth act against every claim the archive already makes about this man — the same pass that stopped him being published as a new child.
why:
**The earlier entry is left standing, wrong word and all**, because corrections here are shown and not swapped. 

It is worth naming what went wrong: the word was written in a sentence that also carried the correct chain, so **the error and its own refutation were published side by side and neither was read against the other**. At ten thousand pages the likeliest false statement in this archive is one of its own, made in passing, in a paragraph about something else — and it will not be found by looking for it, only by checking every new fact against everything already said about the same person.

what: GIUSEPPE NUNZIO FALCO, 25 March 1824 — a tenth child for generation three
was: Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci were held as the parents of twelve children, gathered from baptisms, marriages and burials, with **no son called Giuseppe and no son called Nunzio**. The Nunziata in the household is a daughter, known only from her marriage in 1855.
now: **GIUSEPPE NUNZIO FALCO, born 25 March 1824 at half past twenty-three hours**, in his parents' own house on **strada Camellara**. «*…è comparso **VINCENZO FALCO**, di anni **trentatré**, di professione **contadino** … che lo stesso è nato da **ANDREANA CRISPI** sua moglie legitima, di anni **ventisette** … il nome di **GIUSEPPE NUNZIO***». Act **31**, folio **139**.
how: The 1824 birth register read end to end, every opening rendered twice over — the year's tavola is covered in the filming, exactly as 1825's is.
why:
**Published as a birth and nothing more.** No later trace of him is held: he is named in no marriage act, and the 1825 death register — read out act by act the same day — does not contain him. A boy who appears once in a register and never again is the ordinary case in this family, and the archive says so rather than quietly assuming he died. 

His mother's age here is the useful thing. **Twenty-seven in March 1824 is exactly right** against her baptism of 30 November 1796 — and she is given **twenty-seven again in December 1828**, when she was thirty-two. The same number four years apart, correct the first time.

what: Two lives closed from both ends, in one volume — Clemente Falco and Giuseppa Cioffi
was: Both children were in this archive **only as deaths**. **Clemente Falco**, son of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, died 19 June 1825 «*di mesi **quindici***». **Giuseppa Cioffi**, daughter of Francesco Cioffi and Maria Falco, died 2 April 1825 «*di mesi **otto***» — the third child that house buried in three years, with **Giuseppe Falco standing for them each time**. Neither had a birth act, and neither had a date.
now:
**CLEMENTE FALCO, born 11 March 1824 at three in the night**, strada Camellara — act 26, folio 134. Fifteen months and eight days before he died: **the register's own arithmetic, to the week**. 

**GIUSEPPA COSSI, born 18 June 1824 at half past three**, strada Camellara — act 73, folio 181. Nine and a half months before she died, recorded as eight.
how: Both found in the same end-to-end read of the 1824 birth register, whose alphabetical tavola is covered in the filming.
why:
An age in months is the one number these clerks get nearly right, and both of these land where they should — which is worth recording, because **this archive has spent a week documenting how badly they guess at the ages of adults**. Giuseppe Falco is forty-eight in this very volume and forty a year later. 

Giuseppa Cioffi's act also dates a move: her family were on **strada Sant'Andrea** in June 1823 and are on **strada Camellara** by June 1824, next door to the Falco who kept declaring their dead.

what: The Arienzo death register of 1841 holds no Falco at all
was: The archive held a parish burial: «*JOANNES FALCO **filius Josephi et Antoniae di Guida**, aetatis suae annorum **24 circiter***», **27 November 1841** — a machine transcript, never checked against the image. It is the record that puts a **second Giovanni** in a household whose other Giovanni was born in April 1825.
now: **There is no civil death act for him.** All ninety acts of the Arienzo death register for 1841 have been read, every one, and **not one Falco is among the dead**. The register runs straight from act 86, a child buried 26 November, to act 87, a tailor of eighty buried 7 December. The days on either side of 27 November are accounted for.
how: ANTENATI `an_ua14343`, images 8–54, swept in four contact sheets at the band where the deceased's name and age sit, then the November acts rendered whole and read.
why:
**Published as a bounded negative so nobody reads this volume again**, and because it changes what the two-Giovanni question is about. Arienzo's civil and parish registers normally agree; a burial with no civil act is unusual enough to be evidence in itself. It now seems more likely that the 1841 transcript is **wrong, or belongs to another parish in the same filmed set**, than that this household really kept two living sons of one name. 

That cannot be settled from here: **the image behind the transcript has not been read**, and reading it needs the FamilySearch viewer.

what: Forty-four marriage indexes this archive wrote down and never opened
was: A research note recorded, in one line, that Antenati holds **44 «Matrimoni, indice» volumes for Arienzo, 1809 = `an_ua14108`, +1/year**. That line was written when the death indexes were found, and **nothing was ever read from it**. Marriages in this family were being reconstructed from death acts, which name a spouse but never a date.
now: **They are the richest finding aid in the whole Arienzo series.** Each is one to four images, and each line gives the **act number, BOTH spouses, each one's patria, BOTH sets of parents, and the date of the church wedding**. A whole year of marriages fits on two pages. Nine years have now been read and **three marriages came out of them**.
how: `python3 tools/antenati.py ids an_ua<14108 + year − 1809>`, then every image rendered at 2100px. The sort order is not stable — **1818 is by FORENAME, 1821 to 1824 by SURNAME** — so a letter has to be found before it can be searched.
why:
**This is the third time the same failure has been published here**: a source found, summarised in a note, and then treated as though the note were the source. The Nudgee graves were already in three files when they were announced as a discovery; three lines had no household while their documents sat harvested elsewhere; and now a finding aid that answers questions on the open-questions page has been sitting in a memo for a week. 

**A source is not held until something has been read out of it.** The note is not the holding.

what: Anna Falco's wedding day, and her husband's parents
was: **ANNA FALCO**, daughter of Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti, baptised 28 October 1795. The archive knew she was married because **her death act said so** — «*moglie di **ARCANGELO CRISCI***», 23 August 1820, strada Camellara — and because his two-day-old son Fortunato was buried in January of the same year. **No wedding date. No parents for him. Nothing before 1820.**
now: **Married before the church on 3 MAY 1818**, and his parents are named: «*fu **NICOLA**, e **CHIARA MAJONE***» — his father already dead. The entry gives her as «*di **PASQUALE**, e **CHIARA RIVETTI***», with no «fu» before either, which is consistent: Pasquale Falco lived until 1834.
how: The 1818 Arienzo marriage tavola, `an_ua14117` — a two-page index sorted by forename, so she is under **A** for Anna.
why:
It closes the shape of a very short life. **Baptised 1795, married at twenty-two, buried a son at twenty-four, dead three months later.** 

**One thing is deliberately left unresolved.** The index writes the groom's surname **COSSI**; the 1820 acts, also read from the image, write **CRISCI**. This archive has already recorded that the two are not reliably separable in this scribe's hand — it happened once before, over a child's burial in 1824. The identification does not depend on it: there is one Anna Falco of Pasquale and Chiara, and one Arcangelo she was married to. **The spelling is reported as found, in both places, and not reconciled.**

what: Two more grandchildren for Matteo Falco, through his daughter Angela
was: **ANGELA FALCO**, daughter of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci, married **CRESCENZO RIVETTI** — a marriage the archive knew only from **his death act** of 1 December 1816, where Giuseppe Falco and Gioacchino Falco declared him as «*parenti*». She was widowed at forty-five and died 17 October 1822. **One child was on record**: Angelandrea Rivetti, buried 12 February 1819.
now: **Two sons, both with wedding dates.** «*7. **RIVETTI GIOVANNI** ed Attarelli Mariangela | Rivetti **Crescenzo**, e **Falco Angela** | A dì **23 Xbre 1821***». And «*18. **RIVETTI PASQUALE** | Rivetti **Crescenzo**, e **Falco Angela** | A **29 Luglio 1824***», his bride Agnese Vetrone of Serfasali. **Angela Falco lived to see the first wedding and not the second** — she died ten months after Giovanni's and twenty-one months before Pasquale's.
how: The Arienzo marriage tavole for 1821 and 1824, both read from the image and both rows magnified to the word before the parents were accepted.
why:
**The founder's line had been traced almost entirely through his sons.** Angela was a name on a death act and a widow in a register; she is now a woman with a household and descendants who married into the Attarelli and the Vetrone. 

And a trap worth publishing: **the 1824 tavola holds a second Pasquale Rivetti**, act 23, son of **PAOLO** Rivetti — who was Crescenzo's brother. Two first cousins of the same name marrying in the same year, in the same town, four months apart. **Nothing but the parents' column tells them apart**, which is exactly why an index that carries both parents is worth more than one that does not.

what: The fourth Maria Falco, named — twenty-four hours after this archive said it could not name her
was: Published here **yesterday** as an open question. A **MARIA FALCO, thirty-three**, wife of **ALFONSO DIGLIO** of strada Camellara, bore a daughter on 30 May 1825. The entry said: «*Which Falco house she comes from is open … Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti baptised a Maria on 30 October 1790, which would make her thirty-four here rather than thirty-three — inside this register's proven margin, and **not enough**.*»
now: **It is her house.** «*…è morta nella sua propria casa **MARIA FALCO, d'anni TRENTADUE, MOGLIE DI ALFONSO DIGLIO**, nata in Arienzo, di professione contadina … **FIGLIA DI PASQUALE FALCO**, di professione contadino, domiciliato ivi, **E DI CHIARA RIVETTI**, domiciliata ivi*» — **25 April 1826**, at nine in the morning, act 22. She was **a daughter of generation four**, and a sister of the Anna Falco whose wedding was published this morning.
how: Not by looking for her. The **1827 marriage tavola** showed **Alfonso Diglio marrying again** — «*Diglio Cesare, e M[anna] Sara*» for parents, and a Cesare Diglio of strada Camellara had witnessed his daughter's birth. A second marriage dates a first wife's death, so the window was **30 May 1825 to 2 April 1827**; the death index for 1826 had her in it, and the act named her parents outright.
why:
**The method is the point.** She was invisible from her own side — no age fits, no baptism can be matched, and this archive holds four women of her name. She became findable through **her husband's second wedding**, which is not a record about her at all. 

Two cautions kept. **Which Maria she is remains open**: this couple baptised a Maria on 13 September 1789 and another on 30 October 1790, and the stated age of thirty-two fits neither. And the declarants are carefully **«vicino della defunta»** — neighbours. The register distinguishes that from «parente», and so does this archive.

what: A fourth child for Angela Falco, and a Falco woman at Paolisi
was: Angela Falco, the founder's daughter, had **one recorded child** yesterday morning and **three** by the evening.
now:
**Four.** «*5. **CIMMINO ANTONIO** ed **RIVETTI LUCIA** | Rivetti **Crescenzo**, e **Falco Angela** | A **7 Febrajo 1825***». **Lucia Rivetti married as an orphan** — her father dead since 1816, her mother since October 1822. 

And separately, in 1826: «*LETTIERI **LUDOVICO** | **PAOLISI** | Lettieri **Antonio**, e **FALCO GIOVANNA***». A son marrying in 1826 puts his mother's birth around **1770–1785** — the founders' generation.
how: The Arienzo marriage tavole for 1825 and 1826, read from the image.
why:
Angela Falco was a name on her husband's death act two days ago. She now has **four children, three wedding dates and two families married into** — the Attarelli, the Vetrone and the Cimmino. 

**The Giovanna Falco of Paolisi is a lead and is filed as one.** She is far too old to be either Giovanna this archive already holds — Gioacchino's daughter of 1797 or Giuseppe's of 1805 — which leaves the founders' own household as the obvious place to look and **no act yet that names her parents**. **Paolisi** went onto this archive's map only last week, on the strength of a place-name in a register; there is now a person standing in it.

what: The marriage-index arithmetic slips after 1835, and the series stops in 1849
was: The rule recorded this morning: **Arienzo marriage indexes, `an_ua14108` + (year − 1809)**, published as continuous.
now: **It holds only to 1835.** `an_ua14135` is **1837, not 1836** — so from 1837 the ark is `14107 + (year − 1809)`. **1836 is missing from the series altogether**, and `an_ua14148` returns no manifest at all. The last index is **1849** (`an_ua14147`); `an_ua14149` onward belong to a different series.
how: Resolving the label of every volume from 1825 to 1852 instead of trusting the formula past the years that had been checked.
why:
**The death indexes slip in exactly the same way, after 1834** — that was already recorded here. Two independent Arienzo series, both drifting by one volume in the mid-1830s, is not a coincidence; something was lost or re-bound from that decade in both. 

Published because an arithmetic rule that is right for twenty-six years and wrong afterwards is **more dangerous than no rule at all**: it returns a real volume for the wrong year, and every negative taken from it would be false.

what: Giovanna Falco married — half of the «two daughters» question closed
was: On the open-questions page: «*GIOVANNA and FRANCESCA MARIA LUCIA, daughters of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, are baptised and neither appears in the Arienzo death registers of 1844–1858. **They married, died before 1844, or left.***» Three possibilities and no way to choose between them.
now: **She married.** «*10. **CRISCI ANIELLO** | Crisci Crescenzo, e Quotolo Angela*» ed «***FALCO GIOVANNA** | **Falco Giuseppe, e Guida Antonia** | A **6 7bre 1829***». Baptised 1805, married at **twenty-four**, to the son of Crescenzo Crisci and Angela Quotolo.
how: The 1829 marriage tavola — a single sheet, filmed sideways, carrying the whole year's sixteen marriages. The month was settled by comparison: two rows below sits «10 **Xbre** 1829», whose X is nothing like this 7.
why:
**FRANCESCA MARIA LUCIA IS STILL OPEN.** Half a question closed is not a question closed, and the page now says so. 

What the answer adds is a pattern rather than a fact. **This is the second Falco woman to marry a Crisci in eleven years** — Anna Falco, daughter of Pasquale, in 1818, and now Giovanna, daughter of Giuseppe, in 1829. The two brides were **first cousins**. The Crisci are already the Falco's nearest neighbours on strada Camellara, already their co-declarants, and already the family a Falco widow's son was buried by. Marrying next door is what these households did.

what: Raffaela Falco married her first cousin — and the «Francesco Falco» this archive could not place is named
was: **RAFFAELA FALCO**, daughter of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, died 20 April 1854 on strada Camellara, «*moglie di **FRANCESCO FALCO***». Her household was published here yesterday with three dead children and this caveat: «*Her husband was also a Falco, which at Arienzo is common enough to **prove nothing on its own**.*»
now: **He was her first cousin.** «*8. **FALCO FRANCESCANTONIO** | **Falco Pasquale, e Rivetti Chiara***» ed «***FALCO RAFFAELA** | **Falco Giuseppe, e Guida Antonia*** | A **16 [Luglio] 1832***». **Giuseppe and Pasquale Falco were brothers**, both sons of Matteo. So their children married, and **Francescantonio is a new son for generation four** — Pasquale and Chiara had no son of that name on record.
how: The 1832 marriage tavola, both rows magnified to the word. The parents' column is what carries it; the surname alone would have proved nothing, exactly as the caveat said.
why:
**It closes a loop the archive had left open on purpose**, and it does it the way the caveat implied it would have to be done — by a record that states both parentages, not by a matching surname. 

It also changes what the three dead children are. **Carmina, Clemente and Pasqualina Falco are Matteo Falco's great-grandchildren through BOTH of his sons at once.** 

**One thing does not fit and is left showing.** Raffaela's death act makes her thirty-four in 1854, so born about 1820 — which would have her marrying at twelve. Both figures are read from the image and they cannot both be right. Her brother Crescenzo's marriage carries a papal dispensation «*super quarto gradu consanguinitatis*», so cousin-marriage in this house is documented; a bride of twelve is not, and the birth year is the likelier error.

what: Michelangelo Falco joined to generation four — and a «parente» from 1831 explained
was: Two households in this archive carried the same man and neither had a father for him: «**Michelangelo Falco (strada Camellara)**» and «**Michelangelo Falco & Mariantonia Vigliotta**», known only from the burials of **two daughters both called Anna** — one at thirteen months in 1831, one at eight days in 1834. The 1831 act records that **VINCENZO FALCO, 38, declared the death «come PARENTE della defunta»**, and the archive noted the word without being able to explain it.
now: **He is Pasquale Falco's son.** «*10. **FALCO MICHELANGELO** | Arienzo | **FALCO PASQUALE, e RIVETTI CHIARA***» ed «***VIGLIOTTI ANTONIA** | **Vigliotti Francesco, e Repetelli Vittoria***», married **December 1828** — the day is behind the fold shadow, the month is not. So **Michelangelo was Vincenzo Falco's brother**, and Vincenzo was standing for his niece.
how: The 1828 marriage tavola. The household was never searched for; it surfaced because every line of the year was read.
why:
**A relationship word this archive recorded three years ago is now a relationship.** «Parente» has been treated here as evidence of kinship without degree — deliberately, because the registers use it loosely — and this is the first time an independent record has come back and said which kinship it was. 

It also gives **Mariantonia Vigliotta her parents**, and adds a household of generation four that had been sitting unattached in the middle of strada Camellara the whole time. The marriage index writes her **Antonia Vigliotti** where the death acts write **Mariantonia Vigliotta**; both are kept.

what: A second Matteo Falco — the founder's name given again, twenty-five years on
was: Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida baptised a **Mattheus** in **1807**, named for his grandfather the founder. **He died on 28 August 1809.** No later Matteo was on record in this house.
now: **There was another.** «*3. **FALCO MATTEO** | Arienzo | **FALCO GIUSEPPE, e GUIDA ANTONIA** | A **24 Gennajo 1834***», married **CRISCI ALESSANDRA**. A **ninth child** for the household.
how: The 1834 marriage tavola, the row magnified to the word.
why:
**The second necronym in one household, and the sixth in this family.** Maddalena was given again in 1827 after the first Maddalena died in 1825; Matteo is given again after 1809. The pattern that has repeatedly warned this archive against merging two children of one name has now also **found** one. 

**A likely link is left unproven.** The bride's mother is written «[Quo]tolo Angela», and **Aniello Crisci — who married this man's sister Giovanna five years earlier** — was son of «Crisci Crescenzo, e Quotolo Angela». Brother and sister marrying brother and sister is exactly what these households did. But **the father's forename here is lost to the fold shadow**, and Angela Quotolo is not a rare name at Arienzo, so it is filed as a resemblance and not a fact.

what: Both daughters married. The question is closed, and it was always one answer
was: «*What became of **TWO daughters**?*» — **GIOVANNA** (b. 1805) and **FRANCESCA MARIA LUCIA** (b. 1812), daughters of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, absent from fifteen years of death registers. «*They married, died before 1844, or left.*» Giovanna was answered this morning; Francesca was still open at lunchtime.
now:
**«*1. **CRISCI RAFFAELE** | Arienzo | Crisci Giuseppe, e [Quo]tola Paola*» ed «***FALCO FRANCESCA** | Idem | **Falco Giuseppe, [Gui]da Antonia** | A **5 GENNAJO 1839***».** Baptised 1812, married at **twenty-six**. 

Both daughters married. **Both married Crisci.**
how: The 1839 marriage tavola — the very first entry of the year, act 1, found on the first page read.
why:
**The answer was never «what happened to them» but «who did this house marry».** Three of Giuseppe Falco's children married into the Crisci: Giovanna to Aniello in 1829, Matteo to Alessandra in 1834, Francesca to Raffaele in 1839. Add Anna Falco, his niece, in 1818, and that is **four Falco–Crisci marriages in twenty-one years**. 

The Crisci are the family this archive already knew as the Falco's neighbours on strada Camellara, their co-declarants, and the household that buried a Falco child. They were also, repeatedly, the family the Falco married. **Two households on one street, tied four times in a generation** — and every one of those ties was invisible until the marriage indexes were opened this week. 

The index writes her simply **FRANCESCA**; her baptism names her **Francesca Maria Lucia**, and there is no second Francesca in the household.

what: Angelandrea Falco, born 1826, is the man who married Maria Cimmino — a refusal lifted
was: When **Angelandrea Falco's birth act of 12 September 1826** was published, the archive refused to join him to anyone: «*NOT JOINED to the **ANGELO** Falco who married Maria Cimmino in 1847 or the **ANDREA** Falco who married Maria Carmela — this household already contains both, each known only from a marriage act, and «Angelandrea» may be **either or neither**.*»
now: «*3. **FALCO ANGELANDREA** | Arienzo | **Falco Vincenzo, e Crisci Andreana***» ed «***CIMMINO MARIA** | Cimmino Alessandro, e Solli [Rosa]*». **The civil index writes the exact name of the birth act**, with the same parents and the same bride. **Angelo of the parish act and Angelandrea of the birth act are one man**, married at twenty.
how: The 1847 marriage tavola, act 3 — the first page of the year.
why:
**The refusal was right and lifting it is right, and both for the same reason.** In 1826 there was no record that connected the names; the parish act said Angelo, the birth act said Angelandrea, and joining them would have been a guess. A second, independent register now uses the birth act's name for the bridegroom, and the guess becomes a reading. 

**Only half the ambiguity is gone.** The **ANDREA Falco** who married Maria Carmela, daughter of Onofrio and Angela Imbimbo, is still a separate son and still joined to nothing. 

And a discrepancy is left standing: this tavola gives the church wedding as **24 March 1847**, the parish record held here gives **17 April 1847**. Both are recorded. The archive has seen civil and parish disagree about a wedding day before — four days apart, in 1844 — and does not choose between them.

what: Every marriage in two households, dated — and the Angelo/Andrea/Angelandrea tangle undone
was: **Vincenzo Falco's sons** were a knot the archive refused to cut: an **ANGELO** who married Maria Cimmino, an **ANDREA** who married a Maria Carmela with no surname, and an **ANGELANDREA** born 12 September 1826 who «*may be either or neither*». **Crescenzo Falco's** marriage was dated «*c. 1831–46*» — a fourteen-year window, derived entirely from the fact that the dispensation naming «*Papa nostro **GREGORIO***» must mean Gregory XVI.
now:
**ANDREA FALCO married MARIA CARMELA BUONO on 24 MAY 1846** — her surname supplied for the first time — and **ANGELANDREA married MARIA CIMMINO in MARCH 1847**. Two men, two years, two wives. The tangle is undone. 

**CRESCENZO FALCO married ANGELA MARIA MORGILLO on 3 FEBRUARY 1845**, her father Gennaro Morgillo. Fourteen years to a day.
how: The 1845 and 1846 marriage tavole, each row magnified before it was accepted.
why:
**Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida now have a dated wedding for every child who married**: Giovanna 1829, Raffaela 1832, Matteo 1834, Francesca 1839, Crescenzo 1845 — and Don Giovanni, who took orders and did not. A household reconstructed entirely from burials three weeks ago now has a marriage calendar. 

One thing this does **not** explain. Crescenzo's dispensation was for the **fourth degree of consanguinity** — he and Angela Maria Morgillo were related closely enough to need Rome's permission — and **no Falco–Morgillo link has been traced**. The archive holds two Angelo Morgillo, the Monticello brothers and the San Gaetano brothers, and none of them yet connects. **A dispensation is a statement that a kinship exists. It is not a statement of what it was.**

what: Angela Falco had five children, and the Falco married the Crisci five times
was: **Angela Falco**, the founder's daughter, had **one recorded child** yesterday morning — Angelandrea Rivetti, buried in 1819 — and her marriage to Crescenzo Rivetti was known only from **his death act**.
now:
**Five children, four of them with wedding dates.** **Angela Maria** married Clemente Cossi on **26 November 1816**; **Giovanni** on 23 December 1821; **Pasquale** on 29 July 1824; **Lucia** on 7 February 1825; and **Angelandrea** died in 1819. 

Angela Maria's date is the one that tells you something. **Her father died on 1 December 1816 — five days after her wedding.**
how: The Arienzo marriage tavole for 1816, 1821, 1824 and 1825, each row magnified before the parents were accepted.
why:
**Crescenzo Rivetti's death act is the document this archive has leaned on hardest in this corner** — it names the marriage, and it records Giuseppe Falco and Gioacchino Falco declaring him as «*parenti*», which is how Angela was placed in the founder's family at all. It now also has a date five days after a wedding in the same house. 

And the wider count. **The Falco of strada Camellara married the Crisci five times**: Margarita Falco, born about 1776, married Domenico Crisci — the earliest, and she had sat in this archive among the twelve people with **no parent, no spouse, no child and no sibling attached**, until her son Angelo's wedding of 29 November 1819 surfaced. Then Anna in 1818, Giovanna in 1829, Matteo in 1834, Francesca in 1839. **Five ties across two generations, between two households on one street** — and every single one of them was invisible until the marriage indexes were opened this week.

what: Maria Falco's wedding day, 1813 — the marriage the sweep was looking for
was: Yesterday's coverage note named the two marriages the marriage-index sweep had **not** found and said where they had to be: «*MARIA FALCO (b. 1789 or 1790) to **ALFONSO DIGLIO** … Neither appears anywhere in 1816–1849, which is read*», so both were expected in **1809–1815**.
now: **«*13. **ALFONSO DIGLIO** | Arienzo | Di **CESARE, ed ANNA MANNA*** » ed «***MAGGIA FALCO** | Arienzo | Di **PASQUALE, e CHIARA RIVETTI*** | A **19 9bre 1813***».** She married at twenty-three or twenty-four, bore Clementina in May 1825, and died eleven months after that.
how: The 1813 tavola, filmed sideways — rotated, then the row magnified twice, once for the names and once for the month glyph, which is a **9** and not the **X** that appears two rows below it.
why:
**A prediction the archive published, and then met.** The coverage note was written to be falsifiable — it said which two records were missing and which seven years had to contain them — and one of the two turned up in the first of those years read. 

**Her given name is written «MAGGIA».** Everywhere else, including her own death act, she is **MARIA**. The identification does not depend on it: one Alfonso Diglio son of Cesare, one wife, one pair of parents, and a death act that repeats all three. **The spelling is reported as found and not reconciled** — the same treatment as Cossi and Crisci.

what: Alfonso Diglio's mother was ANNA Manna, not Sara
was: Published here **yesterday**, from the 1827 tavola recording Alfonso Diglio's second marriage: «*DIGLIO CESARE, e **M[anna] SARA***». The forename was given with brackets round the surname because the hand was tight, but **Sara was read plainly and stated plainly**.
now: **ANNA MANNA.** The 1813 entry for his **first** marriage reads «*Di **CESARE**, ed **ANNA MANNA***» in a markedly clearer hand, twelve years closer to the event.
how: Found by carrying on with the sweep, not by rechecking: the 1813 row named the same father and a different mother, and two readings of one woman cannot both stand.
why:
**The wrong reading came from the harder image, and it was published without saying so.** The 1827 entry sits in a fold shadow; the 1813 entry does not. The archive's own rule is to settle a disputed letter against a control in the same hand, and no control was sought here because the word did not look disputed. 

It is a forename in a household not of this line, and it changes nothing else. **It is corrected in public anyway**, because a reader who finds Sara in one entry and Anna in another deserves to be told which one this archive stands behind and why.

what: A fourth Falco stock at Arienzo — Sebastiano Falco and Colomba Montefusco
was: This archive distinguishes **three** Falco stocks: the *contadini* of **strada Camellara** who are this line; the gentry house of **Don Francesco Falco and Donna Maddalena Stellato**, with a nun and a priest in it; and the soap-makers of **San Felice a Cancello**. Its standing position is that **the surname identifies nobody**.
now: **A fourth.** «*8. **LUIGI FALCO** | Arienzo | Di **SEBASTIANO, e COLOMBA MONTEFUSCO***» ed «***GIUSTINA PETRILLO** | Fu Sabatino, e Brigida Cossi*», married **1815**. **Neither Sebastiano Falco nor Colomba Montefusco appears anywhere in this archive** — not in the households, not in the register, not among the 549 people.
how: The 1815 marriage tavola, read while looking for something else entirely.
why:
**Published because the archive's position costs something to hold.** Saying «the surname identifies nobody» is easy when the other Falco are safely elsewhere; it is worth more when a fourth household turns up in the same parish, in the same decade, with a son marrying a local woman. 

And a trap avoided by arithmetic alone: **the Luigi Falco of strada Camellara was baptised in December 1819** to Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci. He was four years from being born when this Luigi married. The names match perfectly and the men cannot be the same.

what: Generation three married on 15 October 1814 — and a daughter found yesterday was named for her grandmother
was: **VINCENZO FALCO and ANDREANA CRISCI** are the couple this whole line descends through, and the households file has carried **an em-dash in the date column** for their marriage since the archive began. The parish act names the parties and no day: «*Vincentium Falco **filium Paschalis, e Clarae Rivetta**, e Andreanam Crisci **filiam Arcangeli, e [Rosae] Ruggiero***» — the bride's mother in **brackets**, this archive's mark for a reading it does not trust.
now: **«*16. **VINCENZO FALCO**, ed | Arienzo | **Pasquale, e Chiara Rivetti** | A **15 OTTOBRE 1814***» ed «***ANDREANA CRISCI** | Arienzo | **Arcangelo, e SARA RUGGIERO***».** He was **twenty-two**, baptised 1 February 1792; she was **seventeen**, baptised 30 November 1796. And her mother is **SARA**, not Rosa.
how: The 1814 marriage tavola, reached on the last unread block of the series. The row was magnified twice — once for the groom's line and the date, once for the bride's parents.
why:
**The forename is the part that pays.** Yesterday this archive published a new daughter for this couple: **SARA FALCO, born 19 December 1828** — the only Sara in the household, found in a tavola whose F group ran across a page break. She was named **for her mother's mother**, and neither fact could be seen without the other. 

It also sharpens a caution rather than removing it. The midwife who declared Sara's birth was **GELSOMINA RUGGIERO, sixty**, and a Gelsomina Ruggiero stood *matrina* at this couple's son Raffaele's baptism in 1818. With Andreana's mother now firmly a **Ruggiero**, a kinship is **more likely than it was**. It is still not claimed, and it will not be until an act says so.

what: Read the tavola's own heading, not the catalogue label
was: Every year in this sweep has been addressed by **arithmetic on the ark** and trusted on **Antenati's catalogue label** — «*Arienzo > 1814*» and so on.
now: **The volume catalogued 1814 contains a tavola headed «*nell'Anno 1812*» on one leaf and a 1814 tavola on the next**, with the left-hand page of the opening a blank printed **1813** form. Three years in three leaves of one volume.
how: Noticed only because the dates in the entries disagreed with the folder the file had been saved into.
why:
**Every tavola states its own year in its heading, and that is the only figure worth trusting.** The ark arithmetic already failed once in this series — `an_ua14135` is 1837, not 1836 — and the death indexes slip the same way after 1834. This is the third instance and the first where the mismatch is *inside a single volume*. 

**A negative taken from the label rather than the heading is worthless**: it would say «no Falco married in 1814» on the strength of a page about 1812. Every year reported as read on the searched page was checked against its own heading before it was written down.

superseded.what: WITHDRAWN — the 1814 volume does NOT mix three years. That was my misreading of a single digit
superseded.note: **The instance was invented.** The heading reads **1814 on both leaves**; a 4 was read as a 2, and the general rule was then built on top of the misreading. **The advice survives and the evidence for it does not** — the ark arithmetic really does slip at `an_ua14135` and the death indexes after 1834, so the rule stands on two real instances, not three.

what: WITHDRAWN — the 1814 volume does NOT mix three years. That was my misreading of a single digit
was: Published here **earlier today**, as a method note: «*The volume catalogued 1814 contains a tavola headed «nell'Anno **1812**» on one leaf and a 1814 tavola on the next … **Three years in three leaves of one volume**.*» It was offered as the third proof that Antenati's catalogue labels cannot be trusted.
now: **It is 1814 on both leaves.** Magnified, the heading reads «*Tavola Annuale Alfabetica de Matrimonj celebrati in questo Comune di Corpo d'Arienzo nell'Anno **1814***» — and the entry dates with it. **I read a 4 as a 2**, in the heading and in every date under it, and then built a general rule on top of the mistake. The only genuinely 1813 thing in the volume is a **blank pre-printed form** on the facing page, which is leftover stationery and not a tavola at all.
how: By doing the thing the withdrawn note recommended: going back and magnifying the tavola's own heading, instead of trusting a glance at a low-resolution page.
why:
**The advice was right and the evidence for it was invented.** «Read the tavola's own heading» remains the correct rule — the ark arithmetic really does slip at `an_ua14135`, and the death indexes really do slip after 1834. But those two are real and this third one was not, and **a rule supported by a fake instance is worse than a rule with two**, because the next reader cannot tell which of the three to check. 

The error has a shape this archive has recorded before and did not avoid: **a conclusion drawn from the harder image, published before the easy confirmation was done.** That is the same failure as «Manna Sara» this morning, twice in one day. The fix is not more care in general; it is a specific rule — **when a reading founds a general claim, magnify it first**, every time, no exceptions.

what: The Arienzo marriage indexes are finished — 1809 to 1849, forty volumes, and what the last negative means
was: A week ago these forty volumes existed in this archive as **one line in a research note**. Three days ago the first one was opened. The sweep has been chasing, among other things, the marriage of the **MARIA FALCO who was twenty-five in June 1824** and whose husband was **FRANCESCO COSSI**.
now:
**Every year from 1809 to 1849 has been read** — each one checked against **its own tavola heading**, not the catalogue label, and each one carried to its closing certificate where the register states the year's total. **1836 does not exist in the series.** 

**Maria Falco's marriage to Francesco Cossi is not in any of them.**
how: 116 images. The early years are sorted by FORENAME, the 1820s and 1830s by SURNAME, and 1829 and 1813 were filmed sideways and had to be rotated before they could be read at all.
why:
**The negative has one likely explanation and it is not a gap in the reading.** Their son Giuseppe Cossi died in March 1824 aged five, so the marriage is no later than about 1819 — and every year from 1809 to 1819 is now read out. But **the Arienzo civil registers begin in 1809**. If they married in 1808 or earlier there is no civil act to find, and **no index will ever hold them**. 

Her stated age argues against it — twenty-five in 1824 makes her ten in 1809 — but this archive has spent two weeks documenting that these ages are invented at the desk, including a man aged **forty-eight, then forty, then forty-five in thirteen months**. An age that is wrong by eight years would put this marriage comfortably before the registers existed. 

**So the next instrument is the parish marriage register, not another index.** That is where a pre-1809 marriage survives, and it is the same register that still holds Matteo Falco's own wedding, somewhere in the 1760s.

superseded.what: WITHDRAWN — «Giuseppa COSSI». The surname is CIOFFI, and this archive had already corrected it
superseded.note: **The forty volumes were read against a surname this archive had already retired.** The husband of the Maria Falco of strada Camellara is **FRANCESCO CIOFFI**, not Cossi — corrected months ago, re-broken, and re-corrected the same day this negative was published. **So «not in any of them» is a fact about a name, not about a marriage**, and the whole argument that follows, that the couple married before the civil registers began, rests on it. **The indexes must be re-read for Falco × CIOFFI before any of this can stand.**

what: The 1841 burial read from the image — the transcript was right, and the two Giovanni are real
was: Yesterday this archive published that **Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida appear to have had two sons named Giovanni**, and said the likelier explanation was that **the 1841 record was wrong**: «*it is now more likely that the 1841 transcript is wrong, or belongs to another parish in the same filmed set, than that this household really kept two living sons of one name.*» The act had never been read — only a machine transcript of it.
now:
**The transcript was right.** «*Anno Domini **1841** die vero **27. Novembris** obiit **JOANNES FALCO filius JOSEPHI et ANTONIAE DI GUIDA**, aetate sua **annorum 24 circiter**, omnibus Sacramentis munitus et in commendatione animae adjutus, cujus cadaver **in Sodalitate S. Mariae Gratiarum** jacet*», the margin reading **Giovanni Falco**. 

So he was born about **1817**, and he cannot be **Don Giovanni Falco the deacon**, whose birth on 6 April 1825 is fixed by **two** independent registers and who died in 1849. **The household had two living sons of one name for sixteen years.**
how: The FamilySearch image viewer, reached by composing the DeepZoom tiles directly and reading them out of the page — the pane could not be displayed for a screenshot, so the rendered image was carried back as data and decoded locally.
why:
**The archive guessed, said so, and was wrong.** The guess was reasonable — Arienzo's civil and parish registers normally agree, and **there is still no civil act for this death**, which remains genuinely odd. But it was a guess made to avoid an uncomfortable conclusion, and the uncomfortable conclusion is what the act says. 

**The necronym rule does not cover this.** Everywhere else in this family a name returns only after the first child carrying it has died — two Maddalena, two Pasquale, two Raffaele, two Matteo. Here the elder Giovanni was **alive and eight years old** when his brother was christened Giovanni. 

One more detail worth keeping: he died **«omnibus Sacramentis munitus»**, which this register does not say of everyone, and he lies in the **Confraternity of Santa Maria delle Grazie** — the same place recorded for the «*Francisca Crisci, vidua […] Falco*» of 1805 whose identity is still an open question. Two burials, one named place. **Not offered as kinship**; a confraternity buried many families.

what: WITHDRAWN — «Giuseppa COSSI». The surname is CIOFFI, and this archive had already corrected it
was: Published here **this morning**: «*GIUSEPPA COSSI, born 18 June 1824 … to **FRANCESCO COSSI**, 27, contadino of strada Camellara*», read from the 1824 birth act.
now:
**CIOFFI.** Re-rendered at four times magnification, the word after «Francesco» carries **a dot over the letter after the C** and its double letter is an **ff ligature**, not «ss». 

And this archive **had already made this exact correction**, months of work ago, and left it standing in its own household file: «*This archive carried this household as «Francesco COSSI & Maria Falco» from 1823 to 1828. **It is CIOFFI.** The 1825 register, read at full resolution, writes the strada Camellara family with a dotted «i» after the C … and writes the strada Cossi family, in the same volume and the same hand, without one. **Two different families, distinguished by the clerk and conflated by this archive.***»
how: Found not by rechecking the act but by working through the eight people whose parent lists have more than two entries. Four of those eight are this household's children, and their **third parent is the correction row itself**.
why:
**I walked back into a conflation this archive had already climbed out of, using the very letter the correction warns about.** 

The mechanism matters more than the mistake. This archive keeps its reconstructed families in **two files that have drifted apart** — `data/households.tsv`, where the work of the last two days was written, and `site/src/data/households.json`, which is what the site is actually built from. **The correction lives in the JSON. The TSV still carries the retired reading «Francesco Cossi & Maria Falco» as a live household name.** I worked in the TSV, trusted the label, and re-published a retracted claim within hours of it being reaffirmed elsewhere on this site. 

A correction that is only recorded in the file nobody edits is not a correction. It is a note.

what: The eight people with more than two parents, worked one by one
was: `/bloodline` reported **eight people carrying more than two parents** and drew those lines fainter rather than choosing between them. **Pasquale Falco had five**: Agostino Falcone and Elisabetta Sabina from the tree, Andreana Crisci and Vincenzo Falco from the registers, and Matteo Falco from the line. The page called them «competing claims from three kinds of source».
now:
**They were four different conditions, and only two were disagreements at all.**

**1–4. The four children of Francesco Cioffi and Maria Falco.** The third parent is **this archive's own correction row**, kept visible on purpose: the house was carried as «Francesco COSSI» from 1823 to 1828 and was corrected to **CIOFFI**. Both readings are deliberately retained. **Nothing to retire — the graph was reading a correction as a rival claim.**

**5. Pasquale Falco — a real error, now fixed.** Generation two's Pasquale, who died on 1 October 1834 **aged seventy-four** as Chiara Rivetti's husband, had been merged with **two great-grandsons of the same name**: the infant baptised 24 March 1830 who died at three in 1833, and the second infant who lived ten days in December 1834. The merge gave a man of seventy-four a baptism of 1830, two deaths that were not his, and **VINCENZO FALCO — his own son — as his father.** The three child rows are now named apart. 

**6–7. Antonio and Raffaele Falco.** Their four parents were **one couple under two slugs**, tree and register, which the builder had **refused to merge** — Vincenzo because merging him «*would make someone their own ancestor*», which was true, and which was a symptom of the Pasquale error above. With Pasquale split, **Vincenzo merges** and the false note on Raffaele's father is gone. Andreana stays doubled: **there are two Andreana Crisci in the tree** and the archive will not merge on a name alone.

**8. Vincenzo Morgillo.** Three parents from two houses. **Gaetana Laudato is not his mother** — she was born about 1738 and he about 1799, and she is in that household as Simone Morgillo's widow, three generations up. The rest is a homonym: a second Vincenzo Morgillo is a child of Giuseppe Morgillo and Gelsomina Rivetti. **Not retired, because nothing yet says which Vincenzo is which.**
how: Reading the person-graph builder's own log rather than only its output. It had been saying so all along: «*1 REFUSED: vincenzo falco (would make someone their own ancestor)*» and «*merges refused (same name, no date agreement): 8*».
why:
**Most of what looked like conflicting evidence was the archive's safety machinery working.** The builder refuses to merge two people on a matching name, refuses a merge that would close an ancestry loop, and marks a superseded tree claim instead of hiding it. Every one of those refusals appears downstream as «more than two parents», and a page that counts parents cannot tell a refusal from a disagreement. 

**One real error was hiding inside all that noise**, and it was upstream of three of the eight: an eighteenth-century man wearing his great-grandsons' baptism and burials. 

**What is still wrong and is left showing: there is no generation three.** `line.json` names it — Vincenzo Falco — but no person record carries it, because the line file spells his wife «*Adriana (Andreana) Crisci*» and the matcher requires the spouse to agree with the household, which says «Andreana Crisci». Until that is reconciled, every note generated about generation four's parentage will say the archive identifies generation three as «someone else». **That is a wrong sentence on a live page and it is not mine to quietly rewrite.**

what: The contested parents now carry their verdict on the record, not only in prose
was: The chart at `/bloodline` could say only **that** eight people's parents disagree, and how many kinds of source were involved. It could not say **which** claim this archive stands behind, because the reasoning lived in prose and the edges themselves carried nothing.
now:
**Every contested edge carries a verdict and a reason**, written in `site/src/data/parent-verdicts.json` and applied by the person-graph builder. Three kinds: **retired** for a claim disproved or superseded, **same-as** for a second record of someone already listed and deliberately unmerged, and silence for an accepted parent. **All eight people are now down to two accepted parents or fewer.**

**Two claims were disproved outright today, both on Vincenzo Morgillo.** **GAETANA LAUDATO** was «*di anni settantotto*» at her death in March 1816, so born about **1738**, and she stands in that house as **Simone Morgillo's widow** — a generation above its head. Vincenzo was twenty-nine in May 1828, born about **1799**. She was sixty-one at his birth and is not his mother. **GIUSEPPE MORGILLO** is the father of a **different Vincenzo Morgillo — an infant of FOUR DAYS who died on 25 January 1816 in strada Salvatorella**. This one lived in strada Cappuccini and declared two deaths at the Capuchin monastery in the 1820s. Merged on the forename alone.
how: Following the reading offered on the chart: that the repeated third parent across four Cossi siblings, and the same shape on Vincenzo Morgillo, looked like **one systematic error rather than several** — and the suggestion to check whether the extra parent was a godparent, a witness or a second marriage misread. For the Morgillo it was none of those: **it was a dead infant of the same name.**
why:
**The archive was already right about most of this and simply could not say so.** The Cossi third parent is a correction it published itself; the doubled Andreana is a merge it refuses on principle; the Falcone pair is an ancestor it examined and dropped. Only Vincenzo Morgillo held real errors, and both were the same kind — **a name doing the work that a date and a street should do.** 

**The merges are still not made.** «Andrea / Andreana Crisci» and «Andreana Crisci» are marked as one woman under two spellings and left as two records, because there are **two Andreana Crisci in the tree** and no date yet separates them. That is a judgement for whoever next reads the register, and the record now says so in those words instead of leaving the chart to guess.

what: Alfonso Diglio's second wife was ANNA MARIA CRISCI, not Cossi — found by auditing my own week
was: Published here yesterday, from the 1827 marriage tavola: Alfonso Diglio «*married again on 2 April 1827 to **ANNA MARIA COSSI**, daughter of Salvatore Cossi*». That remarriage is what dated the death of his first wife, Maria Falco, and so it is load-bearing.
now: **CRISCI.** At eight times magnification the word is **C–r–i–sc–i**: a narrow **r** after the C and a **dotted i**, with no round «o». Set beside the 1818 entry for Arcangelo **Cossi**, magnified the same way, the difference is plain — that one is C–**o**–ss–i, a round letter with no dot.
how: Not by rechecking this entry, but by **auditing every surname I read in this hand over the past two days** after re-breaking the Cioffi correction earlier today. Three readings were in the ambiguous class. One was already wrong and fixed this morning, one was confirmed right, and this is the third.
why:
**The audit was worth running and I should have run it unprompted.** Three readings, two errors, and the third only confirmed because it was tested rather than assumed. 

**The date does not move.** Alfonso Diglio still remarried on 2 April 1827, which still puts Maria Falco's death before it, and her death act of 25 April 1826 still names her parents outright. What changes is the bride's family, and with it any future attempt to trace her. 

The deeper point is that this parish hand carries **three surnames that collapse into one shape** — COSSI, CRISCI and CIOFFI — and this archive has now been caught by all three in a single week. The test that separates them is not judgement, it is magnification: **the dot after the C, the round o, the r.** That is now the standing rule for this hand.

what: Two days of findings reach the site — the household files are one file again
was:
This archive kept its reconstructed families in **two files that had drifted apart**: `data/households.tsv`, which its own README and research notes call the family file, and `site/src/data/households.json`, **which is what the site is actually built from**. Nothing synced them. The TSV held **66 households**, the JSON **53**, and they differed in both directions — **12 households existed only in the JSON, 25 only in the TSV**. 

So **Sara Falco, Giuseppe Nunzio Falco, Clementina Diglio, Giuseppa Cioffi, the Angelandrea join, Maria Falco's identification, five children for Angela Falco and generation three's own wedding day were described in the corrections log and were not in the archive's data at all.**
now:
**Merged, additively — nothing in either file was deleted.** `households.json` goes from 53 households and 209 members to **77 and 337**. The person graph goes from **549 people to 626**, and the site from **10,147 pages to 10,284**. 

**And `npm run check` now refuses a release whose TSV is ahead of the JSON**, naming the rows that would not reach the site.
how: A dry run first, printing exactly what would be added and confirming nothing would be removed; then the merge; then the gates. The merge itself **introduced three duplicates** — one Chiara Rivetti under two spellings, two Pasquale Falco rows that had already been split apart earlier today — because the de-duplication keyed on the exact person string. Found by comparing every added name against the existing names in the same household, and repaired.
why:
**This is the failure that produced all the others this week.** A retracted reading survived in the TSV as a live household name, and I read it, trusted it and **republished a correction the archive had already made** — the Cioffi household, twice in one day. 

The general shape is worth naming: **an archive that keeps its working file and its published file apart will, given time, publish from whichever one is stale.** The corrections log said the right thing the whole time; the data said nothing at all. 

The guard is the durable part. A note describing this problem would have been read by nobody; a check that fails the build will be read by whoever next writes a row.

what: Generation three exists again — one bracket was hiding it
was: **No person in this archive carried generation three.** The line file names it — **VINCENZO FALCO** — and the person graph never bound the two, so the direct line ran 1, 2, **—**, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The consequence was live on the site: every note generated about generation four's parentage read «*This archive does not [make Vincenzo Falco a parent of generation 4]: it identifies generation 3 as **someone else***» — **a sentence that was not true, about the man the whole line descends through.**
now:
**All nine generations are assigned.** The matcher requires the ancestor's name AND the spouse's to agree. `line.json` spells her «*Adriana **(Andreana)** Crisci*»; every act spells her **ANDREANA CRISCI**; and the archive's own name-cleaning routine **strips brackets before the comparison**, so the file's only surviving form was «Adriana Crisci» and the two never met. 

The name-variant helper now reads the **unclean** name and emits the bracketed alternative as well — the same thing it already did for slashes, «*Andrea / Andreana Crisci*». **No «someone else» note survives, and no one in the archive has more than two accepted parents.**
how: By instrumenting the matcher rather than reasoning about it. The first fix was written in the right place and did nothing, because the function's second line had already thrown the brackets away — the test only found that out when the debug line printed `gen_of= None` beside a name that matched.
why:
**A punctuation mark between two spellings of one woman's forename cost this archive a generation of its own direct line**, and the visible symptom was a page confidently denying a parentage it asserts everywhere else. 

The fix is small and the lesson is not: this file cleans names to keep old URLs alive, and that same cleaning silently governs whether two records can ever be recognised as one. **Anything that normalises a name for one purpose will be used for another.** 

Two smaller things fell out of the same pass. **Three «people» who were couples** — rows where a marriage was recorded against «Vincenzo Falco & Andreana Crisci» as though that were a person — are re-attributed to the husband. And the builder's refusal to merge **Pasquale Rivetti** with his own grandfather of the same name is left standing: that refusal is the protection, and both men keep their own record.

what: The two Andreana Crisci are separated — and the deacon gets his own death back
was: The family tree holds **two women called Andreana Crisci**, and the person graph refused to merge either with the registers' Andreana, because **this archive does not merge two records on a matching name**. Her page was drawn twice, and both Antonio and Raffaele Falco listed her twice over.
now:
**Separated by husband, and the right one merged.** Tree `4512467` — «*Andrea / Andreana Crisci (Falco)*» — is married to **VINCENZO FALCO**, and its own note carries her baptism: «*baptised ADRIANA, 30 November 1796, daughter of **Arcangelo Crisci and Sara Ruggiero***». That is the reading the **1814 marriage index** gave independently yesterday. Tree `4512381` is married to a different man, **Gioacchino / Guglielmo Falco**, and stays a separate woman. 

The merge was not forced: it fell out of fixing generation three. The builder already held a rule for exactly this — «*the couple chooses*» — and it had never been able to run, because it depends on the same bracket-blind name comparison. **Merges refused fall from eight to five; merged-from-both rises from ten to twenty-nine.**
how: Reading the two tree records side by side and separating them on the husband, then rebuilding — at which point the archive's own dormant rule did the work.
why:
**Three more duplicates fell out of the same pass, and one of them was hiding a man's death.** 

**LUIGI FALCO** was two records in one household — a baptism of December 1819 under «Luigi (Aloysius) Falco» and a death of 16 December 1864 under «Luigi Falco». One man, forty-five years, two people. 

Worse: **the burial of 27 November 1841 was sitting on DON GIOVANNI THE DEACON'S record.** The old machine-transcript row was still filed under the plain name, so the elder brother's death and the deacon's birth of 6 April 1825 were on one page — the exact conflation this archive spent yesterday proving false. Re-attributed. 

And the deacon's **own** death act — read from the image on 13 September, «*DON GIOVANNI FALCO … di professione DIACONO*», 26 November 1849 — **was in the corrections log and in no data file at all.** It is in the household now. Its declarants are **Gennaro and Francesco Cioffi** of strada Camellara, which is the same family whose surname this archive mis-read twice this week.

what: The elder Giovanni Falco is not in the birth registers of 1816 or 1817
was: His burial was read from the image yesterday: «*JOANNES FALCO filius Josephi et Antoniae di Guida, aetate sua **annorum 24 circiter***», **27 November 1841**. That puts his birth between November 1816 and November 1817 if the age is anywhere near right, and he is the brother whose existence forced this archive to accept **two living sons named Giovanni** in one house.
now:
**Both years are read out, act by act, and he is in neither.** 

**1817** (`an_ua14414`, 109 acts, images 4–46): **not one Falco in the entire year.** 
**1816** (`an_ua14413`, 62 acts, images 4–64): **one Falco act only** — Domenico Falco, born 25 November to **Giuseppe Falco, 36, massaro di campo of STRADA COSTA**, and Gelsomina Vigliotta. That is the OTHER Giuseppe Falco, already held, and no Giovanni.
how: The declarant band swept across every opening of both volumes — this form puts a whole act on one half-page, so both halves carry a separate «*è comparso …*».
why:
**A negative worth the reading, because it narrows a question this archive opened yesterday.** Three things remain possible and the archive prefers none: the stated age is wrong, which this register does constantly; he was born in a year not yet read — 1815, or 1818 to 1820; or his birth is **only in the parish register** and never reached the comune. 

**The 1817 result is the stranger one.** Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida were an active household — a daughter Maddalena on 7 June 1818, sons through the 1820s — and **the whole of 1817 holds no Falco birth at all**, from any of the four Falco houses this archive tracks at Arienzo. A year that empty is itself a fact about the volume, not only about the family. 

**Citation slip corrected in passing:** this archive cites Domenico Falco's act as `img59l`. It is on **image 60**, left page.

## TWO SENTENCES OF THIS ENTRY ARE WRONG, AND THEY ARE LEFT STANDING ABOVE — 21 September 2026

**«1817: not one Falco in the entire year» is false.** The year holds **SALVATORE DIGLIO, act 49, 15 May**, to Alfonso Diglio and **MARIA FALCO**; and **GIOVANNA MORGILLO, act 69, 22 September**, to Carlantonio Morgillo and **ROSA FALCO**, a daughter of the founders — **an act this archive has cited from this very volume since before that reading was made.**

**«1816: one Falco act only» is also false.** The year holds **two**: act 116, Domenico Falco, as stated — and **act 56, 25 April, RAFFAELE FALCO**, to **VINCENZO FALCO** and **ANDREANA CRISCI**, which this archive cites as `an_ua14413 img30l act56`.

**So the argument collapses even though the conclusion survives.** «*A year that empty is itself a fact about the volume*» was built on an emptiness that was not there. **What remains true is the only thing this entry needed: there is no GIOVANNI FALCO in either year.** Both volumes have now been read act by act at the combined band, for work-list row 86.

**The fault is the one row 29 exists to find**: an entry published as a negative, never walked back, and contradicted by the archive's own household file on the day it was written.

what: The printed year on a Bourbon form is not the year of the act
was: Volumes in this series have been identified by **ark arithmetic** and by the catalogue label, and — when those were doubted — by reading the year off the act itself.
now:
**Reading the year off the act is not enough either.** These registers were printed in batches with a year already set in type. When the stock outlasted the year, **the clerk struck the printed word and wrote the true year above it by hand**: «*L'Anno mille ottocento ~~sedici~~ **diciassette** a' dì sedici del mese di Febrajo*». 

So `an_ua14414` reads **sedici** in print on every page and **is the register of 1817**. Likewise `an_ua14415` is printed *sedici* and is **1818**.
