**The correction published yesterday said a correction nobody can reach from the thing it corrects is a note, not a correction. For a day, that is exactly what these were.** The notices rendered, the prose was right, and every «→» went to the top of the site.

**Two separate faults, and the second is the instructive one.** The encoding mismatch is an ordinary bug. **But `u()` prepending a base to a fragment is a helper doing precisely what it was built to do, to an input nobody imagined giving it** — and the kit component calls it on a field whose name, `href`, promises it will take a fragment. 

**The archive is midway through moving its pages onto shared components**, and this is the second time in a day that a page lost something in the move: the front-page chart lost the treatment of zero, and this page lost its links. **Both were caught by a gate rather than by a reader.**

what: THE TWO MICHELE FALCO ARE ONE MAN — the first act out of the unindexed marriage registers, and it names a generation
was: This archive held **two separate Michele Falco households** on strada Camellara and was careful to keep them apart: **Michele Falco × ANTONIA VIGLIOTTA**, known by a daughter Chiara who died in 1846 aged seven and a Carmela who died in 1859; and **Michele Falco × MARIA GIOVANNA D'AMBROGIO**, known by a daughter Antonia born 19 November 1850 and two children who died in 1859. **Neither was claimed as kin, and the archive did not know whether they were one man or two.**
now:
**One man and two marriages.** Arienzo, *Matrimoni* **1850**, act 6, **12 February 1850**: «*…**MICHELE FALCO maggiore, di anni QUARANTATRE, nato in ARIENZO, di professione COLONO, domiciliato in STRADA CAMELLARA** … **VEDOVO DI ANTONIA VIGLIOTI** … e **GIOVANNA D'AMBROGIO MAGGIORE, di anni TRENOVE**, di professione contadina*». **HER AGE IS THIRTY-NINE, NOT NINETEEN** — re-read at the leaf's full 3,200 pixels on 20 September 2026. The numeral's initial is a tall ascender crossed by a diagonal, a **t**; this hand's **d**, in «CHIARA RIVETTI DEFUNTA» four lines above it in the same pen, is a small closed bowl. «Trenove» is the clerk's contraction of *trentanove*. **And the act says so twice**: she is «MAGGIORE», of age, and no consent of her mother is taken — a nineteen-year-old would have been «MINORE», as Andreana Crisci is in 1814. So she was born about **1811**, not about 1831.

**The d'Ambrogio daughter Antonia was born 19 November 1850 — nine months after this wedding.**

**And it names his parents, a generation this archive did not have for this house:** «*figlio di **RAFFAELE FALCO DEFUNTO**, di professione simile, domiciliato ivi, e di **CHIARA RIVETTI DEFUNTA**, di professione filatrice*».
how: **Work-list row 34, on its first volume.** The «Matrimoni, indice» series stops at 1849 and the registers after it have no finding aid at all — only 1854, 1855 and 1856 had ever been opened, each for one question. **1850 is the first year read for its own sake, and act 6 of 11 is a Falco.**
why:
**CHIARA RIVETTI is a name this archive already has, and this is almost certainly not her.** Generation two's wife Chiara Rivetti was the widow of **PASQUALE** Falco, died 13 September 1843 aged eighty, and bore Pasquale children from 1789 to 1802 — **so she cannot have been married to a Raffaele Falco when this Michele was born about 1807.** Either a second Chiara Rivetti, on a street where the Rivetti are dense and intermarry with the Falco repeatedly, or Michele's stated age is badly wrong. **Nothing is merged and nothing is chosen** — and after this afternoon's measurement of what a stated age is worth, «badly wrong» is not the long shot it looks.

**The method point is the one worth keeping.** Forty index volumes were read to 1849 and every Falco marriage in them published. **The first register year opened past the index produced a Falco in its sixth act, a household merger, and two new names.** The index gives the couple and the parents; the register gives the ages, the streets, the trades, which parents were dead, and the word *vedovo* — which is what joined two households the index could never have joined.

**There are fifteen unread years after this one.**
by: the first marriage register read after the index series ends

what: THE ARIENZO MARRIAGE RECORD IS COMPLETE, 1809 TO 1858 — and the series is six years shorter than this archive assumed
was: The «Matrimoni, indice» series stops at **1849**, and this archive recorded that after it «*the register IS the index*» — expecting, and writing on the work list, **fifteen unread years**.
now:
**Nine.** `an_ua14213` + (year − 1809) reaches **1858 = `an_ua14262`** and then stops: `14263`, `14264`, `14265` and `14268` return **no manifest**, and by `14272` the arks have moved on to a different series altogether — the *Morti* indexes, where `14272` is 1810.

**All nine are now read act by act, and they hold ONE Falco marriage.** 1850, eleven acts, **act 6: MICHELE FALCO**. 1851 (24 acts), 1852 (two bound registers, about nine acts then thirty), 1853 (29), 1857 (32), 1858 (36) — **no Falco in any of them.** 1854, 1855 and 1856 were read earlier and gave three Falco weddings.

**So the Arienzo civil marriage record is complete from 1809 to 1858**: forty index volumes and nine registers. **A Falco who married at Arienzo in that half-century is either found or does not exist.**
how: Work-list row 34, read to the end of the series rather than to the end of the plan.
why:
**Two open questions move, and one of them moves a long way.**

**PASQUA FALCO'S SECOND MARRIAGE of 30 December 1880** — known only from the margin of her own birth act — **cannot be in this series at all.** It is twenty-two years past its end. It must be sought in the post-1865 *Stato civile italiano* for Arienzo, which this archive has never located for this comune, or in collection 2043630. **A marginal annotation reached a marriage that the register series cannot.**

**LUIGI FALCO** is now a much sharper negative. Born 21 December 1819, dead at Arienzo on 16 December 1864, five days short of forty-five, and **he is in none of the forty indexes nor any of the nine registers.** If he married it was after 1858 or it was not at Arienzo. His death act will say *celibe*, *coniugato* or *vedovo*, and that is the cheapest test left.

**And the method note is about scope, not method.** The row was written as «there is no index at all» and assumed the reading job ran to 1865 because the DEATH registers do. **Different series in the same fondo end in different years, and the arithmetic tells you which** — three failed manifests and one ark that turned out to belong to another series settled it in under a minute, before any of the six unread years were opened.
by: reading to the end of the series rather than the end of the plan

superseded.what: WITHDRAWN — the Arienzo marriage series does NOT end in 1858. I read a rate-limit refusal as an absence
superseded.note: **Wrong. The series runs to 1865 and those volumes are digitised** — `an_ua14264` is Matrimoni 1860, 38 images. The four «no manifest» probes were **403s from a rate-limiting host**, which `antenati.py` could not tell from an absence. **1859–1865 are unread.** The six years this entry reports as read were genuinely read.

what: GENERATION THREE WAS ALIVE IN DECEMBER 1864 — twenty years later than anything this archive held, and his death is not on Antenati at all
was: **VINCENZO FALCO**, generation three, baptised 1 February 1792. His latest dated sighting was **7 March 1844**, in his son Raffaele's civil marriage act at San Felice a Cancello. His death has been hunted for months: the Arienzo civil death registers read act by act to 1858, the parish collection's **703 Falco pages** enumerated, and nothing. And **LUIGI FALCO**, his son, was a work-list row — born 21 December 1819, dead 16 December 1864 at forty-five, with **no marriage anywhere** in forty index volumes and nine registers.
now:
**Luigi's death act, read from the image** — it was a FamilySearch index stub until today. Arienzo *Morti 1864*, atto 47: «*…è morto nella sua casa **LUIGI FALCO = MARITO DI CAROLINA CIMMINO** — nato in Arienzo, di anni **quarantuno**, di professione **industriante**, domiciliato **Contrada Capodiconca**, figlio di **VINCENZO**, di professione **colono**, domiciliato **alla CAMELLARA**, e di **ANDREANA CRISCI**, domiciliata ivi*».

**NEITHER PARENT IS MARKED DEAD.** And this register marks the dead, systematically: on the same opening, **act 41** gives «*figlio di **fu** Nicola … e della **fu** Colomba Capezzo*», **act 43** «*del **fu** Giuseppe … e della **fu** Cecilia Silvestri*», **act 45** «*del **fu** Don Stefano … e della **fu** Donna Faustina Cimmino*», **act 49** «*del **fu** Filippo … e della **fu** Lucrezia Varrecchia*». **Four dead parents marked on one sheet, and these two not.**

**So Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci were alive on 16 December 1864, on strada Camellara.** He was seventy-two.

**And 1865 has now been read end to end — 147 acts, no Falco death at all.** Antenati's Arienzo death series **stops at 1865**. **So generation three died in 1866 or later, and his death act is not in this archive's reach.** That is an answer, not a gap.
how: Work-list row 41, which asked only where Luigi's marriage was. His death act answered that — «*marito di Carolina Cimmino*» — and then answered a much older question in its parentage clause.
why:
**This archive has a standing rule that the absence of «fu» proves nothing**, written after three acts of one archpriest killed the inference. **This is the other instrument.** A civil register that writes «fu» four times on one opening and omits it twice is not being silent; it is recording. The rule is about PARISH Latin, and it has been quietly doing damage to civil readings ever since.

**Two work-list rows close and one changes shape.** Luigi was married — to **CAROLINA CIMMINO**, a woman this archive did not know existed, and since the Arienzo marriage record is now complete 1809–1858 with no Falco–Cimmino in it, **they married after 1858 or not at Arienzo.** And the hunt for Vincenzo's death moves off Antenati entirely: **1866 onward is the post-Unification *Stato civile italiano***, which this archive has never located for Arienzo.

**One more thing fell out of 1865.** Act at image 82 has «*e **MATTEO FALCO** di anni cinquantanove*» as a declarant — **the second Matteo Falco, alive in December 1865**, born about 1806. He is a sighting, not a death.
by: a death act read for its marriage clause

what: Arienzo deaths 1865 — 147 acts, read end to end, and not one Falco
was: The Arienzo civil death registers were read out for **1844–1858** and **1859**, and the series was known to stop at **1865**. The remaining years were the only untried route to **Vincenzo Falco**'s death, and to **Giuseppe Falco of Antonia di Guida**'s.
now:
**1865 (`an_ua14367`, 86 images) holds 147 acts and NO FALCO DEATH.** The year was confirmed from the manuscript title page — «*Dal primo Gennajo a tutto il dì trentuno Dicembre mille ottocento sessantacinque*» — and the volume has **no tavola at either end**, so it was read act by act at the band where the deceased's name sits.

**What it does hold:** «*e **MATTEO FALCO** di anni cinquantanove*» as a **declarant** in December — the second Matteo Falco, alive at about fifty-nine. And **ANGELO MAJONE**, 56, declaring in October — **Pasqua Falco's first husband, alive** nine years after their wedding and fifteen before she married again as, on the ordinary reading, his widow.
how: Seven contact sheets of twenty-four bands each, at the «è morto nella sua casa [NAME]» line.
why:
**This is the end of the road on Antenati for this question, and that is worth stating plainly.** With 1865 read and Vincenzo Falco alive in December 1864, **his death is in 1866 or later — in the post-Unification *Stato civile italiano*, which this archive has never located for Arienzo.**

**A namesake caution, recorded because the next reader will want it to be her.** Act at image 68 buries a **MARIA CARFORA** at Arienzo on 24 October 1865. **She is not generation seven's grandmother** — that Maria Carfora is of **Forchia** and was bearing children from 1883. This archive has already been caught twice reading a woman as «Maria Carfora» because it wanted her to be.
by: reading the last volume in the series

what: WITHDRAWN — the Arienzo marriage series does NOT end in 1858. I read a rate-limit refusal as an absence
was: Published here today: «*`an_ua14213` + (year − 1809) reaches **1858 = `an_ua14262`** and then stops: `14263`, `14264`, `14265` and `14268` return **no manifest**… So «after 1849» is **NINE** years, not fifteen*», and, on that, «*the Arienzo civil marriage record is **complete from 1809 to 1858**… a Falco who married at Arienzo in that half-century is either found or does not exist*».
now:
**The series runs to 1865, and those volumes are digitised.** `an_ua14264` is **Arienzo, Matrimoni, 1860, 38 images**; `an_ua14267` is **1863, 24 images**. The year facet for the town says the same: **Nati, Matrimoni and Morti all run 1809–1865.**

**The four «no manifest» results were 403s.** This host rate-limits, and a 403 page contains no manifest link either — so `tools/antenati.py` reported a refusal in exactly the words it uses for a volume that does not exist. **I had diagnosed that rate limiting twenty minutes earlier, on the holdings endpoint, and did not carry it across to the ark probes.**

**So 1859–1865 are UNREAD** — seven years, not zero. What survives: **1850, 1851, 1852, 1853, 1857 and 1858 really were read act by act**, and act 6 of 1850 really is Michele Falco.
how: The holdings endpoint, retried after the rate limit cleared, and its year facet — which lists every year a town has, whether or not the ten shown include it.
why:
**A tool that cannot tell «refused» from «absent» will manufacture negatives, and this archive runs on negatives.** `antenati.py` now stops on a 403 and says so in those words: *RATE LIMITED, not missing. Do NOT record a negative from this.*

**The error had every warning attached to it in advance.** This archive's own memory says the ark arithmetic has been wrong three times in one week and that only the manuscript identifies a volume. I used a failed fetch — weaker than arithmetic, weaker than a catalogue label — to close a series.

**And the shape is the one this page keeps recording: a negative published before its instrument was calibrated.** Yesterday it was a blank margin that meant nothing until a control was run. Today it is a missing manifest that meant nothing until the host stopped refusing.
by: the holdings endpoint, once it stopped returning 403

what: THE ANNECCHINO GAIN A GENERATION, AND THE CARFORA TURN OUT TO BE AN ARIENZO FAMILY — from a Falco sweep that was not looking for either
was: **MARIA CARFORA**, generation seven's grandmother, has three closed routes to her parents — her own birth act unlinked among too many Forchia candidates, her marriage inside the Forchia filming gap of 1866–1930, her death absent from 59 indexed Carfora death acts. **All three were run at FORCHIA.** And **SABATINO ANNECCHINO and MARIANTONIA CARFORA** were a household this archive knew only from four daughters born 1861–1866; their marriage had never been found.
now:
**Arienzo, *Matrimoni* 1860, act 3, 20 January 1860** — found while sweeping the year for Falco: «*sono comparsi nella Casa Comunale **SABBATINO ANNECCHINO**, di anni **trentaquattro**, nato in **FORCHIA**, contadino, domiciliato in Forchia, figlio di **fu CARMINE ANNECCHINO** … e di **fu ROSA CEGLIA** … e **MARIA ANTONIA CARFORA**, di anni **ventinove**, **NATA IN ARIENZO**, figlia di **fu [?]ERIO CARFORA**, contadino, e di **fu PASQUA MORGILLO***».

**Four new people and a generation.** Sabatino's parents **CARMINE ANNECCHINO** and **ROSA CEGLIA** — Ceglia has never appeared in this archive under any spelling. Her parents **[?]erio CARFORA** and **PASQUA MORGILLO**, all four dead by January 1860.

**And Maria Antonia Carfora was born at ARIENZO**, not Forchia.
how: Work-list row 34, sweeping the 1860 Arienzo marriage register for Falco. Act 3 of 25 is not a Falco at all.
why:
**The three shut routes to Maria Carfora's parents were all run at Forchia, and here is a Carfora house at Arienzo** — a *contadino* who married a **MORGILLO**, in the generation born about 1800. That does not reach generation seven's grandmother, who is two generations later; **it opens a place to look that this archive had no reason to try.**

**The recurring forename is worth holding onto and NOT resolving.** Sabatino's father is a **CARMINE ANNECCHINO** dead before 1860; generation seven's wife's father is a **CARMINE ANNECCHINO** fathering children from 1883. **Two men, two generations apart, one name** — which is either a family naming pattern pointing at a descent, or the commonest trap in this archive. **Nothing is joined.**

**The bride's father's forename is left unread.** At four times magnification it is «[L/t]erio» and resolves no further. This archive leaves one widow's surname deliberately blank for the same reason, and a guessed forename on a new grandparent would be worse than a gap.

**The method note: a sweep run for one surname pays in others.** Twenty-five acts were read looking for FALCO, and the year's yield was an ANNECCHINO marriage that unlocks a generation on the line this archive can least reach.
by: a Falco sweep that found an Annecchino

what: A NEW CHILD FOR GENERATION THREE — STANISLAO FALCO, a shepherd, married in 1861
was: Generation three's children were: Raffaele of 1816 who died an infant, **Raffaele of 1818** who is generation four, **Luigi** 1819, **Giuseppe Nunzio** and **Clemente** 1824, **Angelandrea** 1826, **Sara** 1828, and daughters **Nunziata**, **Maddalena** and a **second Maddalena**. The list ended there.
now:
**Arienzo, *Matrimoni* 1861, act 16, 19 September 1861**: «*sono comparsi nella Casa Comunale **STANISLAO FALCO**, di anni **VENTIQUATTRO**, nato in **ARIENZO**, di professione **PASTORE**, domiciliato in Arienzo, figlio di **VINCENZO FALCO**, contadino, e di **ANDREANA CRISCI** … e **FILOMENA DI LUCIA**, di anni ventitré, nata in Arienzo*». Church celebration **23 September 1861** at **Sant'Andrea Apostolo**.

**A *pastore* — a shepherd — in a house of contadini**, and the first of that trade in this family.

**And his parents are again unmarked.** «*figlio di VINCENZO FALCO, di professione contadino, domiciliato in Arienzo, e di ANDREANA CRISCI, domiciliata ivi*» — while the bride, in the very next clause, is «*figlia di **fu** [Luigi] di Lucia*». **Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci were alive on 19 September 1861**, three years before the other sighting.
how: Work-list row 34 — the 1861 marriage register, one of the seven years this archive had wrongly written off as not existing.
why:
**Twenty-four in September 1861 gives a birth about 1837, which would make Andreana Crisci about forty.** Late, and recorded as such rather than smoothed: this register's ages are good to about three years and no better — measured on her own husband, six sightings — and she was bearing children into 1828 on the archive's existing reckoning. **The birth act is the test**, and 1837 is `an_ua14406` + 28 = `an_ua14434`.

**The volume also holds a second register, and it is worth more than it looks.** Bound after the twenty-nine marriage acts are the **NOTIFICAZIONI** — the banns. They give each couple with **both sets of parents**, in a clerk's cleaner hand, and they are what supplied **LUIGI DI LUCIA** and **MARTA DI NIZZO** when the marriage act's own writing would not resolve the bride's father.

**More than that: a notificazione is published where a couple LIVES, and the marriage may be celebrated elsewhere.** That is precisely the shape of **NUNZIATA FALCO**, who has a parish wedding date of 13 November 1855 and appears in no Arienzo marriage register. **The banns registers are a new place to look for her**, and for anyone else who married out.
by: the seven years I had wrongly declared not to exist

what: Five more people filed under a second given name — «Angela Rosa» under ROSA, «Gaetano Antonio» under ANTONIO
was: Fixing the Italian index's surname-first order left five register entries still filed under a forename: **«Angela Maria —», «Angela Rosa», «Antonia Rosa, defunta», «Carolina Rosa», «Gaetano Antonio»** — all **double FORENAMES with the surname never recorded**. `sur()` already returned «unknown» for a single bare word for exactly this reason. It did not for two.
now:
**Zero.** The builder now harvests a forename list **from the archive's own data** — the first word of every person filed under a well-attested surname — and returns unknown when every word of a name is one of them, or when the last word is a well-attested forename and the first is not a surname this archive knows.

**That second rule exists because GAETANO and JOANNA appear NOWHERE in this corpus paired with a surname**, so no threshold on a derived list could ever have contained them.
how: Work-list row 61, raised by the surname-first fix as its own leftover.
why:
**A second given name is not a family.** «Carolina Rosa» filed under ROSA invents a Rosa family and puts her in it; the register never gave her a surname and the honest answer is that it did not.

**The list is derived, not written, and that is the point.** A hard-coded forename list is one more thing that must be remembered when the archive grows. This one is rebuilt from `people.json` on every run.

**And it was checked before it shipped**: no word in this corpus is both a frequent forename and an attested surname, so the rule cannot eat a real name. **FALCO is unchanged at 1,478 across the change** — the canary that says a surname fix has not quietly moved somebody.
by: the leftover from the previous fix

what: «SANTA MARIA A VICO» WAS MY GUESS, AND ITS OWN REGISTER EXCLUDES IT — the comune in the margin is not established
was: Published yesterday from the margin of Domenico Clemente Falco's birth act: «*Con atto **6 agosto 1856** at[to] **21** in **S[anta] Maria a Vico** il Falco sposò **DOMENICA VIGLIOTTI** di Giuseppe*» — and, on the strength of it, a household record placing his marriage at **Santa Maria a Vico**, a work-list row to read that act, and a second row to enumerate the comune.
now:
**The register excludes it.** Santa Maria a Vico, *Matrimoni* **1856** — `an_ua55736`, located through the year facet — has **act 21 as DON DOMENICO DE LUCIA, twenty-nine, born San Felice, promised 14 June 1856**. No Falco. And **no act of 6 August**: act 31 is 3 August, act 32 is 9 August.

**At five times magnification the place reads «S[?]basia a Vico» and resolves no further.** Santa Maria a Vico was the only comune of that shape in this district and it is now ruled out by its own book.

**Two other readings moved with it.** The year is **1856**, checked at six times — a cursive 5, not a 9, and a bridegroom born in 1819 marrying in 1896 would be seventy-seven. The bride's father reads **GASPARE**, not the *Giuseppe* first published.
how: Going to the act the annotation names, instead of stopping at the annotation.
why:
**I read a plausible comune into an illegible word and then published it three times** — in a household record, in a correction, and in two work-list rows that sent the next reader to the wrong archive. **The annotation never said Santa Maria a Vico. I did.**

**What survives is still worth having, and is the part that was actually written down:** a Falco of this house married a **DOMENICA VIGLIOTTI** on **6 August 1856**, recorded as **act 21** somewhere ending «*…a Vico*». That is a dated marriage for a man this archive knew only as a newborn.

**And the instrument still works.** A marginal annotation reached a marriage in another comune, which is what it is for. It is the READING of the annotation that failed, not the method — and the failure is the archive's oldest one: **a name I wanted, in a word that would not resolve.**
by: the register the annotation pointed at

what: EVERY FINDMYPAST NOTE IN THIS ARCHIVE NAMES THE WRONG DOMAIN — the subscription answers on .co.uk, and .com.au looks exactly like having no subscription
was: This archive's FindMyPast method, recorded twice, says to search **`www.findmypast.com.au`** — «*navigate the tab and read the rendered table… `sourcecountry=australasia`, `sourcecategory=…`, `_page=N`*».
now:
**The live subscription answers on `www.findmypast.co.uk`.** Hitting `.com.au` redirects to `auth.findmypast.com/login` with **`initialScreen=signUp`** — **a page indistinguishable from having no subscription at all.** The same search on `.co.uk` returns twenty-one rows immediately.

**Two more recorded techniques have expired.** The note says to load a search «*in a hidden same-origin iframe and poll for `tr` elements*»: five iframes reached `readyState: complete` on the right path with **`body.innerText.length === 0`**. **The application does not paint offscreen.** And the render takes **longer than six seconds** — a read issued in the same round trip as the navigation returned `rows: 0` and an empty body for a search that has twenty-one rows.
how: Being handed a subscription and finding the site apparently signed out.
why:
**The failure this prevents is a false nil of the worst kind: one that looks like a verdict.** A signed-out FindMyPast returns a sign-up screen, not an error. An archive that searched `.com.au` on a live subscription would record «nothing found» for every surname it tried and have a plausible-looking page to prove it. **This archive has already published one FindMyPast verdict that was wrong because it was measured signed-out**, and corrected it. This is the same trap wearing a different hat.

**And the two expired techniques are a reminder that a method note rots.** The iframe trick was written on 9 September and was dead within a week; the six-second wait was generous then and is not now. **A method note needs a date on every claim**, which these now have.
by: a subscription that appeared not to work

what: TWELVE BRANCH SURNAMES SWEPT ON FINDMYPAST — one Queensland find, one true nil, and the Arricale leave no trace at all
was: FindMyPast was swept twice in September, both times signed in, and both sweeps covered **six surnames**: Falco, Raffaele Falco, Annecchino, Zampiello, Servodio and Maione. **The families who married into this line were never searched** — the archive's verdict rested on six names out of seventy-seven.
now:
**Twelve more, on a live subscription. Page one only — twenty rows each — and the totals are not captured**, so «no Queensland» below means *not on page one* and is not a nil.

**ARRICALE returns «No results found».** That is the one true nil here, and it matters: **Giovanna Arricale is generation five's wife**, and her family leaves **no trace whatever** in FindMyPast's Australasian holdings.

**CARFORA and VIGLIOTTA are WESTERN AUSTRALIAN** arrivals of 1955–67 — a different migration stream from this Queensland family, the same shape as the Servodio. **ABATIELLO returns five rows and every one is a UNITED STATES WW2 record** mis-tagged into the Australasia filter, exactly as Zampiello did in September. Falcone, Biondo, Mazza, Zavaglia, Cimmino, Zaino and Crisci give passenger lists and US war records and nothing in Queensland on page one.

**THE ONE QUEENSLAND FIND: CONCETTA MILITANO, on the Australia Electoral Rolls at INNISFAIL** — Herbert division 1939 and 1941, Leichhardt 1949 and 1959.
how: Work-list row 65, on the subscription David opened on 16 September.
why:
**The Militano find is a lead and is not claimed as a link.** Innisfail is **North Queensland, about fourteen hundred kilometres from Brisbane**, and this archive has already met exactly this pattern and refused it: the FindMyPast **Maione** cluster sits at **Winton and Charters Towers**, also North Queensland, and was logged as unconnected. **A shared surname and a shared state is not evidence in a country this size.** And the Militano reach this family through a marriage in the **living** generations, so the living-people rule governs anything published about them.

**Five record sets turned up that the September note's list of «holdings worth remembering» does not have** — NSW Deceased Estate Files, Australia Parish Deaths & Burials, Victoria Wills & Probate, Victoria Petty Sessions, Britain & Ireland Incoming Passenger Lists. **That list said four. There are at least nine.**

**What this does NOT establish is a verdict**, and the distinction is the whole point of publishing it. Page two of every one of these is unread.
by: a subscription, and the surnames nobody had tried

what: FOUR REGISTER ACTS BEHIND FOUR INDEX ENTRIES — one word settles a separation, and a woman gets her trade after five sightings of her age
was: Forty **index** volumes were read for 1809–1849 and thirteen Falco marriages published from them. The index gives the couple and both sets of parents. **Only one of the thirteen registers had been opened.**
now:
**Four now: 1845, 1846, 1847 and 1848.** Each confirms its index entry exactly and adds what an index cannot carry.

**1846, act 14: ANDREA FALCO, maggiore, TWENTY-FOUR**, contadino of strada Camellara, marrying Maria Carmela Buono. **1847: ANGELANDREA FALCO, MINORE**, contadino of strada Camellara, marrying Maria Cimmino.

**That one word settles a separation this archive was carrying on the index alone.** Majority was **twenty-one**, so «minore» puts Angelandrea under it — and his birth act of **12 September 1826** makes him twenty years and six months in March 1847. Andrea is **maggiore at twenty-four in May 1846**, so born about **1822**. **They are two men, four years apart, and the acts say so in a single word each.**

**And ANDREANA CRISCI has a trade at last: FILATRICE, a spinner** — given in both acts. This archive has her stated age five times and had never once had her occupation.

**1848, act 20** supplies a forename the index withheld: the Airola household carried in its very NAME a bracket — «*Pietro Falco & [Carbone]*» — because the index read «*CARBONE […]*». The register reads «*e di **CAMILLA CARBONE detta […]**, di professione filatrice*». **She is Camilla**, and she carries a «detta» alias that still does not resolve.
how: Work-list row 36 — the registers behind the indexes, read for 1846, 1847 and 1848 after 1845 was read yesterday.
why:
**Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci are named as living in both the 1846 and the 1847 act**, with trades and domiciles and no «fu», in a form whose next clause marks the bride's father dead when he is. **That fills the middle of a gap** this archive has been closing from both ends — 7 March 1844, then nothing until 19 September 1861 and 16 December 1864. **It is now 1844, 1846, 1847, 1861, 1864.**

**A date conflict is recorded rather than resolved.** The 1847 act gives the church celebration as **29 March 1847**; this archive also holds «*Angelo Falco … m. Maria Cimmino*» on **17 April 1847** from a parish ark — **the same bride, three weeks apart**. Both are kept until something decides between them.

**And the Airola Falco stay unclaimed.** «*nato in **AIROLA***», father Pietro Falco «*defunto*», a household this archive holds precisely so nobody joins him to the line by the surname. **The new detail changes nothing about that refusal** — it just means the refusal is now made about a woman with a first name.

what: «ZIO DEL DEFUNTO», not «vicino» — the register named the kinship four years earlier than this archive said, and in a stronger word
was: This archive has said, in the household file and in its own prose, that the Falco who kept appearing over the dead children of **Francesco Cioffi and Maria Falco** was never given a relationship: «*The register calls him «vicino» each time and never «parente», so nothing states a relationship*», and, of the act of 24 October 1828, «*After five acts calling him only a neighbour, the register states the kinship. This is the evidence the archive's open question on the third Maria Falco was waiting for.*» The 1824 act was transcribed «*PASQUALE FALCO … vicino del defunto, e GIUSEPPE FALCO …*».
now: **The act of 25 March 1824 enters BOTH Falco declarants as «ZIO DEL DEFUNTO» — uncle of the dead child — and writes the word twice, once for each brother.** Re-read at the leaf's full resolution, the word before «del defunto» is three letters. The same clerk writes the six-letter «vicino della defunta» on this household's acts of **20 June 1823** and **2 April 1825**, and those two acts sit in the same file as the control. So the register states kinship in **1824**, not 1828, and it states a **closer** kinship than «parente».
how: Worklist row 60 — re-magnifying four death acts that were transcribed before this archive had the Cossi / Crisci / Cioffi test. The word was not what row 60 went looking for.
why:
**The misread word is load-bearing twice over.** It made the 1828 «parente» look like a first, when it was a second and a weaker one; and it made three appearances by one man look like a pattern awaiting a statement, when the statement was in the middle of them all along.

**What it does NOT settle, and this matters more than what it does.** Read strictly, «zio del defunto» makes **Maria Falco a sister of Pasquale Falco (baptised 24 October 1767) and of Giuseppe Falco** — and therefore a **daughter of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci**, the couple at the head of this line. Her own stated age forbids it. She is **twenty-five in June 1824**, born about 1799, and Francesca Crisci was bearing children by 1767. Either that age is one of this register's inventions — and this archive holds the same clerk making Giuseppe Falco **forty and forty-five four days apart** — or «zio» is doing the loose collateral work that «parente» does in 1828.

**The word is recorded. The pedigree is refused.** A register that says «uncle» twice is better evidence than a register that says «relative» once, and neither is a birth act.
by: this archive, auditing its own transcriptions

what: The four Cioffi death acts were re-magnified: every «COSSI» in them was this archive's misreading, not the register's spelling
was: The four death acts of this household — **20 June 1823**, **25 March 1824**, **2 April 1825** and **23 October 1828** — were transcribed «COSSI», and one of them «*GIUSEPPE **CRISCI(?)***» with a question mark nobody resolved. When the household NAME was corrected to CIOFFI, the four transcriptions were left alone under a note saying «*The act's own wording is quoted above unchanged*».
now: **The act's own wording was never COSSI.** All four acts are **CIOFFI** at full magnification, in every place the surname appears — the child, the father, and in 1828 the second declarant and the officiating eletto as well. The test is the one this archive wrote down after being caught by all three names in a single week: **the dotted i after the C, the round o, and the tall ff ligature with its long descender**, against which Crisci shows a narrow r and no round o, and Cossi a short double-s with no ascender.
how: Rendering each leaf at the maximum resolution the host will serve — about 1,660 pixels across a half page — and cropping the single line.
why:
**A note that says «quoted unchanged» is a claim about the manuscript, and this one was false.** It told the next reader that the register spelled the family two ways and that the archive was faithfully reporting both. The register spells it one way. What varied was the reading.

The three new things the re-reading turned up are worth as much as the surname: the **1824 declarants call themselves the child's uncles**; the 1828 act has a **second declarant, Cesare Cioffi, 31, also «parente della defunta»** and almost certainly the father's brother; and it was drawn before **Agostino Cioffi, secondo eletto** — a Cioffi holding municipal office in the comune where this family are labourers.

what: Pasquale Falco signed his own name, and he spelled it PASCALE
was: Nothing in this archive was written by any person in it. Every Falco before the twentieth century existed here only in a clerk's hand.
now: **The death act of 25 March 1824 closes: «*segnato da noi e da uno de' dichiaranti, avendo l'altro cioè GIUSEPPE FALCO dichiarato di non sapere scrivere per non averlo mai imparato*» — and beneath it, in a slow upright hand nothing like the clerk's, stands «PASCALE FALCO».** His own signature, and the Neapolitan form of his name without the *qu*. His brother Giuseppe could not sign.
how: Rendering the foot of the act rather than stopping at the body of it — the transcription in this archive stopped at the parents' names.
why: It is the only line in this archive made by a hand that belongs to the family, and it is on the same act whose one misread word is corrected above. **Two things were at the bottom of a leaf nobody had rendered.**

what: «ivi» means the comune and never the street — settled in two printed forms, and it costs this archive a published finding
was: Both forms leave a blank after «*domiciliato*», and this archive has read the one-word filler «**ivi**» as *in the same street as the person just named*. On that reading, Crescenzo Falco's marriage act of 2 February 1845 — «*domiciliato in strada Sant'Andrea, figlio di GIUSEPPE FALCO … domiciliato **ivi***» — put his father on strada Sant'Andrea, and this archive published that **the household was off strada Camellara by 1845**, after twenty years of birth acts placing it there.
now:
**«ivi» is the comune.** Three acts settle it, in two different printed forms, and each is a single sentence containing the word twice:

**1. The birth act of Giuseppa Cioffi, 18 June 1824, atto 73.** Two witnesses, consecutive: «*Tomaso Esposito … domiciliato **ivi strada Camellara***» and «*Antonio Bernardo … domiciliato **ivi strada Terra Murata***». One word, two streets.

**2. Crescenzo Falco's own marriage act, 1845, atto 3.** The groom is «*domiciliato **ivi strada Sant'Andrea***» — this archive had transcribed «domiciliato **in** strada Sant'Andrea» and dropped the word — and the bride, four lines later, is «*domiciliata **ivi strada Cappuccini***». One word, two streets, one act, one clerk.

**3. The death act of Mariantonia Cioffi, 24 October 1828, atto 54.** The **first** person the act names is «*domiciliato **ivi** strada Camellara*». There is no earlier person to point back to. The only place already named is the comune.

**So a bare «domiciliato ivi» states the comune and says nothing whatever about the street.**
how: Worklist row 47, which asked for exactly this test — «*find acts where ivi follows a person whose street is independently known to differ from the previous person's*» — and three acts already rendered for row 60 turned out to contain it.
why:
**The loss is larger than the one finding.** In the death acts «ivi» is how the deceased's **parents** are recorded, so those acts never gave the parents' address; they gave the street of the house where the death happened, which is the trap this archive already documented for declarants, wearing a different hat.

**And the correction was buried inside a transcription error.** The act says «*domiciliato ivi strada Sant'Andrea*»; this archive wrote «*domiciliato in strada Sant'Andrea*». Losing one three-letter word turned a shorthand for the comune into a preposition, and a reader checking the sentence for sense would have found none to check — it reads perfectly. **This is the second time in two days that a misread word of three letters carried a published conclusion**, the other being «zio» read as «vicino» on the act of 25 March 1824. The rule is now on the method page in both directions: **magnify the small words, and transcribe the ones that look like noise.**

what: Arienzo's lost registers of 1866–1890 are quoted verbatim inside the marriage supplements of 1891–1910
was: Three of this archive's oldest questions all stop at the same wall. **Vincenzo Falco** is alive in December 1864 and absent from 1865. **Giuseppe Falco of Antonia di Guida** is alive in November 1849 and in no volume since. **Pasqua Falco's second marriage of 30 December 1880** is known only from a margin. **Antenati's Arienzo holdings stop at 1865 in every series** — confirmed from the year facet, which lists every year a town holds — and this archive had no instrument that reached past it.
now:
**The registers are gone. Their contents are not.** FamilySearch collection **`2043630`**, «Caserta, Santa Maria Capua Vetere, Civil Registration (Tribunale), 1866–1929», holds Arienzo's **marriage supplements, proclamations and bann supplements for 1891–1910** — *processetti*. **A processetto binds in certified copies of the civil acts of the couple and of their dead parents**, written out in full by the clerk who held the originals. So **the lost years survive inside the surviving ones.**

One surname, swept once: **1,503 hits, 202 distinct Arienzo pages, and seventeen certified extracts of Arienzo civil acts of 1871, 1872, 1873, 1874, 1875, 1878, 1879, 1880, 1881, 1883, 1887 and 1889** — every one of them in the gap.
how: Worklist row 62. The collection facet on a full-text search, read rather than the first collection assumed: `q.anyPlace=Arienzo&q.text=Falco` with no collection filter returns a Collection facet naming every holding that contains the pair, with counts.
why:
**The seventeen land on names the tree could never prove.** This archive holds **MATTEO FALCO × ALESSANDRA CRISCI**, married 24 January 1834, with **nine children and not one document against any of them**. Three of the nine now have an act, and the two sources are independent — a family reconstruction on one side, a clerk's certified copy on the other, machine-read out of a volume nobody has indexed:

- «**FILOMENA FALCO FU MATTEO**», wife of **Antonio Crisci**, on **via Camellara**, 1872 — and the tree had married Filomena to Antonio Crisci.
- «**VINCENZA FALCO FU MATTEO**», wife of **Carmine Morgillo**, piazza Valletta, 1874, 1878 and 1881 — and the tree had married Vincenza to Carmine Morgillo. **Her first recorded daughter is named ALESSANDRA.**
- «**Giuseppe Falco**, 46, agricoltore», husband of **Nicoletta Nuzzo**, via Orticelli, 1887 — and the tree had married Giuseppe to Nicoletta Nuzzo. Forty-six in 1887 is born about 1841, which fits a couple married in January 1834.

**«Fu Matteo» in 1872 dates a death this archive did not have: Matteo Falco was dead before 11 August 1872.**

**NOTHING HAS ENTERED A HOUSEHOLD, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** Every line is a machine transcription of a handwritten copy — two removes from the register, and the same OCR renders Arienzo as «Chienno», «Criengo» and «Artento» on those very pages. **A machine transcription is a candidate, exactly as a contact sheet is.** The arks are citable, the images are unread, and the reading is its own work-list row.

**One merge was refused in this pass and it is the reason the pass is trustworthy.** The extracts name a **Pasqualina Falco DI VINCENZO**, married with a daughter born in July 1872. This archive holds a Pasqualina Falco, daughter of **Pasquale Antonio Falco and Maria Amalia Guida**, with a birth act of 1877. **Different father, impossible dates, two women** — and they would have been one if the check had been left until after the write-up.

**And a clean nil to stop the next search.** «Italy, Campania, Births, from 1825 to 2000» (`M9J1-SZX`) is a collection this archive had never searched. It holds **no Arienzo pages at all**: 563 hits for Falco, every one placed in a neighbouring comune. Measured from `recordPlace` on all 563, not from the hit count — the mistake that once published a «1,621-page» negative that was really 229.

what: The Carfora were living on strada Camellara — the family this archive placed at Forchia was next door all along
was: Every route to Maria Carfora's parents was run at **Forchia**, because that is where this family was assumed to belong, and all three shut. The Arienzo marriage act of 20 January 1860 then named **«fu [?]ERIO CARFORA», contadino of Arienzo**, and **«fu PASQUA MORGILLO»** — and this archive wrote that the Carfora were «*a family this archive never knew to look for*» at Arienzo, with **not one Arienzo Carfora record to its name**.
now:
**Three Carfora households in a single year of one register, and two of them on STRADA CAMELLARA.** The whole of the 1831 Arienzo birth volume was swept on the declarant line:

- **ANIELLO CARFORA, 31, contadino, «domiciliato in questo Comune STRADA CAMELLARA»** × **ORSOLA PORRINO**, 30 — son Antonio, 10 January 1831.
- **RAFFAELE CARFORA, 37, contadino** × **FRANCESCA CIOFFI**, 28 — son Pietro, 12 September 1831.
- **ANTONIO CARFORA, 26, contadino, strada Camellara** × **GIUSEPPA PERRECA**, 23 — daughter **Maria Rosa**, 4 November 1831.

**Strada Camellara is the Falco's street**, and has been the spine of this archive for two months.
how: Work-list row 63. A contact-sheet sweep of all ninety-seven acts of `an_ua14428` over the «*è comparso*» band, then each hit rendered at the leaf's full resolution and read line by line.
why:
**It is the «wrong comune» error, and it is the same shape as the «wrong surname» error this archive was caught by last week.** Forty marriage volumes were once read against a surname that had been retired; here, three routes were run against a town that was only half right. **A negative is a statement about where you looked.**

**And the archive walked past them.** The 1831 volume was in reach the whole time, and the Carfora were on the one street this archive knows better than any other.

**MARIA ANTONIA IS NOT AMONG THE THREE, AND THAT IS NOT YET A NEGATIVE EITHER.** She was twenty-nine in January 1860, so born about 1831, and the November girl on strada Camellara is **MARIA ROSA** — read at magnification, mother **Giuseppa Perreca**, not Pasqua Morgillo. **This archive does not turn one girl into another because the year and the street are right.** Nor can the sweep close the year: it read the declarant line, and **a large minority of these acts are declared by a midwife**, whose acts name the father further down the page. **The sweep is triage, exactly as a contact sheet is.**

what: The 1841 civil register has an eleven-day hole and the Falco burial is inside it — the nil was never evidence
was: The parish buried **JOANNES FALCO** on **27 November 1841**, and the act has been read from the image. This archive then reported that **«all ninety acts of the civil death register for that year hold no Falco at all»**, and called it «*an anomaly with something behind it, not a gap*», on the ground that **«Arienzo's two registers normally agree»**.
now:
**They do not agree, because the civil register is not continuous, and it says so itself.** Read act by act from the image, the death dates run:

| act | death |
|---|---|
| 84 | 19 November |
| 85 | 23 November |
| 86 | **26 November** |
| 87 | **7 DECEMBER** |

**The comune registered nothing at all between 26 November and 7 December 1841. Joannes Falco was buried on 27 November.**

**And it is not a one-off.** A fortnight earlier the same register does the same thing: **act 80 is a death of 30 October, act 81 a death of 13 November — fourteen days.** Two silences, of a fortnight and of eleven days, in a single autumn, in a volume that otherwise enters a death every two or three days in that season.

**Two smaller corrections fall out of the same read.** The volume ends at act **91**, not ninety — «all ninety acts» was one act short. And the tavola leaf bound after the last act is filmed with its ink almost wholly lost and the facing page transferred onto it in mirror: **it is not readable, and it is not recorded as absent.**
how: Work-list rows 12 and 56, which asked for exactly three tests — a numbering gap, a supplementary list, a back-reference from 1842. The numbering is unbroken, the list is illegible, and the third test was never needed: the dates in the acts already read give the answer.
why:
**A negative is a statement about the instrument, and this archive had not examined the instrument.** «No Falco in the 1841 civil register» was treated as a fact about the Falco. It is a fact about a register that lost eleven days in the relevant fortnight and fourteen days in the one before it.

**The rule generalises and this archive should apply it backwards.** Every civil-death nil drawn from these Arienzo volumes needs the dates either side of the window checked before it is allowed to mean anything. That is the same discipline as reading `recordPlace` before quoting a hit count, and the same discipline as not recording a negative from a rate-limited 403.

**One thing came out of the volume that was not being looked for.** Atto 82 is declared by «*ANTONIO CARFORA, di anni **trentasei**, contadino, domiciliato in **strada Camellara***» — and the 1831 birth volume, swept the same day for a different row, has him at **twenty-six on the same street**. **Ten years apart, ten years older, in a register series this archive has spent two months proving invents ages.** Found from opposite directions, in two volumes, on one day.

what: A fourth child of Matteo Falco and Alessandra Crisci, and a granddaughter the tree never had
was: **MATTEO FALCO × ALESSANDRA CRISCI**, married 24 January 1834, stood in this archive's tree with **nine children and not one document against any of them.** This morning three of the nine got an act, from certified extracts bound into the Arienzo marriage supplements of 1891–1910.
now:
**A fourth.** The proclamation of 1908 names «*FERRARA AGNESE, di anni **venticinque**, contadina, residente in Arienzo, figlia di **GIOVANNI**, di anni **sessanta**, colono, residente in Arienzo, e figlia di **MARIA FALCO**, contadina, residente in Arienzo*». The tree holds **Giovanni Ferrara** married to **Maria Falco (Ferrara)**, daughter of Matteo and Alessandra — with `records: 0` against both of them.

**They are named together, both alive at Arienzo in 1908**, he born about 1848 — and the act carries **a daughter, AGNESE, born about 1883, whom the tree does not hold at all.**
how: A second sweep of collection `2043630`, this time on **Carfora** rather than Falco, run for a different row entirely. 171 more Arienzo pages, 347 in all.
why:
**Filomena, Vincenza, Giuseppe, and now Maria.** Four of nine, each confirmed by a source the tree never saw, each agreeing with the tree on the husband it had already assigned.

**It is still a machine transcription of a handwritten copy and the image is unread** — the same standing as a contact-sheet candidate. What has changed is the odds: **four independent agreements is no longer a coincidence about one clerk's handwriting.**

**And the same sweep closed a household from the other end.** Vincenzo Falco and Angela Pellone of **Corso Caudino 80** — a son born December 1880, his own death September 1889 — now have a daughter: «*Falco PASQUALINA, 21, **figlia del fu VINCENZO** … e di **PELLONE ANGELA***», marrying in 1899, her father given as dead. **Three acts, one household, found in two separate sweeps on two different surnames.**

what: Strada Camellara has three house numbers, not one — and this archive was treating the first as the address
was: «**Via Camellara number five**» was published here as «*the first house number ever recovered for strada Camellara*», from the 1883 death act of **Pasquale Falco**, and it has been the only one this archive holds.
now: **Three, inside three years of each other.** A 1906 marriage supplement quotes an Arienzo birth act of about 1879: «*è comparso **PASQUALE FALCO**, contadino, di anni **trentanove** … nella casa posta in **VIA CUMELLARA AL NUMERO UNDICI**, da **MARIA AMALIA GUIDA***» — **the same couple, at number eleven.** And the 1881 birth of Vincenzo Morgillo puts that family at **via Camellara numero nove**.
how: Sweeping FamilySearch collection `2043630` on Carfora for an unrelated row, and reading the extracts rather than the surnames.
why:
**A house number looks like the most precise thing a register can give, and on this street it is not yet.** Pasquale Falco is at number eleven about 1879 and dies at number five in 1883 — either the family moved a few doors, or the street was renumbered between the two, and **nothing this archive holds decides which.**

The practical consequence: **a Camellara house number is not an identifier.** It cannot be used to join two records or to separate them, which is exactly the job it looked ready to do.

what: DOMENICA FALCO — a child of Matteo and Alessandra read from the register at last, and her wedding in the margin
was: **MATTEO FALCO × ALESSANDRA CRISCI** entered this archive as **one line in a marriage index** — «*CRISCI ALESSANDRA … CRISCI [?], QUOTOLO ANGELA*», 24 January 1834, the bride's father's forename lost to a page-fold shadow. The family tree hung **nine children** on that line and this archive had **not one document against any of them**. Three were matched this morning from **machine transcriptions** of certified copies bound into later marriage supplements.
now:
**The fourth — and the first read from the act itself.** Arienzo, *Nati* 1846, image 70: «*è comparso **MATTEO FALCO**, di anni **trentotto**, di professione **COLONO**, domiciliato in **strada Camellara**, quale ci ha presentato una **FEMINA** … il Sacramento del Battesimo è stato amministrato a **DOMENICA FALCO***», born **13 September 1846**, «*da **ALESSANDRA** sua moglie legittima, di anni **trentasei***».

**And the margin of that birth act carries her wedding, twenty-eight years later**: «*(1) **a 10 Ottobre 1874** l'Uff.le dello Stato Civile d'**Arienzo** sposò **DOMENICA FALCO** con **PASQUA[LE]…ANTONIO GUIDA***» — dated by the registrar «*Caserta 31 Luglio 1884*».

**The tree calls her «Domenica Falco (GUIDA)», and had nothing but family memory to say it.**
how: Work-list row 43, which was looking for a different couple's children altogether and swept all 110 images of the 1846 birth volume to do it.
why:
**The margin reaches past the end of the archive's own sources.** Antenati's Arienzo registers stop in **1865**. This marriage is **1874**, and it is legible only because a clerk in Caserta went back to an 1846 leaf in 1884 and wrote on it. **A birth act is not only a birth act.**

**One thing is deliberately left unread.** The mother's surname on this act is a single flourished capital running into the next word, and it **cannot be resolved on this filming**. This is the exact trio — **Crisci, Cossi, Cioffi** — that has caught this archive three times in one week, so it is recorded as «Alessandra [surname]» and not guessed. **The identification does not need it**: a Matteo Falco of strada Camellara whose wife is called Alessandra, whose daughter is Domenica, and whose daughter marries a **Guida** — three hooks, none of them the contested letter.

**And the sweep found no index to check itself against.** The 1845 tavola is printed and **left blank**; the 1846 tavola was **skipped by the camera**, with the operator's card laid across the frame reading «*THIS INDEX HAS BEEN MICROFILMED ALREADY*» — **the same card this archive found over the 1825 leaf.** Two volumes twenty-one years apart: **the Arienzo birth indexes were filmed as a separate series, and that series has never been located.**

what: A whole Arienzo series this archive had never opened — the register of people who died somewhere else
was: When a death could not be found in the Arienzo death register, this archive had two explanations and no third: **the register has a hole**, or **the person died after 1865, where Antenati stops.** Both were used. Neither is wrong. **But there was never a place to look for the case where somebody simply died away from home.**
now:
**There is, and it has been sitting in the holdings list all along.** Antenati's Arienzo «**Diversi**» series — forty small volumes covering 1812 to 1865 — opens on this title page:

> «*Atti per le nascite avvenuti in un viaggio di mare, Per le Ricognizioni, Adozioni, **PERSONE DEFUNTE E FUORI DEL PROPRIO DOMICILIO**, e Morti-Nati*»

**When an Arienzo person died elsewhere, the comune where they died drew the act, and a certified copy came back to Arienzo and was copied in whole** — «*abbiamo ricevuto per mezzo del Signor Sottintendente di questo Distretto copia certificata dal Sindaco e Cancelliere del Comune di …, d'un atto di morte del tenor seguente*». Age, trade, street, both parents, whether they were dead, and the surviving children with their ages. **Nothing is summarised.**
how: Work-list row 10 — hunting the separate filming of the birth tavole, which this is not. The ark block below the marriage indexes was probed one volume at a time and the breadcrumbs read.
why:
**The whole series is about the size of one year of the death register**, one to eight images a volume, and it has never been opened. **Rows 39 and 40 are exactly its shape**: Giuseppe Falco of Antonia di Guida is alive in November 1849 and in no volume since, and his wife is alive in February 1845 and in none either. A man who dies at a masseria in the next district is invisible to every sweep this archive has run.

**The 1825 volume, read from the image, is two acts and both are the kind of record nothing else here would hold.** One is a colono of Arienzo who died at **a masseria in the Nola district** and was declared there by two of his own brothers. The other is a woman of fifty-five who died **«nel Real Stabilimento delle Donne Matte»**, the royal asylum for insane women at Aversa, with her profession, her domicile and **both her parents left blank on the page** — a person whose family the institution did not know.

**AND THE FIRST ACT PAYS FOR THE DISCOVERY TWICE.** «*CRESCENZO CRISCI, di anni cinquantatré, marito di ANGELA QUOTOLO … figlio di ALESSANDRO CRISCI DEFUNTO e di CARMINA SORRINO … ha lasciato superstiti quattro figli, cioè ANIELLO d'anni QUINDICI, SANTE d'anni DODICI, CARMINA d'anni DIECI e MARIA ROSA d'anni CINQUE*». This archive held that couple as **two names in a marriage index** — the parents of the Aniello Crisci who married **Giovanna Falco** in 1829. They now have a dated act, a generation above them, and **Aniello has a birth year: about 1810, so nineteen at his wedding.**

what: The objection to Alessandra Crisci's parentage is removed — and the identification is still not made
was: **ALESSANDRA CRISCI** married **MATTEO FALCO** on 24 January 1834, and the marriage index gives her parents as «*CRISCI [forename lost to the fold shadow], **[QUO]TOLO ANGELA***». This archive noticed that **Aniello Crisci**, who married Matteo's sister Giovanna five years earlier, was son of «*Crisci Crescenzo, e Quotolo Angela*» — brother and sister marrying brother and sister, which is exactly what these households did — and filed it as **«a resemblance and not a fact»**, because the forename cannot be read and Angela Quotolo is not a rare name at Arienzo.
now:
**Crescenzo Crisci's own death act has turned up, and it lists his children.** Four of them: **Aniello 15, Sante 12, Carmina 10, Maria Rosa 5**, in November 1825. **Alessandra is not among them** — which looks at first like the end of the idea.

**It is not, and the act's own arithmetic says why. He was FIFTY-THREE.** A man of fifty-three whose eldest living child is fifteen either married at thirty-eight or **has older children who are not on this list**. These acts record the children who need a tutor — the **minors** — and all four are under sixteen. **An adult daughter would not appear.** Alessandra, marrying in 1834, need only have been born before 1810.
how: The Arienzo «Diversi» register of 1825, read from the image, and then read for what its numbers imply rather than only for its names.
why:
**A resemblance with a hole in it is now a resemblance without one, and that is all it is.** The forename in the 1834 index is still unread, and this archive does not promote a resemblance to a fact by removing an objection to it. **What has changed is that the next reader should stop treating the four children as a reason to drop the idea.**

The general rule is worth more than the case: **«ha lasciato superstiti N figli» is a list of minors, not a list of children**, and this archive should not read any such list as a complete family.

what: SARA RUGGIERO stops being only a godmother — a wedding of 1793, her father, a death window, and two children
was: **She stands as *matrina* on ten pages of the parish baptism harvest, at the fonts of at least six Falco households, and she is generation three's mother-in-law** — Andreana Crisci's mother, one step off the spine of this line. **Nothing else about her was established.** No birth, no death, no parents, no marriage act. The archive held one age for her, forty-five, from an 1817 birth act, and the sentence «*a woman who appears at six households' fonts is the connective tissue of the whole street, and she is a name and nothing more*».
now:
**Four things at once.**

**THE WEDDING.** «*Anno D[omi]ni Millesimo Septingentesimo nonagesimo tertio **1793**, die vero **vigesima sexta 26 Martii** … R. D. **Joseph Crisci Coadjutor** in matrimonio conjunxit nondum uxoratos **ARCHANGELUM CRISCI FILIUM NICOLAI**, et **SARAM RUGGIERO FILIAM PASCHALIS**, utrosque hujus Archipresbyteralis [Ecclesiae] **S. Andreae***».

**HER FATHER — PASQUALE RUGGIERO** — and the groom's father, **NICOLA CRISCI**: two grandparents of Andreana Crisci that this archive did not have.

**A DEATH WINDOW OF THREE YEARS.** She bore a son in 1817 at forty-five; by **1 June 1820** she is «*quondam*». **Dead between 1817 and June 1820.**

**TWO MORE CHILDREN.** **ANGELA ROSA CRISCI**, married 1 June 1820 to Angelo Clemente Frasca of the parish of Sant'Agnese; **LORENZO CRISCI**, married 25 March 1846 to Maria Angelica Ruotolo, whose mother is a **CARFORA**.
how: Work-list row 45, through FamilySearch's full-text of the Arienzo parish marriage register. The search that found it was the **quoted phrase** «Sara Ruggiero» — 36 hits in the death collection and 38 in the marriage one, where the unquoted surname returns fourteen hundred and three thousand. **Adding words to `q.text` makes the result set GROW, not shrink**: it weights, it does not AND. Only the quotes narrow.
why:
**The dating is what makes it hold together.** She married in March 1793 at about twenty-one and Andreana was baptised in November 1796 — three and a half years, with the wedding on the right side. Nothing had to be assumed to fit.

**AND THE IDENTIFICATION RESTS ON THE COUPLE, NOT THE FORENAME.** This archive holds a **second Arcangelo Crisci**, the one who married Anna Falco, and has already been careful to keep them apart. It is the pairing with Sara Ruggiero — in the 1793 act, and again in both children's acts as «*filiam/filium Archangeli, e quondam Sara Ruggiero*» — that separates them. A forename would not have.

**These are machine transcriptions of a parish hand and the images are not read.** The 1793 act is stronger than most because **the same leaf attests it twice**, once in the year's index line and once in the act. It is still a candidate until the image is rendered.

**One by-product for a different question.** Both 1820 acts marry a bride the writer calls «*meam Parochianam*» to a groom «*ex Parrocchia **Sanctae Agnetis***», two days apart — the first evidence about **Sant'Agnese** that does not come from a film label. And both cite «*Episcopalis Curiae **Sanctae Agathae Gothorum***»: **Arienzo answered to the diocese of Sant'Agata de' Goti**, which is where to write for what the parish does not hold.

what: Maddalena Falco's baptism — and the reason two passes could not find it
was: **«Maddalena Falco's baptism — two passes spent, still unread.»** The work-list row named the ark `3Q9M-CSD3-1381-R` and the date 7 June 1818, and recorded that **two rendering passes went hunting the margin label and neither reached the entry**.
now:
**They reached the margin label because the margin label is all that is on that leaf.** «*[Anno] D[omi]ni 1818, die vero **septima 7 Junii**, R. D. **BLASIUS MANSIONARIUS ARRICALE** Substitutus baptizavit infantem **natam** ex **JOSEPHO FALCO et ANTONIA DI GUIDA** conjugibus hujus Parochiae, **cui dedit nomen MAGDALENA. Matrina fuit DOROTHEA D'ADDIO.** HYACINTHUS Archip. MORGILLO*» — and it is on **`3Q9M-CSD3-13LG-7`**, a different leaf altogether.

**In this parish register the year's index and the year's acts are bound apart.** A search that lands on the index will never reach the act, however many tiles it renders.
how: FamilySearch full text, quoted phrase «Maddalena Falco» — two hits in the whole baptism collection: the label, and the act.
why:
**The godmother is the point.** **DOROTEA D'ADDIO** also stood at **Gioacchino Falco's** font in **1779**. One woman at this family's baptisms across forty years, and a second name to put beside Sara Ruggiero as the connective tissue of the street.

**And it is a lesson about where to look, not about how hard to look.** Two passes of tile-by-tile rendering were spent on a leaf that could not contain the answer. **Before rendering, ask the full text which leaf the words are on.**

what: A surname search of the parish baptisms cannot produce a negative — the machine renders FALCO as FALO and FALIO on a third of the pages
was: This archive has used FamilySearch's full text of the Arienzo parish registers as a **finding aid and as a test of absence**, and work-list row 42 proposed exactly that: «*Test the parish baptisms first*» for **ROSARIA FALCO**, whose birth act is in none of the four civil years she could have been born in.
now:
**The test was run and it is inconclusive, and the collection's own numbers say why.** Same collection, same place filter, one word changed:

| spelling | pages |
|---|---|
| `Falco` | **361** |
| `Falo` | **126** |
| `Falio` | **92** |
| `Zalco` | 7 |
| `Salco` | 6 |
| `Talco` | 3 |

**Two hundred and eighteen pages carry the name in a form that a search for «Falco» never sees — about a third of the corpus.** And the machine is not even consistent within one leaf: an index page renders the same entry as «*Joseph **Zalco** fol: 185*» and «*Joseph **Falco** fol: 185*» a few words apart.

The exact Latin form fares worse still: «*ex Josepho Falco*» returns **two pages in the entire collection**, for a household with at least eight children.
how: Work-list row 42. Counting the mis-renderings instead of trusting the nil.
why:
**A negative is a statement about the instrument**, and this archive has now said that twice in two days — once about a civil register that lost eleven days, and now about a machine that cannot read the family's own name on a third of the pages it has transcribed.

**The practical rule: in this collection, search the FORENAME and the MOTHER, not the surname**, and treat any surname nil as «not found by this method», never as «not there». **ROSARIA FALCO is still not found, and Santa Maria a Vico is still untried.**

what: The ark table published here yesterday was not the Diversi series — and the fix took five requests, not sixty-eight probes
was: Yesterday this archive found the Arienzo «**Diversi**» register — the volume for people who died away from home — and published a table of «*Confirmed arks so far, by asking `tools/antenati.py ids` for the breadcrumb year*»: **`an_ua14056` 1835, `14057` 1837, `14058` 1839, `14059` 1840, `14060` 1846, `14061` 1848, `14062` 1849**, beside three arks from a different burst. It warned, correctly, that «*the arithmetic is not linear and must not be guessed*».
now:
**Those seven arks are not Diversi volumes at all.** The real series is **`an_ua14064` to `an_ua14106`, plus `an_ua57637`–`57638`** — **45 volumes, 1812 to 1865**, every one now mapped to its year.

**The warning was right and I broke it anyway.** Probing an ark returns a breadcrumb — «*Arienzo > 1839*» — and **a breadcrumb gives the town and the year and says nothing about the series**. Seven arks answered with a year, and I wrote them down as Diversi because they sat next to one that was.
how: Reading the holdings list instead of probing. `/search-registry/?localita=Arienzo&tipologia=Diversi` renders each volume as `<li class="search-item" data-id="NNNNN">` with «*Registro: YYYY*» beside it — ten to a page, `&s_page=N` to continue. **Five requests for all forty-five**, against fifty minutes of probing that returned nothing but 403s the day before.
why:
**It is the fourth time in two weeks that this archive has been caught identifying a volume by something other than the volume.** Ark arithmetic was wrong once, the catalogue label once, the printed year on the form once — and now a breadcrumb. **The standing rule already covers it: only the manuscript identifies a register.** What is new is that the holdings list identifies the SERIES, which the breadcrumb never did, and it was available the whole time.

**A second thing was published void and is withdrawn here too.** The 1855 volume was swept on the band carrying the act heading, «*Atto di morte fuori domicilio di …*», and reported as empty. **From 1856 this clerk leaves that printed heading blank and writes only the body** — so the heading sweep returns «no acts» for a volume that has five, and the 1855 nil cannot stand. **It must be swept again across both halves before anything is said about it.**

what: The UK National Archives had never been searched — it is now, and it is closed
was:
**This archive had never looked at the National Archives of the United Kingdom.** Not once: `discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk` appears nowhere in the repository, and the twenty-five sources on the *Sources* page do not include it. Every «National Archives» in this archive is the National Archives of **Australia**.

The only reasoning ever recorded about Britain was to rule out **FreeBMD**: «*FREEBMD indexes the civil registration of ENGLAND AND WALES from 1837. This family has no English generation.*»
now:
**That reasoning was sound and it was too narrow.** Discovery is not English civil registration — it is a catalogue over Kew's own holdings **and some 2,500 other British archives**: aliens' registration, naturalisation, merchant seamen, service records, military police files. None of that was covered by ruling out births, marriages and deaths.

**Searched, and the result is a nil with a denominator.** **Zampiello 0 · Annecchino 0 · Arricale 0 · Carfora 0 · Morgillo 0 · Rivetti 0 · Crisci 1 · Forchia 0 · Arpaia 0.** **FALCO returns 86 and not one can be this family** — eighteen British Army service records, twenty-one merchant seamen registered at UK ports, twelve Home Office files (mostly naturalisations of Italians living in Britain, the nearest being a Luigi Falco born at **Saviano** in 1894), a dissolved company, a lawsuit of 1515, a Lake Como steamer. **«Falco Arienzo» returns 0. «Falco Caserta» returns 0.**

**So the old conclusion holds, and now it is measured rather than assumed.**
how: Prompted from outside, with the API endpoint. **The endpoint as given does not work.** `GET /API/search/records?sps.searchQuery=…` from a plain client returns **«202 Accepted» with an empty body** and the header **`x-amzn-waf-action: challenge`** — an AWS WAF challenge, not a 200 with JSON. It answers a real browser. That is recorded on the *Sources* page so the next person does not spend an hour on a dead curl.
why:
**A source nobody had thought to name is worse than a source that failed**, because nothing records the omission. This one is now on the register with its counts, and it will not be searched again.

**AND IT IS NOT QUITE EMPTY.** One file names the town: **WO 32/22147**, «*Special Investigation Branch investigation: alleged murder of **Herron FG, Private, 1583838, Argyle and Sutherland Highlanders**, **by two Italian civilians at ARIENZO, Italy, 11 March 1945***». Open since 2017, held at Kew, **not digitised**.

**No Falco is named in it and none is assumed.** It is worth ordering because **this archive holds almost nothing from Arienzo in the 1940s** — the civil registers stop in 1865 and the Australian records begin in 1964 — and a military police file names its accused and its witnesses, and its witnesses are townspeople. **A lead about the town, filed as that and not as a family record.**

what: «Arienzo» in the holdings list is a DISTRICT, not a town — a third of the volumes belong to other comuni
was: Yesterday and this morning this archive located the **«Diversi»** series — the register of people who died away from home — and published it as **«45 volumes, 1812 to 1865»** for **Arienzo**, mapped ark by year from `/search-registry/?localita=Arienzo&tipologia=Diversi`. The whole set was treated as this family's town.
now:
**They are not all this family's town.** More than one comune in this district carries «Arienzo» in its name, and the locality filter matches all of them. Read from the volumes' own title pages and act texts:

- `an_ua14064`, `14069`, `14071` — «*Comune di **CORPO D'ARIENZO***». **This family's town.**
- `an_ua57637`, `an_ua57638` (both 1813) — «*Comune di **SAN FELICE D'ARIENZO***».
- `an_ua14068` (1824) — «*ed ufiziale dello Stato Civile del Comune di **SAN CASALE DI ARIENZO***».

**The printed heading of every one of these title pages says «CIRCONDARIO DI ARIENZO», and that is the DISTRICT.** The comune is the line beneath it, filled by hand.
how: Reading each volume's own title page instead of trusting the query that returned it — which is this archive's oldest standing rule and the fourth time in three days it has had to be re-learned.
why:
**It would have produced a false Falco.** This archive holds a documented **Falco household at SAN FELICE A CANCELLO** — soap-makers, 1815 — and has deliberately refused to claim them as kin. A Falco found in `an_ua57637` and attributed to Arienzo would have merged two families that this archive has spent months keeping apart.

**And it changes the size of the job honestly.** «Forty-five volumes of Arienzo Diversi» was never true; some unknown fraction belongs to neighbouring comuni, and **each volume's comune has to be read before anything in it is attributed.** That is slower and it is the only safe way.

**Nothing found so far is affected** — the Crisci of 1812, the d'Addio of 1850 and the Crisci of 1825 are all from Corpo d'Arienzo volumes, checked.

what: The register of people who died away from home is read out — 45 volumes, and no Falco in any of them
was: Three days ago this archive found the Arienzo «**Diversi**» register and wrote that it was **the third explanation** for a death the town never recorded — beside «the register has a hole» and «after 1865, where Antenati stops». **ANTONIA DI GUIDA** is alive on 2 February 1845 and in no volume since; **GIUSEPPE FALCO of Antonia di Guida** on 26 November 1849 and in none since. A man who dies at a masseria in the next district is invisible to every sweep this archive has run.
now:
**All forty-five volumes are read, 1812 to 1865, and the answer is no.** Every act from **1845 to 1865** has been read and its dead named — the whole window both people could fall in — and **there is no FALCO and no DI GUIDA among them**. Four acts in the entire series are still unnamed, and all four are **before 1845**, so none can be either of them.

**The third explanation is spent. What remains for rows 39 and 40 is 1866 or later.**
how: Work-list row 70, over three days: the holdings list read instead of arks probed, each volume's **comune** checked from its own title page, and each volume swept on the body band across both halves rather than the act heading — which from 1856 the clerk leaves blank.
why:
**A negative is only worth having when you can say what it cost to get it**, and this one maps a world. About **thirty-five deaths away from home** for Corpo d'Arienzo, and they show where an Arienzo labourer went and did not come back from: the **Ospedale degli Incurabili** at Naples, **Sant'Agostino degli Scalzi** and the **Real Stabilimento de' Matti** at Aversa, **Acerra**, **Caserta**, **Airola**, a masseria in the **Nola** district — and, once, **LIPARI**.

**PASQUALE PORRINO**, fifty-two, married, a labourer born at Arienzo, died on **31 October 1864 in the hospital of the DOMICILIATI COATTI on Lipari** — internal exile, three years after Unification — and the act came home to the sindaco Raffaele Rivetti.

**CARLO BALLETTA**, soldier of the **1st Dragoons**, died in the **Ospedale della Trinità** on 3 March 1855. His colonel wrote to the sindaco asking him to **tell the soldier's relatives to send someone they trusted** to collect **one ducat and thirty-five grana** — what his kit had fetched when it was sold.

**ANGELO IMBIMBO**, sixty, died in the **Aversa madhouse** on 30 November 1855. The 1845 volume holds **FRANCESCO IMBIMBO, «figlio d'ANGELO»**, dead in the **same asylum** on 4 November 1844. **Father and son, eleven years apart, in the same institution.**

**None of them is a Falco, and that is the finding.** This family stayed, and died, at home.

what: Four different totals for the processetti, all correct, none labelled — and the file that explained them was read by nothing
was: This archive has quoted the size of the *processetti* holding **four different ways**: «**378** volumes across six towns» in the work list, «**321** volumes» in the page's eyebrow and again in its opening card, «**320** volumes» in the same page's closing section, and «**258** volumes across four towns, of which **none have been read**» on the *Searched* page.
now:
**Every one of them was arithmetically right, and every one counted a different set of towns:**

| number | what it counts |
|---|---|
| **378** | all six towns |
| **321** | the five of the **VALLE CAUDINA** — San Felice a Cancello excluded |
| **258** | the four in **BENEVENTO** — Arienzo excluded as well |
| **320** | 321 less the one bundle that has been read |

**Not one of them said which set it meant.** The only place the breakdown existed was `site/src/data/processetti.json` — and **no build script and no page read that file.** The page carried its numbers as typed literals.
how: Auditing the archive for the Mazza fault — evidence keyed to something the build never reads. This file is keyed to a **town**, not a person, so nobody was being told they were undocumented; it was a number rotting instead of a person.
why:
**A number nobody can trace is worse than a wrong one, because it survives being checked.** Each of these four could be defended in isolation, and together they made the holding look like it was shrinking. The page now **derives all four from the six rows** and states the scope every time — «*378 volumes across six towns*», «*320 of the 321 Valle Caudina volumes*» — and renders the table they come from, so the next reader can see which towns are in and which are out.

**One statement was not merely unlabelled but wrong.** *Searched* said the processetti were «*258 volumes across four towns, of which **none have been read***». **One bundle has been read** — Arienzo 1814, bundle 16, the richest document this archive holds — and Arienzo is not one of the four towns in the 258 anyway.

what: GAETANA LAUDATO died in APRIL, not March — and her mother was never unreadable
was: «*GAETANA LAUDATO figlia delli fu **GIACINTO LAUDATO e GIOVANNA —**, VEDOVA DI SIMONE MORGILLO, di anni SETTANTOTTO, contadina, domiciliata nella strada Trave*» — **death 9 MARCH 1816**. She is the oldest person this archive holds by birth, «*born about 1738, the deepest this archive reaches*», so her act is load-bearing for the whole Morgillo pedigree.
now:
